segments.voiceover: Welcome to today's board review on white cell malignancies, covering acute myeloid and lymphoblastic leukemia, myelodysplastic syndrome, and myeloproliferative neoplasms, presented by the National Taiwan University Hospital hematology-oncology division.

Here's our roadmap: AML, MDS, MPN, the overlap syndrome MDS-MPN, and ALL, with a heavy emphasis on AML since it dominates board questions, plus a quick preview of newly approved agents worth recognizing, including quizartinib and gemtuzumab ozogamicin for AML, asciminib for CML, momelotinib for myelofibrosis, and blinatumomab and ponatinib for B-ALL.

This slide organizes the major mutation classes driving AML pathogenesis into four functional groups worth memorizing for boards. First, proliferation and survival signaling: the RAS pathway with NRAS, KRAS, CBL, NF1, and PTPN11, alongside receptor tyrosine kinase mutations like JAK2, MPL, FLT3, and KIT. Second, epigenetic modifiers: DNA methylation genes DNMT3A, TET2, and IDH1 and IDH2, plus chromatin modifiers like ASXL1, EZH2, and KMT2A partial tandem duplications. Third, genes that block differentiation, including transcription regulators CEBPA and RUNX1, and the spliceosome machinery SF3B1, SRSF2, and U2AF1. Finally, cohesin complex genes like STAG2 and CTCF, and a catch-all bucket including TP53, NPM1, and WT1. The board-relevant takeaway is that AML arises from cooperating hits across these categories, typically a proliferation driver plus a differentiation block, and knowing which gene belongs to which functional class helps you predict prognosis and targeted therapy eligibility.

keypoints: RAS/RTK -> proliferation: FLT3, JAK2, KIT
DNMT3A/TET2/IDH1/2 -> epigenetic
CEBPA/RUNX1/spliceosome -> blocks differentiation
TP53, NPM1, WT1 -> other high-yield genes
segments.voiceover: Group these by function: proliferation drivers like FLT3 and JAK2, epigenetic regulators like DNMT3A and IDH1/2, differentiation blockers like CEBPA, RUNX1, and the spliceosome genes, and don't forget TP53 and NPM1, both critical for ELN risk stratification.

This is the European LeukemiaNet 2022 risk classification, flagged here as a must-know for boards. Favorable risk includes core-binding factor leukemias, the t 8;21 translocation with RUNX1-RUNX1T1 fusion and inversion 16 with CBFB-MYH11 fusion, plus NPM1 mutation without FLT3-ITD, and in-frame bZIP CEBPA mutations. Intermediate risk covers the t 9;11 translocation with MLLT3-KMT2A fusion, and critically, NPM1 mutated with FLT3-ITD, or wild-type NPM1 with FLT3-ITD, since FLT3-ITD allelic burden shifts favorable NPM1 mutants into intermediate risk. Adverse risk is the largest and most tested category: KMT2A rearrangements other than t 9;11, the t 9;22 translocation meaning BCR-ABL1, inversion 3 or t 3;3 involving GATA2 and MECOM, monosomy 5 or del 5q, monosomy 7, abnormal 17p, complex karyotype, and mutated TP53, which carries the worst prognosis regardless of other findings. The single highest-yield pearl here: NPM1 mutation is only favorable when FLT3-ITD is absent; add FLT3-ITD and it drops straight to intermediate.

keypoints: Favorable: t(8;21), inv(16), NPM1mut w/o FLT3-ITD, CEBPA bZIP
Intermediate: NPM1mut + FLT3-ITD, t(9;11)
Adverse: TP53mut, complex karyotype, -5/-7, t(9;22)
NPM1 + FLT3-ITD flips favorable -> intermediate
segments.voiceover: Remember, NPM1 without FLT3-ITD is favorable, but adding FLT3-ITD makes it intermediate. TP53 mutation and complex karyotype are always adverse, no exceptions.

This slide lists the International Consensus Classification's genetically-defined AML subtypes, which still require a 20% blast threshold, unlike the 10% cutoff used for a subset marked in red on this slide. Acute promyelocytic leukemia with the t 15;17 translocation and PML-RARA fusion tops the list, since it's a hematologic emergency treated without conventional chemotherapy. Other core-binding factor and recurrent translocations follow: t 8;21 with RUNX1-RUNX1T1, inversion 16 with CBFB-MYH11, t 9;11 with MLLT3-KMT2A and other KMT2A rearrangements, t 6;9 with DEK-NUP214, inversion 3 with GATA2 and MECOM, and t 9;22 with BCR-ABL1, which requires distinguishing de novo AML from blast-phase CML. Mutation-defined entities include AML with mutated NPM1, in-frame bZIP CEBPA mutations, and AML with mutated TP53, which requires a single mutation with variant allele frequency over 10% and uses the lower 10% blast threshold. Know that APL and BCR-ABL1 positive AML are the two subtypes where you must actively exclude alternative diagnoses, promyelocytic variants or CML blast crisis, respectively.

keypoints: APL: t(15;17) PML-RARA -> hematologic emergency
t(8;21), inv(16): core-binding factor AML
t(9;22) BCR-ABL1: exclude CML blast phase
TP53mut AML: single mutation, VAF>10%, blast>=10%
segments.voiceover: APL is the must-recognize emergency here. TP53-mutated AML uses a lower 10% blast cutoff in ICC, while everything else still needs 20%.

Continuing the ICC scheme, this slide covers the myelodysplasia-related category, which uses the lower 10% blast threshold. AML with myelodysplasia-related gene mutations requires one of nine genes: ASXL1, BCOR, EZH2, RUNX1 highlighted in red, SF3B1, SRSF2, STAG2, U2AF1, or ZRSR2, essentially the spliceosome and chromatin genes typically seen in secondary or antecedent MDS. AML with myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic abnormalities includes complex karyotype with three or more clones, del 5q, monosomy 7 or del 7q, trisomy 8 highlighted in red, del 12p, isochromosome 17q, abnormal 17p, del 20q also highlighted in red, and isodicentric X. These overlapping categories matter because they signal biology closer to antecedent MDS, generally conferring worse prognosis and influencing transplant decisions. Finally, AML not otherwise specified is the residual category for cases lacking any defining lesion, and myeloid sarcoma is the extramedullary mass-forming presentation, which is diagnosed as AML regardless of marrow blast percentage.

keypoints: 9 genes: ASXL1, BCOR, EZH2, RUNX1, SF3B1, SRSF2, STAG2, U2AF1, ZRSR2
Cytogenetics: complex karyotype, del(5q), -7, +8, del(20q)
Myeloid sarcoma = AML regardless of marrow blast %
segments.voiceover: Myelodysplasia-related gene mutations and cytogenetics both signal secondary-type biology and worse outcomes. Myeloid sarcoma is always AML, no blast percentage required.

This flowchart shows how the International Consensus Classification assigns diagnosis hierarchically once you have at least 10% myeloid blasts or blast equivalents. You work left to right through decreasing priority: first check for AML-defining recurrent genetic abnormalities, if absent, check for TP53 mutation with VAF at least 10%, if absent, check for the nine myelodysplasia-related gene mutations, if absent, check for myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic abnormalities, and if all are negative, the diagnosis is AML not otherwise specified. At each of these last four branch points, the blast percentage then determines the final label: 10 to 19% blasts gives an MDS/AML diagnosis, while 20% or more gives the corresponding AML diagnosis. Only the first branch, AML-defining recurrent genetic abnormalities, bypasses this split and is called AML directly regardless of blast count. Finally, three diagnostic qualifiers can be appended to any of these diagnoses: therapy-related, arising after prior MDS or MDS/MPN, or associated with a germline predisposition syndrome. This hierarchy is exam-favorite material because it tests whether you understand that TP53 mutation status is checked before myelodysplasia-related mutations, meaning TP53 always takes priority.

keypoints: Order: AML-defining lesion -> TP53mut -> MDS-related mutation -> MDS-related cytogenetics -> NOS
10-19% blasts = MDS/AML; >=20% = AML
TP53 checked before myelodysplasia-related genes
Qualifiers: therapy-related, prior MDS, germline predisposition
segments.voiceover: Memorize the priority order: genetic-defining lesion first, then TP53, then myelodysplasia-related mutations, then cytogenetics, then NOS. Remember TP53 outranks the myelodysplasia-related gene panel.

This is the same ICC hierarchy, now annotated with the key differences from the WHO classification, a favorite source of trick questions. First, WHO eliminated the blast cutoff entirely for AML with defining genetic alterations, meaning even blasts below 10% can qualify, whereas ICC still requires at least 10% blasts for that category. Second, WHO does not use TP53 mutation as its own hierarchical branch point the way ICC does. Third, WHO's myelodysplasia-related gene mutation list does not include RUNX1, so that gene is ICC-specific for this category. Fourth, for myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic abnormalities, WHO does not list trisomy 8 or del 20q, while ICC does not include del 11q, monosomy 13, or del 13q, so the two systems' cytogenetic lists are not interchangeable. Finally, WHO frames its terminal category around AML defined by differentiation rather than ICC's not-otherwise-specified label. On boards, expect questions that hinge on exactly these discrepancies, so know which classification system the question is asking about before you answer.

keypoints: WHO: no blast cutoff for genetically-defined AML
WHO doesn't branch on TP53; ICC does
RUNX1 in ICC's MDS-gene list, not WHO's
Cytogenetics differ: WHO omits +8/del(20q); ICC omits del(11q)/-13/del(13q)
segments.voiceover: The exam trap is mixing up WHO and ICC criteria. WHO drops the blast cutoff for genetic AML and doesn't use TP53 as a branch point; ICC does both, and their myelodysplasia-related gene and cytogenetic lists differ slightly too.

This slide lays out the fifth edition of the WHO classification of AML, and it's worth knowing cold for boards. The big conceptual shift is on the left column: AML with defining genetic abnormalities. For most of these entities, you no longer need to hit the twenty percent blast threshold, the genetics alone are diagnostic. The classic ones are still here, APL with PML-RARA, core binding factor AML with RUNX1-RUNX1T1 or CBFB-MYH11, and AML with NPM1 mutation. But note the exceptions marked with an asterisk, BCR-ABL1 fusion, CEBPA mutation, and myelodysplasia-related AML still require that twenty percent blast cutoff, because those categories overlap biologically with other diseases like CML or MDS. On the right side is the older, morphology-based approach, AML defined by differentiation, which still requires blasts of twenty percent or more, things like AML without maturation or acute monocytic leukemia. The takeaway for exams is simple, genetics trumps morphology whenever a defining mutation or fusion is present.

keypoints: Genetic-defined AML usually skips the twenty percent blast requirement
Exceptions needing twenty percent blasts, BCR-ABL1, CEBPA, MDS-related AML
Core binding factor and APL fusions remain classic defining lesions
Differentiation-based AML categories still need twenty percent blasts
New entities added, KMT2A, MECOM, and NUP98 rearrangements
segments.voiceover: Remember, genetic abnormalities generally bypass the blast percentage rule, except for BCR-ABL1, CEBPA mutated, and myelodysplasia-related AML, which still need twenty percent blasts. The right column, defined by differentiation, is the traditional morphologic classification and always requires twenty percent blasts.

This is a big-picture map of how we treat AML in twenty twenty-six, and the whole thing hinges on two questions, is the patient fit for intensive chemotherapy, and does the leukemia have a targetable mutation. Start with the fit patients on the top left. If they have a FLT3 mutation, you add midostaurin or quizartinib to seven plus three. Core binding factor AML often gets gemtuzumab ozogamicin added. Therapy-related or secondary AML does better with CPX-351, the liposomal daunorubicin-cytarabine combination, instead of standard seven plus three. After induction, consolidation is transplant, high-dose cytarabine, or oral azacitidine for maintenance. Now shift to unfit patients, bottom left, the backbone is venetoclax combined with a hypomethylating agent or low-dose cytarabine. If they carry an IDH1 mutation, ivosidenib gets added to that azacitidine backbone. On the right side is the salvage setting for relapsed or refractory disease. Fit patients typically get FLAG-Ida plus or minus venetoclax, while unfit patients get mutation-directed single agents, gilteritinib for FLT3, ivosidenib or enasidenib for IDH1 or IDH2, and revumenib for NPM1 or KMT2A rearranged disease. The gray boxes just flag agents not currently available in Taiwan.

keypoints: Fitness for intensive chemo and mutation status drive first-line choice
FLT3 mutated fit patients get midostaurin or quizartinib added to seven plus three
Unfit patients get venetoclax plus a hypomethylating agent or low-dose cytarabine
IDH1 mutated unfit patients can add ivosidenib to the backbone
Salvage therapy is increasingly mutation-directed, gilteritinib, ivosidenib, enasidenib, revumenib
segments.voiceover: Keep two axes in mind, fitness for intensive chemo, and presence of an actionable mutation like FLT3, IDH1, IDH2, or NPM1-KMT2A. Those two axes determine essentially every box on this chart, both in the first-line and salvage settings.

This slide is the same treatment landscape you just saw, but now filtered through Taiwan's National Health Insurance reimbursement rules, which is exactly the kind of local, practical detail that shows up on board exams here. Notice the light gray shading appearing in the salvage unfit column, gemtuzumab ozogamicin, venetoclax plus HMA, and gilteritinib are all marked as not reimbursed by NHI in that particular indication, even though they are clinically used and available. Venetoclax combined with FLAG-Ida in the fit salvage setting is shown grayed out too, meaning it's not reimbursed there either. Meanwhile agents like enasidenib and revumenib remain simply not available in Taiwan at all, shown in dark gray, a distinct category from not reimbursed. This distinction matters clinically, a drug can be approved and physically available but still require self-payment or a special application, which changes real-world treatment decisions even when the evidence supports using it.

keypoints: Same treatment map, now annotated with Taiwan NHI reimbursement status
Light gray equals available but not reimbursed by NHI
Dark gray equals not available in Taiwan at all
Salvage unfit agents like gilteritinib and venetoclax plus HMA are not reimbursed
Reimbursement status can limit real-world use despite drug availability
segments.voiceover: Two shades of gray carry different meanings here, light gray means the drug is available in Taiwan but the National Health Insurance won't pay for it in that setting, dark gray means the drug isn't available in Taiwan at all. Recognizing that distinction is a good local-context board question.

Here's the pivotal trial that established venetoclax plus azacitidine as standard of care for older, unfit AML patients, the VIALE-A trial. Four hundred thirty-one patients with newly diagnosed AML who were unfit for intensive induction, median age seventy-six, were randomized two to one to either azacitidine plus venetoclax at four hundred milligrams, or azacitidine plus placebo. The survival curves separate early and stay separated, median overall survival was fourteen point seven months with the combination versus just nine point six months with azacitidine alone, a highly significant difference with a hazard ratio of zero point six six. Response rates tell the same story, complete remission was thirty-six point seven percent versus seventeen point nine percent, and if you include CR with incomplete count recovery, the combined response rate jumps to sixty-six point four percent versus twenty-eight point three percent. This trial is why venetoclax-azacitidine is now the default backbone for unfit AML patients everywhere, and it's a very testable trial, know the name VIALE-A, the population, and those survival numbers.

keypoints: VIALE-A, four hundred thirty-one unfit AML patients, median age seventy-six
Azacitidine plus venetoclax versus azacitidine plus placebo, two to one randomization
Median overall survival, fourteen point seven months versus nine point six months
Complete remission rate, thirty-six point seven percent versus seventeen point nine percent
Hazard ratio zero point six six, p less than zero point zero zero one
segments.voiceover: Memorize VIALE-A as azacitidine plus venetoclax in unfit AML, with a median overall survival benefit of about five months, fourteen point seven versus nine point six, and roughly double the complete remission rate compared to azacitidine alone.

This is the sister trial to VIALE-A, called VIALE-C, and it tests venetoclax paired with low-dose cytarabine instead of azacitidine, again in unfit, newly diagnosed AML patients. Two hundred eleven patients, median age seventy-six, randomized two to one to venetoclax six hundred milligrams plus LDAC, or placebo plus LDAC. Look carefully at the two Kaplan-Meier panels, they show the same trial at two different analysis timepoints. At the primary endpoint analysis, the hazard ratio was zero point seven five but did not reach statistical significance, p equals zero point one one. However, with six more months of follow-up, the benefit became significant, hazard ratio zero point seven zero, p equals zero point zero four. Response rate was clearly better with venetoclax, forty-eight percent versus thirteen percent, and transfusion independence improved too, thirty-seven percent versus sixteen percent. The key teaching point here is that venetoclax plus LDAC is a reasonable option but generally considered less preferred than venetoclax plus azacitidine, partly because the survival benefit was borderline at the primary analysis and only became significant later.

keypoints: VIALE-C, venetoclax plus low-dose cytarabine in unfit AML, two hundred eleven patients
Primary endpoint hazard ratio zero point seven five, not significant, p equals zero point one one
With extended follow-up, hazard ratio zero point seven zero, p equals zero point zero four
Response rate forty-eight percent versus thirteen percent favoring venetoclax
Considered a less robust option than venetoclax plus azacitidine from VIALE-A
segments.voiceover: VIALE-C pairs venetoclax with low-dose cytarabine rather than azacitidine. The survival benefit only became statistically significant after extended follow-up, which is why most clinicians favor the azacitidine combination from VIALE-A as first choice.

This slide is flagged as a must-know exam topic, so pay close attention. FLT3 inhibitors are classified along two independent axes, generation and type. By generation, sorafenib and midostaurin are first generation TKIs, while quizartinib, gilteritinib, and crenolanib are second generation, generally more potent and more selective. The kinome tree diagrams up top visually show target selectivity, notice how gilteritinib and crenolanib have that distinct blue dot marking a unique kinase target, AXL, which contributes to their activity profile. The second axis is functional type. Type one inhibitors are active against both ITD and TKD, or tyrosine kinase domain, mutations, because they bind the active conformation of the kinase, midostaurin is the first-generation example, gilteritinib and crenolanib are second-generation examples. Type two inhibitors only work against ITD mutations, not TKD, because they bind the inactive kinase conformation, sorafenib is first generation, and quizartinib, bolded here for emphasis, is the key second-generation type two inhibitor. This type one versus type two distinction, and which drugs work against TKD mutations, is exactly the kind of detail that shows up on written boards.

keypoints: FLT3 inhibitors classified by generation, first gen versus second gen
First generation, sorafenib and midostaurin, second generation, quizartinib, gilteritinib, crenolanib
Type I inhibitors hit both ITD and TKD mutations, active conformation binding
Type II inhibitors hit only ITD mutations, inactive conformation binding
Sorafenib is the first-generation type II inhibitor, quizartinib is the key second-generation one
segments.voiceover: Two axes to memorize, generation and type. Type one drugs like midostaurin and gilteritinib cover both ITD and TKD mutations. Type two drugs like sorafenib and quizartinib only cover ITD mutations, that gap is a classic board question.

This is the ADMIRAL trial, the pivotal phase three study that got gilteritinib approved for relapsed or refractory FLT3-mutated AML, and it's a very commonly tested trial. Patients with R/R FLT3-mutated AML were randomized to gilteritinib at one hundred twenty milligrams daily, two hundred forty-seven patients, versus investigator's choice salvage chemotherapy, one hundred twenty-four patients. The Kaplan-Meier curve shows clear separation favoring gilteritinib throughout follow-up. Median overall survival was nine point three months with gilteritinib compared to five point six months with salvage chemotherapy, a hazard ratio of zero point six three seven, highly significant at p equals zero point zero zero zero seven. Twelve-month overall survival rates reinforce this, thirty-seven percent alive at one year with gilteritinib versus only seventeen percent with chemotherapy. This is the trial that established single-agent FLT3 inhibition as superior to conventional salvage chemotherapy in relapsed FLT3-mutated AML, and it's why gilteritinib became the standard salvage option for this population.

keypoints: ADMIRAL trial, gilteritinib versus salvage chemo in R/R FLT3-mutated AML
Two hundred forty-seven on gilteritinib, one hundred twenty-four on chemo
Median OS, nine point three months versus five point six months
Hazard ratio zero point six three seven, p equals zero point zero zero zero seven
Twelve-month survival, thirty-seven percent versus seventeen percent
segments.voiceover: ADMIRAL established gilteritinib as superior to salvage chemotherapy in relapsed FLT3-mutated AML, with median overall survival of nine point three months versus five point six months, and roughly double the one-year survival rate.

This slide dives into why FLT3 inhibitors eventually stop working, resistance mechanisms, which is a favorite advanced topic for hematology fellows. The top half is a literature summary organized by drug. For midostaurin, N676K is a described resistance mutation. Crenolanib resistance involves F691L and an extracellular domain mutation K429E. Gilteritinib resistance is driven by F691L. On the right, other FLT3 inhibitors like quizartinib, sorafenib, sunitinib, and pexidartinib show overlapping resistance mutations at F691L and the D835 codon, D835 mutations recur again and again across different inhibitors, making it a hot spot for acquired resistance. The bottom panel is an oncoprint from real patient samples collected after gilteritinib progression. Look at the FLT3-ITD row in blue, five of forty-one patients, about twelve percent, actually lost their FLT3-ITD clone entirely at relapse, meaning a different, ITD-negative clone took over. The red boxes show newly acquired mutations, RAS-MAPK pathway mutations, NRAS, KRAS, BRAF, CBL, PTPN11, were the most common escape route, found in about thirty-seven percent of patients, more common than the FLT3 F691L gatekeeper mutation itself, which appeared in only about twelve percent. Overall, new mutations of any kind emerged in fifty-six percent of patients at progression, underscoring that resistance to FLT3 inhibitors is often driven by bypass pathway activation rather than the FLT3 gene itself.

keypoints: F691L is the most common shared FLT3 gatekeeper resistance mutation across inhibitors
D835 kinase domain mutations recur across quizartinib, sorafenib, sunitinib, pexidartinib
Twelve percent of patients lose the FLT3-ITD clone entirely at gilteritinib progression
RAS-MAPK pathway mutations, about thirty-seven percent, are the leading resistance route
New mutations emerge in fifty-six percent of patients at time of gilteritinib progression
segments.voiceover: F691L and D835 are the classic on-target gatekeeper mutations to know, but the bigger picture is that RAS-MAPK pathway mutations, not FLT3 itself, are the most frequent driver of resistance, found in over a third of patients progressing on gilteritinib.

This is the QuANTUM-First trial design, and it's the reason quizartinib now has a frontline indication. Enrolled patients had newly diagnosed FLT3-ITD positive AML, with at least 3 percent ITD allelic frequency, ages 18 to 75, total of 539 patients. They were stratified by region, age above or below 60, and baseline white count above or below 40, then randomized 1 to 1 on day 7 of cycle 1, plus or minus 3 days. Both arms got standard 7 plus 3 induction, cytarabine days 1 through 7 with daunorubicin or idarubicin days 1 through 3, for up to 2 cycles. Starting day 8, one arm added quizartinib and the other placebo. Consolidation was up to 4 cycles of high dose cytarabine with quizartinib or placebo, and allo transplant was allowed per institutional policy. Responders then moved into a continuation phase, single agent quizartinib or placebo once daily, for up to 36 cycles, essentially maintenance therapy.

keypoints: FLT3-ITD positive AML, N equals 539, randomized 1 to 1
Induction and consolidation add quizartinib or placebo to standard chemo
Continuation phase gives single agent quizartinib or placebo up to 36 cycles
Allo-HSCT permitted during consolidation per institutional policy
segments.voiceover: Key points here. This is FLT3-ITD positive AML, 539 patients randomized 1 to 1. Quizartinib or placebo is layered onto standard induction and consolidation chemotherapy. And critically, responders go on to a long continuation phase of single agent quizartinib or placebo for up to 36 cycles, which functions as maintenance. Allo transplant was allowed during consolidation per local practice.

This is the primary endpoint of QuANTUM-First, overall survival in the intention to treat population. The quizartinib arm, 268 patients, had a median overall survival of 31.9 months, versus 15.1 months with placebo plus standard chemotherapy in 271 patients. That's a 16.8 month improvement in median OS. The hazard ratio was 0.78, 95 percent confidence interval 0.62 to 0.98, p equals 0.032, so a statistically significant and clinically meaningful 22 percent reduction in the risk of death. Looking at the Kaplan-Meier curves, they separate early and the quizartinib curve, in blue, stays consistently above the placebo curve in green throughout follow-up, which extended to a median of about 39 months in both arms. Event rates were 50 percent with quizartinib versus 58 percent with placebo. This is the survival benefit that underlies the FDA approval of quizartinib in newly diagnosed FLT3-ITD AML.

keypoints: Median OS 31.9 months with quizartinib vs 15.1 months with placebo
22 percent reduction in risk of death, 16.8 month OS improvement
Curves separate early and remain separated through long-term follow-up
segments.voiceover: The headline numbers to remember. Median overall survival roughly doubled, 31.9 months versus 15.1 months. Hazard ratio 0.78, statistically significant at p equals 0.032. That translates to a 22 percent reduction in the risk of death, and the survival curves stay separated well beyond 3 years of follow-up, supporting a durable benefit rather than just an early effect.

This slide covers the ALFA-0701 trial, which established frontline MYLOTARG, that's gemtuzumab ozogamicin, in combination with chemotherapy. Patients were randomized 1 to 1 to induction with daunorubicin 60 milligrams per meter squared on days 1 to 3, plus cytarabine 200 milligrams per meter squared days 1 to 7, with or without MYLOTARG dosed at 3 milligrams per meter squared on days 1, 4, and 7, that's the fractionated dosing schedule. If bone marrow blasts remained above 10 percent at day 15, patients got a second induction course, and notably, patients in the MYLOTARG arm did not receive MYLOTARG during that reinduction. Responders proceeded to two consolidation cycles, each with daunorubicin and high dose cytarabine, and the MYLOTARG arm received one additional low dose of MYLOTARG, 3 milligrams per meter squared, on day 1 of each consolidation cycle. The primary efficacy endpoint was event free survival, measured from randomization to induction failure, relapse, or death from any cause.

keypoints: ALFA-0701: DNR plus AraC induction, with or without fractionated MYLOTARG
MYLOTARG dosed 3 mg/m2 on days 1, 4, 7 of induction only, not reinduction
One low dose MYLOTARG added to each of two consolidation cycles
Primary endpoint was event-free survival
segments.voiceover: Remember ALFA-0701 as the fractionated gemtuzumab ozogamicin regimen, 3 milligrams per meter squared on days 1, 4, and 7 added to standard daunorubicin and cytarabine induction. That fractionation is what made MYLOTARG tolerable after the original single high dose formulation was pulled from the market. The drug is also added at a single low dose to each consolidation cycle, and the trial's primary endpoint, event free survival, is the outcome most often quoted for this regimen.

This slide breaks down the ALFA-0701 event free survival benefit by ELN 2017 cytogenetic risk group, and it's a really important nuance for boards. In the ELN favorable group, MYLOTARG plus chemotherapy clearly outperformed chemotherapy alone, with event free survival curves separating early and staying apart, p equals 0.04. In the ELN intermediate group, there's also a meaningful benefit, curves separating similarly, p equals 0.05, right at the edge of significance. But in the ELN adverse risk group, the two curves are essentially superimposed throughout follow-up, p equals 0.74, no benefit at all. So the take home is that gemtuzumab ozogamicin's benefit is concentrated in favorable and intermediate risk cytogenetics, and adverse risk AML, which is CD33 biology aside, tends to be more resistant disease overall, does not appear to benefit from adding this antibody drug conjugate.

keypoints: EFS benefit of MYLOTARG concentrated in ELN-favorable and intermediate risk
ELN-favorable: P equals 0.04, clear separation of curves
ELN-intermediate: P equals 0.05, borderline but favors combination
ELN-adverse: P equals 0.74, curves overlap, no benefit
segments.voiceover: The pattern to memorize. MYLOTARG helps in favorable and intermediate risk cytogenetics, with p values of 0.04 and 0.05 respectively, but provides no measurable event free survival benefit in adverse risk AML, where p equals 0.74 and the curves overlap completely. This risk-stratified benefit is a classic board question about who should actually receive gemtuzumab ozogamicin.

This slide addresses hepatotoxicity, specifically veno-occlusive disease, or VOD, which is the boxed warning for MYLOTARG. Pooling data across trials, several factors increase VOD risk. Higher monotherapy doses of MYLOTARG in adults raise risk. Baseline moderate or severe hepatic impairment before starting MYLOTARG raises risk substantially, patients with that impairment were 8.7 times more likely to develop VOD. Receiving MYLOTARG after a prior transplant increased risk 2.6 fold compared to patients without prior HSCT. And undergoing HSCT after MYLOTARG treatment increased risk 2.9 fold compared with patients who didn't go on to transplant. Because of that transplant-related risk in both directions, two studies offer practical guidance. ALFA-0701 recommended waiting at least 2 months between the last dose of MYLOTARG and proceeding to HSCT. And in MyloFrance-1, no patients who underwent HSCT did so within 3.5 months of MYLOTARG therapy, suggesting that's a safer practical interval.

keypoints: MYLOTARG carries a boxed warning for hepatotoxicity, including VOD
Baseline moderate/severe hepatic impairment raises VOD risk 8.7-fold
MYLOTARG after HSCT: 2.6x risk; HSCT after MYLOTARG: 2.9x risk
Suggested interval between last MYLOTARG dose and HSCT is roughly 2 to 3.5 months
segments.voiceover: For boards, focus on the boxed warning itself, veno-occlusive disease with MYLOTARG. The biggest risk multiplier is pre-existing hepatic impairment, nearly a 9-fold increase. Transplant timing matters in both directions, MYLOTARG before or after HSCT each roughly triples VOD risk. Practically, plan on spacing MYLOTARG and HSCT by about 2 to 3.5 months based on the ALFA-0701 and MyloFrance-1 experience.

This slide maps out AML maintenance therapy options for patients who achieve complete remission after intensive chemotherapy but do not go on to allogeneic transplant. Right now, only Onureg, which is oral azacitidine, is FDA approved in this setting, based on overall survival benefit shown in the QUAZAR trial published in the New England Journal in 2020. Other HMA-based maintenance strategies have been studied, injectable azacitidine and decitabine showed disease free survival benefit, and azacitidine plus venetoclax and Onureg plus venetoclax, that's the VIALE-M trial, are being explored. For FLT3 mutated patients specifically, FLT3 inhibitor maintenance is an option, midostaurin for one year based on the 2017 New England Journal data, or quizartinib for up to three years based on the 2023 Lancet QuANTUM-First data we just covered. Now, an important caveat about QUAZAR, 68 percent of enrolled patients had received no consolidation or only one cycle before starting Onureg, and patients who did receive consolidation actually had a statistically inferior reduction in hazards of death compared to those with no consolidation at all. Also, the optimal duration of maintenance was never defined in that trial.

keypoints: Onureg (oral azacitidine) is the only FDA-approved maintenance option, non-HSCT setting
Alternative HMA options: azacitidine, decitabine, azacitidine plus venetoclax
FLT3-mutated patients can receive midostaurin (1 year) or quizartinib (3 years) maintenance
QUAZAR caveat: most patients had minimal consolidation, and duration was undefined
segments.voiceover: Key takeaway, in patients who don't proceed to transplant, Onureg is the only FDA-approved maintenance drug, proven in the QUAZAR trial. If the patient is FLT3 mutated, FLT3 inhibitor maintenance, midostaurin or quizartinib, is an alternative pathway. But remember the QUAZAR caveat for boards, most patients in that trial had little to no consolidation therapy, which complicates how generalizable the survival benefit is, and the ideal maintenance duration remains unknown.

This slide covers AML maintenance therapy in the post-transplant setting, and the key message up front is that no drug is currently FDA approved here. For patients without allo-HSCT, options mirror the prior slide, HMA maintenance with azacitidine, azacitidine plus venetoclax from the VIALE-T trial, or Onureg being studied in the AMADEUS trial. But there's an important pitfall to recognize, patients with the highest risk disease, meaning active graft versus host disease or significant cytopenias, are often unable to tolerate maintenance therapy after transplant, and those are exactly the patients destined for worse outcomes anyway. That selection bias can artificially inflate the apparent benefit of post-HSCT maintenance in observational analyses. For patients who do proceed to allo-HSCT, FLT3 inhibitor maintenance has the most evidence, quizartinib from the QuANTUM-R and QuANTUM-First trials showing an overall survival benefit, sorafenib showing relapse free survival and reduced relapse rate benefits across two separate trials, and gilteritinib data published in Lancet Hematology in 2024.

keypoints: No FDA-approved maintenance therapy currently exists in the post-HSCT setting
Non-transplant options: azacitidine, azacitidine plus venetoclax, Onureg
Post-HSCT options for FLT3-mutated disease: quizartinib, sorafenib, gilteritinib
Pitfall: sickest post-HSCT patients often can't tolerate maintenance, biasing benefit estimates
segments.voiceover: Two things to hold onto here. First, unlike the non-transplant setting, nothing is FDA approved for maintenance after allo-HSCT yet, though FLT3 inhibitors like quizartinib, sorafenib, and gilteritinib have the strongest supporting data for FLT3 mutated patients. Second, watch for the selection bias pitfall, patients too sick from graft versus host disease or cytopenias to receive maintenance are also the ones most likely to relapse, which can make maintenance look more effective than it truly is.

This is the study design for QUAZAR AML-001, the pivotal trial behind Onureg. It was an international, multicenter, placebo controlled, double blind phase 3 study across 148 sites in 23 countries. Key eligibility criteria at screening included patients in first complete remission or CR with incomplete count recovery after intensive chemotherapy with or without consolidation, age 55 or older, de novo or secondary AML, ECOG performance status 0 to 3, intermediate or poor risk cytogenetics, ineligibility for transplant, and adequate marrow recovery. Randomization was 1 to 1 within 4 months of achieving CR or CRi, stratified by age group, prior MDS or CMML history, cytogenetic risk, and whether consolidation was given. Patients received CC-486, that's oral azacitidine, 300 milligrams once daily for 14 days of each 28-day cycle, or matching placebo. Response was assessed every 3 cycles, patients with 5 to 15 percent marrow blasts could get an optional extended 21-day dosing schedule, and those exceeding 15 percent blasts stopped treatment. All patients were followed long-term until death, withdrawal, study termination, or loss to follow-up.

keypoints: QUAZAR AML-001: international phase 3, placebo-controlled trial of CC-486 (Onureg)
Eligibility: first CR/CRi, age 55+, intermediate/poor risk cytogenetics, transplant-ineligible
Dosing: CC-486 300 mg once daily for 14 days of each 28-day cycle vs placebo
Blast-based algorithm: extend to 21 days if 5-15% blasts, stop if over 15%
segments.voiceover: For boards, know the QUAZAR skeleton. This is the phase 3 trial of oral azacitidine, brand name Onureg, in older patients age 55 and up, with intermediate or poor risk AML in first remission who are not transplant candidates. The regimen is 300 milligrams daily for 14 days each 28-day cycle versus placebo, with a built-in escalation to 21 days if blasts creep up to 5 to 15 percent, and treatment stops if blasts exceed 15 percent.

This is the pivotal QUAZAR AML-maintenance trial, looking at overall survival from randomization with a median follow-up of forty one point two months. Patients in remission after intensive chemotherapy were randomized to oral azacitidine, drug code CC dash four eight six, versus placebo. The stratified P value is zero point zero zero zero nine, with a hazard ratio of zero point six nine, meaning a thirty one percent reduction in the risk of death. Median overall survival was twenty four point seven months with oral azacitidine compared to fourteen point eight months with placebo, a difference of nine point nine months. This established oral azacitidine as standard of care maintenance therapy for AML patients in first remission who are not proceeding to transplant, and it's a key trial for boards.

keypoints: QUAZAR AML trial: oral azacitidine maintenance after remission
Median OS twenty four point seven months versus fourteen point eight months with placebo
Hazard ratio zero point six nine, P equals zero point zero zero zero nine
Nine point nine month survival benefit, practice changing
segments.voiceover: Remember QUAZAR, oral azacitidine maintenance after remission, extends median overall survival from fourteen point eight to twenty four point seven months, a hazard ratio around zero point seven, and it's now standard maintenance therapy for patients not going to transplant.

This slide breaks down the QUAZAR overall survival benefit by how many consolidation cycles patients received before starting maintenance. Across all three subgroups, no consolidation, one consolidation, and two or more consolidations, oral azacitidine prolonged survival compared to placebo. Median overall survival ranged from twenty one to twenty eight point six months with oral azacitidine, versus only ten point nine to seventeen point six months with placebo. Interestingly, the hazard ratio was most favorable, zero point five five, in patients who received no consolidation at all, suggesting the benefit of maintenance is preserved or even more pronounced when consolidation chemotherapy was skipped or not tolerated. This is useful for boards because it shows the drug's benefit is consistent regardless of prior consolidation intensity.

keypoints: OS benefit with oral azacitidine held across all consolidation subgroups
No consolidation: HR zero point five five, most favorable
One consolidation: HR zero point seven five
Two or more consolidations: HR zero point seven five
Benefit independent of consolidation intensity
segments.voiceover: Across consolidation subgroups from none to two or more cycles, oral azacitidine consistently prolonged survival versus placebo, with the strongest hazard ratio, zero point five five, seen in patients who had no consolidation at all.

This is the SORMAIN trial data, showing that sorafenib maintenance therapy reduces relapse and death after allogeneic transplant for FLT3 dash ITD positive AML. Panel A shows relapse free survival, with a hazard ratio of zero point three nine and a log rank P value of zero point zero one three favoring sorafenib. At twenty four months, relapse free survival was eighty five percent with sorafenib compared to fifty three point three percent with placebo, which is a striking absolute difference. Panel B shows overall survival, with sorafenib giving ninety point five percent survival at twenty four months versus sixty six point two percent with placebo, hazard ratio zero point five one six. This trial established that FLT3 inhibitor maintenance after transplant meaningfully reduces relapse risk in FLT3 ITD positive AML, and sorafenib was the first agent to show this benefit, predating gilteritinib data.

keypoints: SORMAIN trial: sorafenib maintenance post allo-HCT in FLT3-ITD AML
Twenty four month RFS eighty five percent vs fifty three point three percent, HR zero point three nine
Twenty four month OS ninety point five percent vs sixty six point two percent
Sorafenib was first FLT3 inhibitor shown to improve post-transplant outcomes
segments.voiceover: SORMAIN showed sorafenib maintenance after transplant nearly doubles relapse free survival in FLT3 ITD positive AML, from about fifty three percent to eighty five percent at two years, with a clear overall survival benefit too.

This is the MORPHO trial of gilteritinib maintenance after allogeneic transplant in FLT3 dash ITD positive AML, and it's an important contrast to the sorafenib data. The primary endpoint, relapse free survival in the overall population, was not statistically significant, hazard ratio zero point six seven nine, P equals zero point zero five one eight, just missing significance. Overall survival was similar between arms. However, in a pre-specified subgroup analysis using a sensitive FLT3 ITD measurable residual disease assay with a threshold of ten to the negative sixth, gilteritinib clearly improved relapse free survival in MRD positive patients, hazard ratio zero point five one five, while there was no benefit in MRD negative patients. The note in red reminds us this is not an FDA approved indication and is not reimbursed by Taiwan's National Health Insurance, so it's important for exam purposes to distinguish gilteritinib maintenance, which failed its primary endpoint, from sorafenib maintenance, which succeeded.

keypoints: MORPHO trial: gilteritinib maintenance after allo-HSCT missed primary RFS endpoint
Overall population HR zero point six seven nine, P equals zero point zero five, not significant
MRD positive subgroup benefited: HR zero point five one five
MRD negative subgroup: no benefit
Not FDA approved for this indication, not reimbursed
segments.voiceover: MORPHO's gilteritinib maintenance missed its primary relapse free survival endpoint overall, but a pre-specified MRD positive subgroup, using a very sensitive ten to the minus six assay, did benefit. It's not an approved indication, so distinguish this from the positive sorafenib SORMAIN result.

This table, flagged as a must-know exam topic, contrasts the two classic patterns of therapy related AML. Alkylating agent or radiation related t-AML has a long latency period of five to seven years, often preceded by a myelodysplastic phase, and is characterized by loss of chromosome five or deletion five q, loss of chromosome seven or deletion seven q, and complex karyotype. TP53 mutations are common, the clinical course is insidious with cytopenias, and prognosis is generally poor. In contrast, topoisomerase two inhibitor related t-AML, caused by drugs like etoposide or anthracyclines, has a much shorter latency of only one to three years, usually presents as de novo AML without a preceding MDS phase, and is associated with balanced translocations such as KMT2A rearrangements at eleven q two three, RUNX1 dash RUNX1T1, or PML dash RARA. KMT2A rearrangements are the common molecular feature, onset is abrupt with leukocytosis, and prognosis is intermediate, depending on which translocation is present. This latency period and cytogenetic pattern distinction is a very frequently tested board concept.

keypoints: Alkylator or radiation t-AML: five to seven year latency, MDS phase, minus five/minus seven, complex karyotype, TP53 mutated, poor prognosis
Topoisomerase two inhibitor t-AML: one to three year latency, de novo, balanced translocations like KMT2A, RUNX1 dash RUNX1T1, PML dash RARA
KMT2A rearrangements common with topo II inhibitors; TP53 common with alkylators
Marked as a frequently tested exam topic
segments.voiceover: Two patterns of therapy related AML: alkylator or radiation exposure gives a long latency, an MDS phase, minus five or minus seven, and TP53 mutations with poor prognosis; topoisomerase two inhibitor exposure gives a short one to three year latency, de novo presentation, and balanced translocations like KMT2A, with intermediate prognosis.

This flowchart summarizes the full treatment algorithm for confirmed acute promyelocytic leukemia. Diagnosis is confirmed with peripheral blood and bone marrow karyotype, FISH, and RT-PCR for t fifteen;seventeen, PML dash RARA, and its fusion variants. For induction, low or intermediate risk patients receive ATRA plus arsenic trioxide, or ATRA plus chemotherapy if arsenic isn't available, while high risk patients add gemtuzumab ozogamicin or idarubicin to ATRA plus ATO. Throughout induction, clinicians must watch for differentiation syndrome, treated with steroid prophylaxis and dexamethasone, monitor for ATO related QT prolongation by keeping potassium above four and magnesium above one point eight with twice weekly EKGs, watch for fluid overload, and consider CNS prophylaxis in high risk patients or those with prior CNS hemorrhage. A bone marrow assessment at week four should show blasts below five percent before moving to consolidation. After consolidation, RT-PCR on peripheral blood determines the monitoring path: if negative, low and intermediate risk patients get CBC surveillance without routine molecular monitoring, while high risk patients get CBC and RT-PCR every three months with consideration of maintenance therapy. If RT-PCR is positive, confirmed relapse triggers salvage with ATRA plus chemotherapy, arsenic trioxide plus gemtuzumab, and consideration of hematopoietic stem cell transplant.

keypoints: Induction: ATRA plus ATO for low/intermediate risk; add GO or idarubicin for high risk
Watch for differentiation syndrome, ATO-related QT prolongation, and fluid overload
BM assessment at week four; consolidation continues until blasts less than five percent
Post-consolidation RT-PCR guides monitoring: negative goes to surveillance, positive triggers relapse management
Relapse treatment includes ATRA/chemo, ATO plus GO, and consideration of HSCT
segments.voiceover: APL treatment: ATRA plus arsenic trioxide for low and intermediate risk, adding gemtuzumab or idarubicin for high risk, with vigilance for differentiation syndrome and QT prolongation. After consolidation, RT-PCR determines whether patients go to routine surveillance or are managed as relapse with salvage therapy and possible transplant.

This table covers APL with variant translocations, a favorite board topic because it tests whether you know which variants respond to ATRA and which don't. PLZF dash RARA, from t eleven;seventeen at q two three;q twenty one point one, occurs in about one percent of APL and is classically refractory to ATRA, this is the single most important variant to remember. NPM dash RARA, from t five;seventeen, occurs in about zero point five percent and is responsive to ATRA therapy. NuMA dash RARA, from t eleven;seventeen at q thirteen;q twenty one point one, is also responsive to ATRA. STAT5B dash RARA, arising from an interstitial deletion of chromosome seventeen, is refractory to ATRA, similar to PLZF. Finally, BCOR dash RARA, from t X;seventeen at q eleven;q twenty one point one, has only been reported in a single case, and while initially clinically responsive to ATRA, that patient had several relapses despite standard chemotherapy plus ATRA. The key teaching point for exams: PLZF and STAT5B fusions are refractory to ATRA, while NPM and NuMA fusions remain ATRA responsive.

keypoints: PLZF dash RARA, t eleven;seventeen: refractory to ATRA, one percent prevalence
NPM dash RARA, t five;seventeen: responsive to ATRA
NuMA dash RARA, t eleven;seventeen q thirteen: responsive to ATRA
STAT5B dash RARA: refractory to ATRA
BCOR dash RARA: rare, initially responsive but relapsed
segments.voiceover: For variant APL translocations, remember PLZF dash RARA and STAT5B dash RARA are refractory to ATRA, while NPM dash RARA and NuMA dash RARA remain ATRA responsive. PLZF is the classic refractory variant tested on boards.

This slide presents two sample board exam questions with answers, testing practical AML treatment decisions. Question two asks: for a seventy five year old or younger AML patient with cardiac, pulmonary, or hepatic comorbidity, what treatment is appropriate? The options are three plus seven, FLAG-ida, CPX-351, glasdegib with or without low dose cytarabine, or none of the above. The correct answer is D, glasdegib with or without low dose cytarabine, reflecting that patients with significant organ comorbidities are often unfit for intensive induction regimens like three plus seven or FLAG-ida, and a lower intensity, better tolerated option such as glasdegib is preferred. Question three asks about FDA approved indications for targeted therapy in AML. The correct answer is B, ivosidenib can be used in frontline therapy in IDH1 mutated AML, which reflects its FDA approval for previously untreated AML in patients seventy five or older or with comorbidities precluding intensive chemotherapy. The distractors are important to recognize as wrong: enasidenib is not approved frontline, gilteritinib is not approved for induction, and quizartinib is approved for newly diagnosed rather than relapsed refractory FLT3 mutated AML.

keypoints: Comorbid, unfit AML patient: glasdegib plus/minus low dose cytarabine is appropriate, not intensive induction
Ivosidenib is FDA approved for frontline therapy in IDH1 mutated AML
Enasidenib is not approved frontline; distinguish from ivosidenib
Gilteritinib is not approved for induction therapy
Quizartinib is approved for newly diagnosed, not relapsed refractory, FLT3 mutated AML
segments.voiceover: Two testable points here: unfit AML patients with organ comorbidities get glasdegib rather than intensive induction, and among FDA approved targeted agents, only ivosidenib is approved for frontline use in IDH1 mutated AML, so watch out for distractors like enasidenib and gilteritinib in induction.

This page reviews two exam questions on acute myeloid leukemia therapy. The first asks about frontline AML treatment, and the correct answer is none of the above. Venetoclax plus azacitidine works across FLT3 and IDH mutated AML regardless of whether midostaurin, ivosidenib, or enasidenib were given, so those pairing statements are false. Oral azacitidine, from the QUAZAR AML-001 trial, prolongs overall survival as maintenance in older patients who achieved remission with induction chemotherapy but were not going on to transplant, so tying its benefit to patients who also received allogeneic transplant is incorrect. And sorafenib maintenance after transplant, from the SORMAIN trial, showed a relapse free survival benefit for FLT3 ITD AML, not a clearly proven overall survival benefit. The second question asks which statement about therapy related AML is wrong, and it's the one describing latency. Alkylating agent related AML has the longer latency, around five to ten years, while topoisomerase two inhibitor related AML develops much sooner, typically within one to three years. This question reversed those latencies.

keypoints: Venetoclax azacitidine benefits FLT3 and IDH mutated AML independent of prior targeted therapy
QUAZAR trial: oral azacitidine maintenance improves survival mainly in patients not proceeding to transplant
SORMAIN trial: sorafenib after transplant improves relapse free survival, not proven overall survival
Topoisomerase two inhibitor related AML has a short latency, one to three years
Alkylating agent related AML has a longer latency, five to ten years
segments.voiceover: Remember, venetoclax based regimens work across FLT3 and IDH mutated AML no matter what targeted therapy came before. The QUAZAR trial's survival benefit for oral azacitidine maintenance applies to patients who did not go to transplant. SORMAIN showed sorafenib maintenance improves relapse free survival after transplant, but overall survival benefit is not firmly established. And don't mix up the latencies, alkylating agents take longer to cause secondary AML than topoisomerase two inhibitors do.

This page covers AML pathogenesis genes and prognostic factors. Question twelve asks which mutated gene is most prevalent in cytogenetically normal AML, and the answer is NPM1. NPM1 mutations are found in about a third of all AML cases and are even more common in patients with a normal karyotype, often paired with FLT3 ITD mutations. Question thirteen asks which factors are unfavorable for outcome, and the answer combines GATA-1 expression together with adverse cytogenetics, specifically monosomy five or seven, deletion five q or seven q, exaggerated hyperdiploidy of more than forty seven chromosomes, trisomy eight, translocation between chromosomes six and nine, trisomy eleven, and complex karyotypes with multiple abnormalities. Notably, NPM1 mutation by itself, without FLT3 ITD, is actually a favorable marker, and early blast clearance during induction is a good prognostic sign, not an unfavorable one, which is why those two options were excluded from the correct answer.

keypoints: NPM1 is the most common mutation in cytogenetically normal AML
NPM1 mutation alone, without FLT3 ITD, predicts favorable prognosis
Unfavorable cytogenetics include monosomy 5 or 7, complex karyotype, and translocation six nine
Early blast clearance during induction predicts a good outcome, not a poor one
segments.voiceover: For boards, remember NPM1 is the single most common mutation in cytogenetically normal AML. On its own, without FLT3 ITD, NPM1 mutation actually predicts a favorable outcome. The unfavorable side includes monosomy five or seven, hyperdiploidy, trisomy eight, translocation between chromosomes six and nine, trisomy eleven, and complex karyotypes. And don't be fooled, early blast clearance during induction therapy is a good sign, not a bad one.

This page reviews three exam items on AML and MPAL. Question fourteen tests APL treatment, and the wrong statement claims high risk APL, meaning white count over ten times ten to the ninth per liter, should be induced with ATRA and arsenic trioxide alone. High risk APL actually needs an anthracycline added to ATRA, since ATRA-ATO alone is validated mainly for low to intermediate risk disease. Question fifteen tests FLT3 inhibitor pharmacology, and the wrong statement swaps type one and type two inhibitors. Type one inhibitors, like midostaurin, gilteritinib, and crenolanib, block both FLT3 ITD and TKD mutations, while type two inhibitors, like sorafenib and quizartinib, only block FLT3 ITD. Question thirty one covers mixed phenotype acute leukemia. The correct statements are that T myeloid MPAL shares a gene expression profile with early T-cell precursor ALL, and B myeloid MPAL frequently carries ZNF384 fusions. High CD19 expression alone doesn't diagnose B lineage, and MPAL is generally treated with ALL-based, not AML-based, chemotherapy.

keypoints: High risk APL needs anthracycline plus ATRA, not ATRA-ATO alone
Type one FLT3 inhibitors block both ITD and TKD; type two block ITD only
T myeloid MPAL resembles early T-cell precursor ALL by gene expression
B myeloid MPAL often carries ZNF384 fusions
MPAL is generally treated with ALL-based chemotherapy
segments.voiceover: Three quick contrasts to lock in. High risk APL needs an anthracycline added to ATRA, ATRA plus arsenic alone is for low risk disease. Type one FLT3 inhibitors like midostaurin and gilteritinib hit both ITD and TKD mutations, type two inhibitors like sorafenib only hit ITD. And for mixed phenotype acute leukemia, T myeloid cases resemble early T-cell precursor ALL genetically, B myeloid cases often carry ZNF384 fusions, and treatment generally follows ALL-based protocols.

This page has two clinical vignettes testing the 2022 classification updates. The first describes a 65 year old woman with pancytopenia, 16% myeloblasts, a TP53 mutation, a RUNX1 mutation, and translocation between chromosomes six and nine in most metaphases. Under ICC ELN 2022, the answer is AML with recurrent genetic abnormality. Translocation six nine, producing the DEK NUP214 fusion, is a defining lesion that classifies the case as AML even below the usual twenty percent blast threshold, and it takes priority over the co-occurring TP53 and RUNX1 mutations. The second vignette describes a 75 year old man with de novo AML on venetoclax and azacitidine, whose marrow shows trisomy eight, trisomy thirteen, loss of the Y chromosome, an NPM1 mutation, and FLT3 ITD with unknown allelic ratio. The correct answer is intermediate risk under ELN 2022. Loss of the Y chromosome is excluded from complex karyotype counting since it's often age related, leaving too few abnormalities for a complex karyotype. And under ELN 2022, the FLT3 ITD allelic ratio no longer changes the risk category for NPM1 mutated AML, so this combination lands in intermediate risk regardless.

keypoints: Translocation six nine with DEK NUP214 defines AML even under twenty percent blasts
Recurrent genetic abnormalities take priority over comutations like TP53 or RUNX1 for diagnosis
Loss of Y chromosome is usually excluded from complex karyotype counting
ELN2022 dropped FLT3-ITD allelic ratio as a risk modifier
NPM1 mutated plus FLT3-ITD is intermediate risk under ELN2022 regardless of allelic ratio
segments.voiceover: Two ELN2022 updates to memorize. First, defining recurrent genetic abnormalities like translocation six nine with DEK NUP214 establish an AML diagnosis even under the twenty percent blast cutoff, overriding co-mutations. Second, ELN2022 no longer uses the FLT3 ITD allelic ratio to set risk, so NPM1 mutated AML with FLT3 ITD is intermediate risk either way. And remember, isolated loss of the Y chromosome doesn't count toward a complex karyotype.

This page repeats two classic exam themes. Question seven asks which statements about FLT3 mutations are wrong, and three of the four are. FLT3 mutations link to higher peripheral blast counts and a normal karyotype, but not specifically to FAB M1 morphology, so that's wrong. The one true statement is that FLT3 ITD does not affect complete remission rate after standard induction, it mainly drives relapse risk, not induction response. Claiming FLT3 ITD carries higher prognostic significance after age seventy is also wrong, since its impact is generally attenuated in older patients. And the phase three MORPHO trial of gilteritinib maintenance after transplant did not meet its primary endpoint of relapse free survival in the overall population, benefit appeared mainly in patients with detectable measurable residual disease. Question twenty is the familiar therapy related AML item, and the wrong statement again reverses the latency periods, alkylating agents actually cause secondary AML after a longer latency than topoisomerase two inhibitors do.

keypoints: FLT3 mutations link to blast count and normal karyotype, not specifically FAB M1
FLT3-ITD presence does not lower complete remission rate after induction
FLT3-ITD prognostic impact is attenuated, not increased, in patients over seventy
MORPHO trial missed its primary RFS endpoint overall; benefit was in MRD positive patients
Alkylating agents cause AML after a longer latency than topoisomerase two inhibitors
segments.voiceover: Key FLT3 facts for boards. FLT3 ITD doesn't change your complete remission rate after induction, it's a relapse risk marker. Its prognostic weight actually shrinks in patients over seventy, it doesn't grow. And the MORPHO trial of gilteritinib maintenance missed its overall relapse free survival endpoint, benefit was confined to MRD positive patients. Finally, keep the t-AML latency straight, alkylating agents take longer to cause leukemia than topoisomerase two inhibitors.

This page covers ELN 2022 updates and targeted therapy pharmacology, both recurring exam favorites. Question six asks which changes from ELN 2017 to ELN 2022 are correct, and it's the first two. The FLT3 ITD allelic ratio was dropped from the risk model entirely, so a patient's risk category no longer depends on whether the ratio is high or low. And CEBPA mutant AML now qualifies as favorable based on having an in-frame mutation affecting the bZIP region, regardless of whether it's mono-allelic or bi-allelic, a shift from the old requirement of biallelic mutation. The other two statements are false, hyperdiploid karyotypes with multiple trisomies are actually excluded from the complex karyotype adverse category, not included, and AML with myelodysplasia related gene mutations, things like ASXL1, RUNX1, or SRSF2, is explicitly classified as adverse risk under ELN 2022, contrary to what the statement claims. Question nineteen repeats the FLT3 inhibitor pharmacology question, and the wrong statement is again the one that swaps type one and type two inhibitor mechanisms, type one inhibitors block both ITD and TKD mutations, type two inhibitors block ITD only.

keypoints: ELN2022 removed FLT3-ITD allelic ratio from risk stratification
CEBPA favorable prognosis now depends on bZIP in-frame mutation, mono or bi-allelic
Multiple trisomies or hyperdiploidy are excluded from the complex karyotype adverse group
Myelodysplasia-related gene mutations are classified as adverse risk in ELN2022
Type one FLT3 inhibitors block ITD and TKD; type two block ITD only
segments.voiceover: Two ELN2022 changes to nail down. The FLT3 ITD allelic ratio is gone from risk stratification, and CEBPA favorable status now just needs a bZIP in-frame mutation, mono or biallelic. On the flip side, multiple trisomies don't count as complex karyotype anymore, but myelodysplasia related gene mutations still land patients in the adverse risk group. And keep FLT3 inhibitor types straight, type one blocks both ITD and TKD, type two blocks ITD only.

This page pairs a repeat question on therapy related AML with an ELN 2022 risk stratification question. Question eight's wrong statement claims that ICC 2022 sets therapy related AML apart as its own unique diagnostic entity called myeloid neoplasms post cytotoxic therapy. Actually, the ICC approach attaches post cytotoxic therapy as a qualifier onto the underlying AML diagnosis rather than creating a separate category, that distinction is what the WHO fifth edition does instead. Question sixteen asks which ELN 2022 risk statement is wrong, and it's the one classifying AML with mutated NPM1 plus translocation six nine and DEK NUP214 fusion as intermediate risk. Translocation six nine is an adverse cytogenetic marker under ELN 2022, and it overrides a favorable NPM1 mutation, so this combination should be classified as adverse risk, not intermediate. The other listed scenarios are correctly assigned, bZIP in-frame CEBPA is favorable, wild type NPM1 with high FLT3 ITD allelic ratio is intermediate, mono-allelic TP53 with a measurable variant allele fraction is adverse, and core binding factor AML with t(8;21) and a KIT mutation stays favorable despite the KIT mutation.

keypoints: ICC 2022 treats therapy-related AML as a qualifier, not a separate entity, unlike WHO fifth edition
Translocation six nine with DEK NUP214 is adverse risk under ELN2022, even with NPM1 mutation
bZIP in-frame CEBPA mutation remains favorable risk
KIT mutation does not downgrade core binding factor AML with t(8;21) from favorable
segments.voiceover: Don't mix up ICC and WHO on therapy related AML, ICC uses post cytotoxic therapy as a qualifier, WHO fifth edition makes it a separate entity. And for ELN2022 risk, translocation six nine with DEK NUP214 is adverse regardless of NPM1 status, it overrides the otherwise favorable NPM1 mutation. Remember too that a KIT mutation doesn't knock t(8;21) core binding factor AML out of the favorable group.

This page closes out the AML complications theme with differentiation syndrome and hyperleukocytosis. Question two asks which statements about differentiation syndrome are correct, and it's three of the four. Differentiation syndrome is not caused by anthracyclines alone, it's a complication of ATRA or arsenic trioxide therapy in acute promyelocytic leukemia, so that first statement is wrong. The correct features are respiratory distress with pulmonary edema or infiltrates and a pleural or pericardial effusion on chest imaging, that adding concurrent cytotoxic chemotherapy actually lowers the risk of differentiation syndrome, and that at the earliest suspicion you should start dexamethasone at 0.5 to 1 milligram per kilogram, up to 10 milligrams per dose, every 12 hours. Question five asks about hyperleukocytosis, and all four statements are correct. Leukostasis risk depends on both the underlying disease and the absolute white count, the classic target organs are brain, lungs, kidneys, and penis, causing priapism, hyperleukocytosis can produce spurious lab results like pseudohyperkalemia, pseudohypoxemia, pseudohypoglycemia, and abnormal coagulation tests, and red cell transfusions should be limited before cytoreduction because raising the hematocrit worsens blood viscosity and leukostasis risk.

keypoints: Differentiation syndrome comes from ATRA or arsenic trioxide therapy, not anthracyclines alone
Concurrent cytotoxic chemotherapy lowers differentiation syndrome risk
Treat suspected differentiation syndrome early with dexamethasone 0.5 to 1 mg per kg every 12 hours
Leukostasis targets brain, lungs, kidneys, and penis
Limit red cell transfusion in hyperleukocytosis to avoid worsening viscosity
segments.voiceover: For differentiation syndrome, remember it's driven by ATRA or arsenic trioxide, not anthracyclines, adding chemotherapy actually lowers the risk, and you treat early with dexamethasone at 0.5 to 1 milligram per kilogram every 12 hours. For hyperleukocytosis, know the classic target organs, brain, lungs, kidneys, and penis, watch for spurious labs like pseudohyperkalemia, and hold back red cell transfusions before cytoreduction so you don't worsen blood viscosity.

This page reviews two board exam questions on high risk AML genetics. The first asks which alterations are commonly seen in therapy related AML, and the answer includes all four listed findings, loss of chromosome five, loss of chromosome seven, TP53 mutations, and complex karyotypes, since therapy related AML classically carries these adverse cytogenetic and molecular changes after prior chemotherapy or radiation exposure. A key teaching point noted here is that under current risk models, adverse risk cytogenetic abnormalities occurring alongside an NPM1 mutation now override the otherwise favorable NPM1 signal and push the patient into the adverse risk category. The second question presents a sixty year old woman with prior breast cancer treated with mastectomy and adjuvant therapy, who develops AML with a translocation between chromosomes 11 and 23 producing a KMT2A rearrangement, plus an NPM1 mutation and a FLT3 internal tandem duplication. The correct answer identifies this as AML with an ICC defining recurrent genetic abnormality, since the KMT2A rearrangement itself is a defining lesion regardless of the treatment history or the co-occurring NPM1 and FLT3 mutations.

keypoints: Therapy related AML: -5, -7, TP53, and complex karyotype are all classic adverse findings
Adverse cytogenetics plus NPM1 mutation now defines adverse risk, not favorable
KMT2A rearrangement is an ICC AML-defining recurrent genetic abnormality
Prior cancer treatment history alone does not override a defining genetic lesion
segments.voiceover: Remember, therapy related AML shows -5, -7, TP53 mutation, and complex karyotype together. And when adverse cytogenetics coexist with NPM1 mutation, the case is now classified as adverse risk. Also, a KMT2A rearrangement is itself an ICC defining lesion, regardless of treatment history.

This page covers two more questions on AML genetics and targeted treatment. Question sixteen asks which statement is true about AML with cytogenetic abnormalities or mutations, and the correct answer is that FLT3 internal tandem duplication is associated with a high peripheral blast count and a normal karyotype, and while its presence does not affect the complete remission rate, it strongly predicts a higher relapse rate. The distractors are wrong for specific reasons, the RUNX1 RUNX1T1 fusion from translocation eight twenty one is actually associated with large atypical granules and Auer rods rather than peripheral monocytosis, KMT2A rearrangements have over forty translocation partners but the prognosis varies widely by partner rather than uniformly being worst with translocation nine eleven, and NPM1 mutations cluster in exon twelve rather than exon five. Question four asks which statement about treating FLT3 ITD or TKD mutated AML is incorrect, and the answer is that midostaurin has strong evidence for use during induction and consolidation, but its benefit as maintenance therapy alone is not well established, unlike gilteritinib which has clearer evidence supporting post transplant maintenance, especially in patients with detectable measurable residual disease.

keypoints: FLT3-ITD: high blast count, normal karyotype, does not lower CR rate but raises relapse risk
KMT2A has over 40 partners with prognosis varying by partner, not uniformly worst
NPM1 mutations cluster in exon 12, not exon 5
Midostaurin evidence supports induction and consolidation, not clearly maintenance
segments.voiceover: Key points here, FLT3 ITD raises relapse risk without lowering CR rate, and NPM1 mutations are an exon twelve story, not exon five. For treatment, midostaurin is proven in induction and consolidation, while maintenance benefit is better supported for gilteritinib, particularly with detectable MRD after transplant.

This page presents two more high yield questions. Question twenty asks which statement about targeted therapies in AML is wrong, and the answer is the statement about quizartinib. Quizartinib is actually a first generation, type two FLT3 inhibitor, and its pivotal trial combining it with standard seven plus three induction enrolled only patients with FLT3 internal tandem duplication, not FLT3 TKD mutations, so claiming a survival benefit across both mutation types is incorrect. The other statements about glasdegib, gilteritinib, midostaurin, and gilteritinib maintenance based on measurable residual disease status are all accurate. Question twenty seven asks which statement about acute promyelocytic leukemia is wrong, and the answer concerns variant RARA translocations. While the classic translocation between chromosomes 15 and 17 produces the PML RARA fusion that responds beautifully to ATRA, variant translocation partners such as NPM1, NUMA1, ZBTB16, and STAT5B do not all respond well to ATRA, in fact the ZBTB16 and STAT5B fusions are well known to confer ATRA resistance, so it is wrong to say all variant translocations respond effectively to ATRA therapy.

keypoints: Quizartinib is a first-generation, type II FLT3 inhibitor tested only in FLT3-ITD disease
APL classically shows t(15;17) producing the PML-RARA fusion, highly ATRA-sensitive
Variant RARA fusion partners like ZBTB16 and STAT5B confer ATRA resistance
Not all APL variant translocations respond equally well to ATRA
segments.voiceover: Two traps to remember, quizartinib's proven benefit is specific to FLT3 ITD disease, not TKD. And in APL, while classic PML RARA responds beautifully to ATRA, variant partners like ZBTB16 and STAT5B are known to be ATRA resistant.

This page has a single detailed question on targeted therapies for AML, asking which statement is wrong. The answer is the statement describing type one and type two FLT3 inhibitors, and it has the definitions reversed. In reality, type one FLT3 inhibitors bind the kinase in its active conformation and can inhibit both FLT3 internal tandem duplication and FLT3 TKD mutations, while type two inhibitors only bind the inactive conformation and therefore only inhibit FLT3 ITD, not TKD mutations, since a TKD mutation in the activation loop prevents that inactive conformation from forming. The other statements on this slide are accurate teaching points worth remembering, oral azacitidine, known as CC 486 or Onureg, prolongs overall and relapse free survival as maintenance therapy in older AML patients after achieving first remission, quizartinib, crenolanib, and gilteritinib are considered second generation FLT3 inhibitors with greater specificity and fewer off target effects, midostaurin remains the first approved drug for newly diagnosed FLT3 mutated AML, and venetoclax combined with low dose cytarabine is approved for patients over seventy five or those unfit for intensive chemotherapy.

keypoints: Type I FLT3 inhibitors block active conformation, inhibiting both ITD and TKD mutations
Type II FLT3 inhibitors only bind inactive conformation, inhibiting ITD alone
Oral azacitidine (CC-486) prolongs survival as post-remission maintenance in older AML
Venetoclax plus low-dose cytarabine suits patients over 75 or unfit for intensive chemotherapy
segments.voiceover: The trap on this page is the type one versus type two FLT3 inhibitor definition, type one hits both ITD and TKD, type two only hits ITD. Also remember oral azacitidine as maintenance therapy, and venetoclax with low dose cytarabine for older or unfit patients.

This page covers two questions, one on a recent clinical trial and one on ELN 2022 risk stratification. Question thirty nine references a 2025 Blood paper comparing venetoclax plus decitabine against intensive chemotherapy as induction in young patients with newly diagnosed AML, and asks which description is wrong. The answer is the statement claiming infection rates were similar between the two groups, when in fact the trial showed differences in infection risk between the venetoclax decitabine arm and the intensive chemotherapy arm. The other statements, about similar remission rates overall, a higher composite remission rate in adverse risk or U2AF1 mutated patients with venetoclax decitabine, lower serious adverse events, and similar one year event free survival, are all accurate per the trial. Question nineteen asks which statement about ELN 2022 risk stratification is wrong, and the answer involves NPM1 mutated AML with the translocation between chromosomes six and nine producing the DEK NUP214 fusion. Even though NPM1 mutation alone is typically favorable, the DEK NUP214 fusion is itself an adverse risk defining lesion, so this combination should be classified as adverse risk, not intermediate risk as the statement claims.

keypoints: VEN-DEC vs intensive chemo trial: infection incidence actually differed, not similar
VEN-DEC showed higher CRc in ELN-2022 adverse-risk or U2AF1-mutated patients
DEK::NUP214 fusion from t(6;9) is adverse-risk defining even with NPM1 mutation present
NPM1 mutation alone does not override an adverse cytogenetic partner lesion
segments.voiceover: Two takeaways, in the 2025 venetoclax decitabine trial infection rates were not simply similar between arms. And under ELN 2022, DEK NUP214 fusion keeps a case adverse risk even when NPM1 is mutated, since that translocation trumps the favorable NPM1 signal.

This page asks which combination of statements about genomic targets and their commercially available agents in AML is correct. Statement one, that FLT3 internal tandem duplication mutations raise relapse risk and worsen outcomes while FLT3 TKD mutations are prognostically neutral, is true. Statement two, that sorafenib and midostaurin have shown efficacy in both de novo and relapsed refractory AML, is also true. Statement three, that venetoclax as a single agent and in combination with chemotherapy has shown early promising results in adult AML, is true as well. Statement four, however, claims that adding up front gemtuzumab ozogamicin provides no benefit in pediatric AML, and this is false, since pediatric trials such as AAML0531 demonstrated that adding gemtuzumab ozogamicin to induction chemotherapy actually improved outcomes in children with AML. So the correct combination is statements one, two, and three together, giving answer B.

keypoints: FLT3-ITD worsens outcomes and raises relapse risk; FLT3-TKD is prognostically neutral
Sorafenib and midostaurin show efficacy in both de novo and relapsed refractory AML
Venetoclax shows promising results as monotherapy and in combination in adult AML
Gemtuzumab ozogamicin actually improves outcomes when added to pediatric AML induction
segments.voiceover: Statements one, two, and three are all correct, FLT3 ITD is adverse while TKD is neutral, sorafenib and midostaurin work in both de novo and relapsed disease, and venetoclax shows early promise in adults. The trap is statement four, gemtuzumab ozogamicin actually does help in pediatric AML.

This is the presentation outline slide, marking a section transition. The deck covers five major white blood cell malignancy topics, AML, MDS, MPN, MDS slash MPN overlap syndromes, and ALL, and with MDS highlighted here, we are now moving into the myelodysplastic syndrome section.

This slide summarizes the mutation landscape in myelodysplastic syndrome.
