The left panel ranks individual genes by mutation frequency, with ASXL1 as the single most commonly mutated gene at around twenty percent, followed by TET2, SF3B1, RUNX1, STAG2, and TP53 each in the twelve to fourteen percent range, then DNMT3A, SRSF2, and U2AF1 in the eight to ten percent range, with many additional genes such as BCOR, CEBPA, EZH2, IDH2, NRAS, and NPM1 mutated at lower but still clinically relevant frequencies. The right panel groups these same genes into functional pathway categories, and here epigenetic modifiers as a group are affected most often, in about forty six percent of cases, followed by the spliceosome complex at roughly thirty four percent, chromatin modifiers at about twenty nine percent, and DNA methylation related genes at around twenty seven percent. Transcription factors, tumor suppressors, cohesin complex genes, and activated signaling pathways round out the list at lower frequencies. The overall message for boards is that MDS is driven predominantly by epigenetic and splicing machinery mutations rather than classic activated signaling mutations, which helps distinguish its biology from more proliferative myeloid neoplasms.

keypoints: ASXL1 is the single most frequently mutated gene in MDS, around 20 percent
Spliceosome genes SF3B1, SRSF2, and U2AF1 are collectively very common
By pathway, epigenetic modifiers (46%) and spliceosome complex (34%) dominate
MDS biology is driven by epigenetic and splicing mutations, not activated signaling
segments.voiceover: For boards, remember ASXL1 tops the individual gene list at about twenty percent, and by functional category, epigenetic modifiers and the spliceosome complex dominate the mutation landscape, which is the signature that distinguishes MDS biology from more proliferative myeloid neoplasms.

This is the fifth edition WHO classification of MDS, and it is heavily tested, so pay close attention. WHO splits MDS into two groups. The first group is MDS with defining genetic abnormalities. MDS with low blasts and isolated 5 q deletion requires blasts under 5 percent in the marrow and under 2 percent in blood, plus a 5 q deletion alone or with only one other abnormality other than monosomy 7 or 7 q deletion. MDS with low blasts and S F 3 B 1 mutation requires the absence of 5 q deletion, monosomy 7, or complex karyotype, with an S F 3 B 1 mutation present. MDS with biallelic T P 53 inactivation allows blasts up to 20 percent, usually shows a complex karyotype, and requires either two or more T P 53 mutations, or one mutation with evidence of T P 53 copy number loss or copy neutral loss of heterozygosity. The second group is morphologically defined MDS. Hypoplastic MDS has blasts under 5 percent marrow and under 2 percent blood. MDS with increased blasts is split into I B 1, with 5 to 9 percent marrow blasts or 2 to 4 percent blood blasts, and I B 2, with 10 to 19 percent marrow blasts, 5 to 19 percent blood blasts, or the presence of Auer rods. MDS with fibrosis spans 5 to 19 percent marrow blasts and 2 to 19 percent blood blasts. There is also a footnoted category, MDS with low blasts and ring sideroblasts, defined by wild type S F 3 B 1 with at least 15 percent ring sideroblasts.

keypoints: Two WHO groups: defining genetic abnormalities versus morphologically defined
Genetic group: MDS minus 5q, MDS S F 3 B 1, MDS biallelic T P 53
Multi hit T P 53 definition drives the biallelic T P 53 category
Morphologic group: hypoplastic, increased blasts I B 1 or I B 2, and fibrosis
Auer rods or 10 to 19 percent blasts push a case into I B 2
segments.voiceover: Remember the two arms of fifth edition WHO MDS. Genetically defined disease includes isolated 5 q deletion, S F 3 B 1 mutation, and biallelic T P 53 inactivation, the last one allowing blasts up to 20 percent. Morphologically defined disease includes hypoplastic MDS, increased blasts split into I B 1 and I B 2, and MDS with fibrosis. The key exam trigger is Auer rods or blasts reaching 10 to 19 percent, which automatically classifies a case as I B 2.

This slide covers part one of the International Consensus Classification, or ICC, approach to MDS, and it is also a favorite exam topic. The ICC groups T P 53 mutated myeloid neoplasms along a blast count spectrum. MDS with mutated T P 53 requires any degree of cytopenia and 0 to 9 percent blasts in marrow or blood, with either a multi hit T P 53 mutation, or a single T P 53 mutation with variant allele frequency above 10 percent occurring alongside a complex karyotype that often shows loss of 17 p. MDS slash AML with mutated T P 53 uses the same any cytopenia requirement but blasts rise to 10 to 19 percent, and here any somatic T P 53 mutation with variant allele frequency above 10 percent qualifies, without needing the multi hit criterion or complex karyotype. AML with mutated T P 53 does not require cytopenia at all, requires blasts of 20 percent or more, and again just needs any somatic T P 53 mutation above 10 percent variant allele frequency. The slide then defines multi hit T P 53 mutations precisely. This means either two distinct T P 53 mutations each with variant allele frequency above 10 percent, or a single T P 53 mutation combined with a 17 p deletion on cytogenetics, a variant allele frequency above 50 percent, or copy neutral loss of heterozygosity at the 17 p T P 53 locus. The superscript note clarifies that complex karyotype with loss of 17 p is used as a proxy when T P 53 locus loss of heterozygosity information is not available.

keypoints: T P 53 mutated disease forms a continuum by blast percentage under ICC
0 to 9 percent blasts needs multi hit T P 53 or high V A F plus complex karyotype
10 to 19 percent blasts, called MDS slash AML, needs only any T P 53 mutation above 10 percent V A F
20 percent or more blasts is AML with mutated T P 53, cytopenia not required
Multi hit definition: two mutations, or one mutation plus 17p deletion, high V A F, or c n L O H
segments.voiceover: The exam pearl here is that as blast percentage rises, the genetic bar for calling T P 53 mutated disease actually gets lower. Below 10 percent blasts you need the strict multi hit definition or a high variant allele frequency plus complex karyotype. Once blasts reach 10 percent, any somatic T P 53 mutation above 10 percent variant allele frequency is sufficient, whether it is called MDS slash AML or frank AML with mutated T P 53.

This is part two of the ICC classification of MDS, laying out the non T P 53 categories using dysplasia, blast percentage, cytogenetics, and mutations. MDS with mutated S F 3 B 1 requires at least one dysplastic lineage, blasts under 5 percent marrow and under 2 percent blood, cytogenetics that exclude isolated 5 q deletion, monosomy 7 or 7 q deletion, abnormality of 3 q 26.2, or complex karyotype, and an S F 3 B 1 mutation with variant allele frequency at least 10 percent, without multi hit T P 53 or R U N X 1 mutation. MDS with del 5 q requires the same low blast range, a 5 q deletion with at most one additional abnormality other than minus 7 or 7 q deletion, and any mutation except multi hit T P 53. MDS not otherwise specified is subdivided by dysplasia count. Zero lineages of dysplasia, combined with minus 7, 7 q deletion, or complex karyotype, and no multi hit T P 53 or high S F 3 B 1, gives MDS N O S without dysplasia. One lineage of dysplasia gives MDS N O S with single lineage dysplasia, and two or more lineages gives MDS N O S with multilineage dysplasia, both excluding multi hit T P 53 and criteria for the del 5 q or S F 3 B 1 categories. MDS with excess blasts, or MDS dash E B, requires 5 to 9 percent marrow blasts or 2 to 9 percent blood blasts, any cytogenetics, and any mutation except multi hit T P 53. Finally MDS slash AML spans 10 to 19 percent blasts, any cytogenetics except AML defining ones, and any mutation except N P M 1, basic leucine zipper C E B P A, or T P 53.

keypoints: S F 3 B 1 and del 5 q categories each need at least one dysplastic lineage and low blasts
MDS N O S is subdivided by dysplasia count: zero, one, or two or more lineages
MDS dash E B covers 5 to 9 percent marrow or 2 to 9 percent blood blasts
MDS slash AML covers 10 to 19 percent blasts and excludes AML defining mutations
Multi hit T P 53 is excluded from essentially every non T P 53 ICC category
segments.voiceover: Notice the pattern across this whole ICC table. Multi hit T P 53 is carved out of every other category, because once it is present the case falls into the T P 53 mutated pathway from the previous slide instead. Also remember that MDS N O S is purely dysplasia driven, zero lineages means without dysplasia, one lineage means single lineage, and two or more means multilineage.

This flowchart walks through the ICC classification algorithm for MDS step by step, starting with blast percentage. The first decision point asks whether marrow or blood blasts fall in the 10 to 19 percent range. If yes, you move to the second decision point, which asks whether AML defining genes are present. If AML defining genes are present, the diagnosis is AML. If they are absent, the diagnosis is MDS slash AML. A side note lists three features that also route into this AML or MDS slash AML pathway even outside the strict blast percentage: T P 53 mutation, MDS related gene mutations, and MDS related cytogenetic abnormalities. If blasts are not in the 10 to 19 percent range, meaning they are lower, the algorithm asks whether multi hit T P 53 is present. If yes, the diagnosis is MDS with mutated T P 53. If multi hit T P 53 is absent, the algorithm checks marrow blasts of 5 to 9 percent or blood blasts of 2 to 9 percent. If that is satisfied, the diagnosis is MDS with excess blasts. This slide sets up the logic that continues on the next slide for the remaining, lower blast count categories.

keypoints: First branch point: are blasts 10 to 19 percent
AML defining genes present with 10 to 19 percent blasts equals AML
AML defining genes absent with 10 to 19 percent blasts equals MDS slash AML
Multi hit T P 53 at lower blast counts equals MDS with mutated T P 53
5 to 9 percent marrow or 2 to 9 percent blood blasts equals MDS with excess blasts
segments.voiceover: Walk the algorithm left to right. Blast percentage of 10 to 19 splits into AML versus MDS slash AML depending on AML defining genes. Below that range, multi hit T P 53 status is checked next, and only after that does the algorithm look at the 5 to 9 percent marrow or 2 to 9 percent blood blast threshold for MDS with excess blasts.

This is the continuation of the ICC classification algorithm, picking up where the previous slide left off, after blasts have been confirmed as below the excess blasts threshold, meaning under 5 to 9 percent marrow or under 2 to 9 percent blood. The next check is for a 5 q deletion. If a 5 q deletion is present, the algorithm then asks whether minus 7 or 7 q deletion is also present. If minus 7 or 7 q deletion is absent, the diagnosis is MDS with del 5 q. If a 5 q deletion is not present at all, the algorithm moves to S F 3 B 1 mutation status with variant allele frequency at least 10 percent. If S F 3 B 1 is mutated, it checks for minus 7, 7 q deletion, abnormality of 3 q 26.2, or complex karyotype. If none of those are present, the diagnosis is MDS with mutated S F 3 B 1. If S F 3 B 1 is not mutated, the algorithm checks R U N X 1 mutation status, and if R U N X 1 is also absent, the pathway loops back toward MDS with mutated S F 3 B 1 by exclusion in this diagram's dashed arrows. Several dashed arrows converge on MDS N O S without dysplasia whenever high risk cytogenetics like minus 7, 7 q deletion, abnormality of 3 q 26.2, complex karyotype, or R U N X 1 mutation are present alongside no dysplasia. Finally, the rightmost branch asks about dysplasia directly. If dysplasia is absent, the case again falls into MDS N O S without dysplasia, and if dysplasia is present, the case is further split into MDS N O S with single lineage dysplasia or MDS N O S with multilineage dysplasia depending on how many lineages are affected.

keypoints: 5 q deletion without minus 7 or 7 q deletion equals MDS with del 5 q
S F 3 B 1 mutation without high risk cytogenetics equals MDS with mutated S F 3 B 1
Minus 7, 7 q deletion, 3 q 26.2 abnormality, complex karyotype, or R U N X 1 route toward MDS N O S without dysplasia
Presence of dysplasia splits MDS N O S into single lineage or multilineage subtypes
This algorithm is the direct continuation of the excess blasts branch from the prior slide
segments.voiceover: This slide completes the lower blast count arm of the ICC algorithm. Clean 5 q deletion or clean S F 3 B 1 mutation, without high risk cytogenetic partners, gives you the named molecular subtypes. High risk cytogenetics such as monosomy 7, complex karyotype, or R U N X 1 mutation redirect the case toward MDS N O S without dysplasia, while the presence and extent of dysplasia further separates the remaining N O S cases.

This flowchart shows the fifth edition WHO classification algorithm for MDS, which runs in parallel to the ICC algorithm you just saw but follows a different order of checks. The first branch point asks whether biallelic T P 53 is present. If yes, the diagnosis is MDS dash bi T P 53. If no, the algorithm checks for increased blasts. If blasts are increased, it then asks whether fibrosis is present. Fibrosis present leads to MDS dash f. Fibrosis absent leads to MDS dash I B 2 or MDS dash I B 1, depending on the specific blast range. If blasts are not increased, the algorithm checks for a 5 q deletion. Deletion present leads to a check for minus 7 or 7 q deletion; if that is absent, the diagnosis is MDS dash 5 q. If there is no 5 q deletion, the algorithm checks S F 3 B 1 mutation status. If S F 3 B 1 is mutated and minus 7, 7 q deletion, or complex karyotype is absent, the diagnosis is MDS dash S F 3 B 1. If none of the genetic or blast based categories apply, the final branch asks whether the marrow is hypoplastic. Hypoplastic marrow leads to MDS dash h. Non hypoplastic marrow defaults to MDS dash L B, which stands for low blasts. The dashed arrows show that high risk cytogenetics, minus 7, 7 q deletion, or complex karyotype, redirect cases away from the S F 3 B 1 or del 5 q categories and toward the hypoplastic or low blast pathway instead.

keypoints: Order of checks: biallelic T P 53, then blasts, then del 5 q, then S F 3 B 1, then hypoplastic
Biallelic T P 53 present equals MDS dash bi T P 53, checked first
Increased blasts plus fibrosis equals MDS dash f, otherwise I B 1 or I B 2
Clean del 5 q or clean S F 3 B 1 without high risk cytogenetics get their named category
Default pathway ends at MDS dash h if hypoplastic, or MDS dash L B if not
segments.voiceover: Contrast this with the ICC algorithm. Fifth edition WHO checks biallelic T P 53 status first, before even looking at blast percentage, whereas ICC starts with blast percentage. After that, WHO checks increased blasts, then del 5 q, then S F 3 B 1, and finally falls back to hypoplastic MDS or the low blast catch all category, MDS dash L B.

This table lines up WHO and ICC classification side by side against the same clinical inputs, blast counts, cytogenetics, and mutations, which is a great way to cross check your understanding before boards. For marrow blasts under 5 percent and blood under 2 percent, a 5 q deletion gives MDS dash 5 q under WHO and MDS dash 5 q under ICC, essentially the same label. An S F 3 B 1 mutation gives MDS dash S F 3 B 1 under both systems. Other genetic profiles in this low blast group give MDS dash L B under WHO, which maps to MDS N O S without dysplasia or with single or multilineage dysplasia under ICC. For marrow blasts 5 to 9 percent with blood 2 to 4 percent, WHO calls this MDS dash I B 1, while ICC calls the same range MDS dash E B. For marrow blasts 10 to 19 percent with blood 5 to 19 percent, WHO calls this MDS dash I B 2, and ICC calls it MDS slash AML. Running across the top of both systems, biallelic T P 53 under WHO becomes MDS dash bi T P 53, and under ICC becomes MDS dash T P 53, and cases with fibrosis get MDS dash f under WHO regardless of blast count. The highlighted orange row emphasizes that when AML with recurrent cytogenetic abnormality criteria are met at the 10 to 19 percent blast range, ICC labels the case MDS slash AML or AML with recurrent cytogenetic abnormality, while the T P 53 column separately captures MDS dash T P 53 or AML dash T P 53 depending on blast percentage.

keypoints: Low blast group: MDS dash 5q and MDS dash S F 3 B 1 labels align closely between WHO and ICC
WHO MDS dash L B corresponds to ICC MDS N O S subtypes
5 to 9 percent blasts: WHO I B 1 equals ICC MDS dash E B
10 to 19 percent blasts: WHO I B 2 equals ICC MDS slash AML
Biallelic or mutated T P 53 tracks separately across both systems at any blast count
segments.voiceover: Use this table as your quick conversion chart. The biggest naming differences appear at higher blast counts, where WHO uses I B 1 and I B 2 based purely on percentage, while ICC uses MDS dash E B and MDS slash AML, and also carves out a separate AML with recurrent cytogenetic abnormality pathway that WHO does not use in quite the same way.

This slide reviews treatment options for low risk MDS patients. The diagram on the left shows where each drug acts inside the cell. Luspatercept blocks TGF beta signaling at the cell surface. Lenalidomide acts on cdc25C, PP2A, and the CK1 alpha I K Z 1 complex, and is especially effective in patients with the 5 q deletion. Azacitidine, a hypomethylating agent, inhibits DNMT in the nucleus. Imetelstat inhibits telomerase. Deferasirox chelates iron and reduces reactive oxygen species generated from iron overload. Roxadustat inhibits the HIF prolyl hydroxylase enzyme, stabilizing hypoxia inducible factor to stimulate erythropoiesis. On the right, the clinical approach for low risk MDS is organized into three goals. First, maintaining quality of life through G dash C S F and transfusions. Second, avoiding iron deposition using deferasirox. Third, and importantly, improving anemia, using agents that are largely not covered by Taiwan's national health insurance, including E S A, luspatercept, hypomethylating agents, A T G or cyclosporine A as immunosuppressive therapy, lenalidomide specifically for chromosome 5 q deletion, and imetelstat. Finally, for improving platelet counts, T P O, meaning thrombopoietin receptor agonists, is used.

keypoints: Low risk MDS treatment has three goals: quality of life, avoiding iron overload, improving anemia
G dash C S F and transfusions support quality of life
Deferasirox chelates iron to prevent deposition and reduce reactive oxygen species
Anemia agents include E S A, luspatercept, H M A, A T G slash C s A, lenalidomide, and imetelstat
Lenalidomide is specifically effective for MDS with the 5 q deletion, and T P O agents help platelets
segments.voiceover: Focus on the three treatment goals for low risk MDS: quality of life with growth factor and transfusion, iron chelation with deferasirox, and anemia correction with an expanding drug list including E S A, luspatercept, hypomethylating agents, immunosuppression, and imetelstat. Remember that lenalidomide is the go to choice specifically when a 5 q deletion is present, and note that most of these anemia directed therapies are not reimbursed under national health insurance.

This is the Taiwan treatment algorithm for low to intermediate risk M D S, adapted from N C C N guidelines, and it starts after supportive care, iron folate and B twelve replacement, and C M V safe transfusions. The first branch point is cytogenetics. If there's a deletion of 5 q, lenalidomide is the go to agent. Without deletion 5 q, you look at ring sideroblast percentage. Under fifteen percent, or under five percent with an S F 3 B 1 mutation, you check serum erythropoietin. Low E P O favors an erythropoiesis stimulating agent, while high E P O routes you toward either immunosuppression with A T G and cyclosporine if there's good probability of responding, or hypomethylating agents like azacitidine or decitabine if the probability is poor. On the right side, ring sideroblasts fifteen percent or greater point you toward E S A plus G C S F or luspatercept depending on E P O level. The blue bar at the bottom is important for local practice, it marks each drug's Taiwan indication approval and reimbursement status as yes or no, since not everything on the N C C N pathway is actually reimbursed here.

keypoints: Del 5q positive drives lenalidomide as first line
No del 5q: branch by ring sideroblast percent and SF3B1 status
Serum EPO threshold of 500 guides ESA versus HMA or IST choice
Ring sideroblasts 15 percent or more favors ESA+GCSF or luspatercept
Red boxes show Taiwan-specific approval and reimbursement status
segments.voiceover: Remember this flow as a decision tree, first cytogenetics for del 5 q, then ring sideroblast burden, then serum E P O to pick between E S A, immunosuppression, or hypomethylating agents. And don't forget the Taiwan specific reimbursement flags, since board questions here often test what's actually approved locally, not just what's in the N C C N guideline.

This slide looks ahead at where higher risk M D S treatment is heading. Allogeneic transplant remains the dashed line backbone for anyone eligible. Everything else branches off next generation sequencing, which lets you match mutations to targeted drugs, F L T 3 inhibitors for F L T 3 mutations, enasidenib for I D H 2, ivosidenib for I D H 1, and eprenetapopt for T P 53, though that last one is marked with an X since it failed to show benefit. Other pathways like splicing factors, N or K RAS, and T E T 2 point toward investigational agents such as rigosertib or vitamin C. On the right, the H M A plus backbone is being explored with new biomarker guided combinations, but notice how many partners are crossed out, sabatolimab, venetoclax, magrolimab, and pevonidestat all failed to pan out in trials. What did succeed is oral cedazuridine slash decitabine, known as A S T X 7 2 7, giving an oral H M A option, and I R A K 4 inhibitors remain an open question mark.

keypoints: Allograft remains the definitive option for eligible patients
NGS-directed therapy: FLT3i, enasidenib for IDH2, ivosidenib for IDH1
Eprenetapopt, sabatolimab, venetoclax, magrolimab, pevonidestat all failed trials
Oral cedazuridine/decitabine (ASTX727) is an approved oral HMA
Open questions remain around checkpoint blockade and MRD markers
segments.voiceover: The exam relevant takeaway is knowing which HMA combination trials failed, venetoclax, magrolimab, sabatolimab, and pevonidestat all disappointed in higher risk M D S, while oral cedazuridine decitabine succeeded and is now a real option. Keep NGS driven, mutation targeted therapy in mind as the future direction.

This is flagged as a must test topic, the I P S S Molecular model, or I P S S M, from Papaemmanuil and colleagues in N E J M Evidence. It builds on clinical variables, bone marrow blasts, platelets, hemoglobin, and cytogenetic risk category, then adds molecular data from sixteen genes. The table ranks each gene's adjusted hazard ratio and model weight. The heaviest hitters, with hazard ratios above two, are T P 53 multi hit, M L L P T D, and F L T 3 with I T D or T K D mutations, these carry the most prognostic weight and push patients toward higher risk categories. A second tier of moderately weighted genes includes S F 3 B 1 with the 5 q signature, N P M 1, R U N X 1, N RAS, E T V 6, I D H 2, C B L, E Z H 2, U 2 A F 1, S R S F 2, D N M T 3 A, A S X L 1, and K RAS. Beyond these seventeen named variables, there's a residual term capturing fifteen additional minor genes, so more than ninety percent of patients end up with at least one detectable molecular abnormality feeding into this score.

keypoints: IPSS-M combines clinical, cytogenetic, and 16-gene molecular data
Top weighted adverse genes: TP53 multi-hit, MLL-PTD, FLT3
Second tier genes include SF3B1, NPM1, RUNX1, NRAS, IDH2, ASXL1, and more
A residual term covers 15 additional minor genes
Marked as high yield, expect direct exam questions on this model
segments.voiceover: This slide is explicitly flagged high yield, so memorize the top three genes, T P 53 multi hit, M L L P T D, and F L T 3, as the strongest adverse predictors in I P S S M, and know that the model layers clinical data plus cytogenetics plus a panel of sixteen named genes plus a residual term for minor genes.

S F 3 B 1 mutations are usually considered favorable in M D S, but this slide shows that's not the whole story, outcomes actually split into three distinct categories depending on co-mutation pattern. S F 3 B 1 with the 5 q signature makes up about seven percent of S F 3 B 1 mutant cases. S F 3 B 1 beta, about fifteen percent, occurs alongside B C O R, B C O R L 1, N RAS, R U N X 1, S R S F 2, or S T A G 2, and these co-mutations erase the favorable effect, tracking closely with wild type or even worse outcomes on both leukemia free and overall survival curves. The remaining seventy eight percent, S F 3 B 1 alpha, meaning S F 3 B 1 mutated without those adverse partners, shows the classically favorable, prolonged survival curve well above wild type. The Kaplan Meier curves show hazard ratios around three for S F 3 B 1 beta compared to alpha, both for leukemia free and overall survival, all highly significant.

keypoints: SF3B1 5q variant: about 7 percent of SF3B1-mutant cases
SF3B1 beta, about 15 percent, co-mutated with BCOR, BCORL1, NRAS, RUNX1, SRSF2, or STAG2, loses favorable prognosis
SF3B1 alpha, about 78 percent, retains the classic favorable outcome
Co-mutation pattern, not SF3B1 status alone, determines prognosis
Hazard ratio around 3 for beta versus alpha in both LFS and OS
segments.voiceover: Key exam point, S F 3 B 1 is not uniformly good prognosis, the co-mutation pattern matters. S F 3 B 1 alpha, the majority without adverse partners, keeps the favorable course, but S F 3 B 1 beta with B C O R, R U N X 1, N RAS, S R S F 2 or S T A G 2 behaves like a high risk clone despite the S F 3 B 1 mutation.

This slide presents two practice board questions on M D S management. Question nine asks which statement about low risk M D S management is not correct, and the answer is E, azacitidine has no role in low risk M D S, which is false, hypomethylating agents can still be used in select low risk patients who fail other therapies. The other options are all true, checking E P O and del 5 q status first, giving E S A when E P O is under two hundred, using luspatercept in ring sideroblast M D S, and using A T G for hypoplastic M D S. Question ten moves to high risk M D S and asks which statement is not correct, with the answer being C, the idea that failing azacitidine means decitabine definitely won't work is false, sequential H M A therapy can still have value, and switching between agents in the same class isn't automatically futile. The other statements about transplant first for eligible patients, continuing H M A until progression if transplant ineligible, and oral versus injected H M A not being bioequivalent are all accurate.

keypoints: Q9 answer E: azacitidine does have a role in select low-risk MDS, statement is false
Q9 true statements: EPO and del(5q) first, ESA if EPO under 200, luspatercept for MDS-RS, ATG for hypoplastic MDS
Q10 answer C: HMA failure does not preclude a trial of a second HMA
Q10 true statements: transplant first if eligible, continue HMA if ineligible, oral and IV HMA are not bioequivalent
Both questions test nuanced management decisions across risk strata
segments.voiceover: For question nine, remember azacitidine is not off limits in low risk M D S, that's the false statement. For question ten, remember that failing one hypomethylating agent doesn't rule out trying a second one, sequential H M A therapy remains reasonable, that's why C is the wrong statement here.

This is a starred, high difficulty practice question drawn directly from the N E J M Evidence I P S S M paper. It asks which statement is wrong, and the answer is D. Option D claims D D X 41 mutations are associated with high blast percentages and unfavorable overall survival in M D S with excess blasts, but that's actually backwards, D D X 41 mutated M D S typically behaves more favorably, with lower blast counts and better outcomes than expected, which is one of the more counterintuitive findings from the I P S S M molecular data. The correct statements include that multivariable analysis identified T P 53 multi hit, F L T 3, and M L L P T D as the top adverse genetic predictors, that S F 3 B 1 mutations are favorable but modulated by co-mutation pattern as we just saw, that I P S S M improved prognostic discrimination over I P S S R across all clinical endpoints, and that more than ninety percent of patients carry at least one molecular abnormality.

keypoints: Answer D is the wrong statement
DDX41 mutations are actually associated with favorable, not adverse, outcomes in MDS
TP53 multi-hit, FLT3, and MLL-PTD are the top adverse genetic predictors
IPSS-M improved prognostic discrimination over IPSS-R across all endpoints
Over 90 percent of MDS patients have at least one molecular abnormality
segments.voiceover: The trap in this question is D D X 41, remember it as an exception to the pattern, unlike most high risk mutations, D D X 41 in M D S tends to predict a more favorable course, not an unfavorable one, so any statement calling it adverse is the wrong answer.

This starred question tests how prognostic biomarkers translate into actual treatment decisions in M D S, using a multiple true false format with four statements. Statement one says del 5 q in lower risk anemic patients predicts response to lenalidomide, which is true, that's the classic biomarker driven therapy pairing. Statement two says numerous consensus guidelines exist for treating iron overload despite lacking high quality prospective trial evidence, also true, iron chelation guidance in M D S is largely consensus based rather than randomized trial proven. Statement three says E S A s can be used in transfusion dependent anemia when serum E P O is lower than expected for the hemoglobin level, true as well, that's the standard predictor of E S A responsiveness. Statement four says A S X L 1 and R U N X 1 mutations predict response to hypomethylating agents, and this one is false, these mutations are more associated with adverse prognosis generally, not specifically with predicting H M A response. So statements one, two, and three are correct, making the answer A.

keypoints: Statement 1 true: del(5q) predicts lenalidomide response in lower-risk MDS with anemia
Statement 2 true: iron overload treatment guidelines are consensus-based, not RCT-proven
Statement 3 true: ESA response predicted by low serum EPO relative to hemoglobin level
Statement 4 false: ASXL1 and RUNX1 do not specifically predict HMA response
Correct answer is A, statements 1 plus 2 plus 3
segments.voiceover: Lock in three biomarker pairings here, del 5 q predicts lenalidomide response, low relative E P O predicts E S A response, and note that A S X L 1 and R U N X 1 are prognostic markers of adverse risk in general, not specific predictors of hypomethylating agent response, that distinction is what makes statement four false.

This is an actual question from the 112, or 2023, board exam, testing the I C C 2022 classification of M D S, again using the multiple true false format. Statement one says lower risk M D S has been simplified into three subtypes, two defined mainly by genetic features, S F 3 B 1 mutation and del 5 q, with the remainder classified as M D S not otherwise specified, this is true and reflects the I C C's genetically driven simplification. Statement two defines M D S with excess blasts as five to nineteen percent myeloid blasts in the bone marrow, or two to nine percent in peripheral blood, or one percent documented on two separate occasions, but this blurs together separate I C C thresholds, the actual I C C twenty twenty two peripheral blood range for the lower excess blasts category is two to four percent, not two to nine percent, so this statement is false as written. Statement three claims the prior entity of M D S with ring sideroblasts has been replaced by M D S with S R S F 2 mutation, this is also false, ring sideroblast M D S is actually now defined by S F 3 B 1 mutation, not S R S F 2, that's the trap. Statement four, about multi hit T P 53 predicting aggressive disease and short survival, is true. Statement five, about diagnosing M D S without proven clonality if dysplasia and cytopenia qualify, is also true. So the wrong statements are two and three, matching answer key B.

keypoints: Question tests ICC 2022 classification criteria for MDS
Statement 3 is the key trap: MDS-RS is now defined by SF3B1 mutation, not SRSF2
Statement 2 misstates the ICC peripheral blood blast threshold, actual range is 2 to 4 percent, not 2 to 9 percent
Multi-hit TP53 in cytopenic myeloid neoplasms predicts aggressive, short-survival disease
Answer key marks B, statements 2 and 3, as the wrong pair
segments.voiceover: The key trap to remember, in I C C 2022, ring sideroblast M D S is redefined around S F 3 B 1 mutation status, not S R S F 2, so any statement pairing ring sideroblasts with S R S F 2 is a distractor. Also watch the exact peripheral blood blast cutoff, it's two to four percent for the lower excess blasts category, not the looser two to nine percent range, since these precise numbers get tested directly.

This question tests the two-thousand twenty-two revised classification systems for myelodysplastic syndrome, the International Consensus Classification and the fifth edition World Health Organization classification. Option A is correct, both systems now recommend a unified ten percent threshold for defining dysplasia across all three lineages, replacing the older lineage-specific cutoffs. Option B correctly describes MDS with SF3B1 mutation, low blast counts with at least fifteen percent ring sideroblasts, in the absence of TP53 mutation. Option D is also correct, a patient with two-lineage dysplasia, SF3B1 mutation, and a co-occurring RUNX1 mutation falls outside the SF3B1-defined category and is classified as MDS, not otherwise specified, with multilineage dysplasia. Option E correctly applies the fifth edition WHO criteria for biallelic TP53 inactivation, here demonstrated by two separate TP53 mutations with variant allele frequencies of fifteen and thirty-two percent. The wrong statement is option C. A single TP53 mutation with a normal diploid karyotype, forty-six XY, does not meet the multi-hit requirement that the ICC demands for the category MDS with mutated TP53, which requires either two TP53 mutations, one mutation with seventeen p deletion, or one mutation with copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity. A solitary mutation without a second hit should instead be classified under a low variant allele frequency TP53 category rather than the full multi-hit designation.

keypoints: Unified ten percent dysplasia threshold across ICC and WHO fifth edition
MDS-SF3B1 requires ring sideroblasts and absence of a TP53 mutation
Co-occurring RUNX1 excludes the SF3B1 category, becomes MDS NOS with multilineage dysplasia
Single TP53 mutation with a normal karyotype fails the multi-hit rule for ICC mutated-TP53 MDS
segments.voiceover: Remember four things. Dysplasia threshold is now ten percent for every lineage in both classifications. MDS-SF3B1 needs ring sideroblasts and no TP53 mutation. A second mutation like RUNX1 alongside SF3B1 pushes the diagnosis into MDS not otherwise specified with multilineage dysplasia. And critically, TP53-mutated MDS under the ICC requires a multi-hit state, two mutations, deletion plus mutation, or copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity, so a single mutation with a normal karyotype does not qualify.

This page presents two treatment-selection vignettes for lower-risk MDS. The first, a seventy-eight-year-old woman with isolated deletion five q syndrome, is a classic indication for lenalidomide, option C, which produces high rates of transfusion independence and cytogenetic response specifically in this subgroup by degrading the CK1-alpha protein through cereblon-mediated ubiquitination. The other agents are inappropriate here: allogeneic transplant is reserved for higher-risk disease, anthracycline plus cytarabine is intensive induction chemotherapy for acute leukemia, azacitidine is typically used for higher-risk MDS, and antithymocyte globulin targets hypoplastic marrow rather than deletion five q disease. The second vignette describes a fifty-eight-year-old man with anemia, ring sideroblasts, trisomy eight, and an SF3B1 K700E mutation, findings consistent with MDS with ring sideroblasts. His serum erythropoietin level of five hundred milliunits per milliliter is already elevated, which predicts a poor response to exogenous erythropoietin, ruling out option B. Ferritin is also elevated, so iron supplementation with ferrous sulfate would be inappropriate and potentially harmful. Azacitidine is not first-line for this lower-risk, transfusion-dependent anemia without excess blasts. Lenalidomide works best in deletion five q disease, not this karyotype. The correct choice is luspatercept, option E, a TGF-beta superfamily ligand trap that promotes late-stage erythroid maturation and is specifically approved for transfusion-dependent lower-risk MDS with ring sideroblasts, especially when SF3B1 is mutated.

keypoints: Isolated del(5q) low-risk MDS: lenalidomide is first-line
Lenalidomide works via cereblon-mediated CK1-alpha degradation
High baseline EPO (over 500) predicts poor ESA response
Ring sideroblasts plus SF3B1 mutation favors luspatercept over ESA
segments.voiceover: Two takeaways. For isolated deletion five q low-risk MDS, lenalidomide is the go-to agent, working through cereblon-mediated degradation of CK1-alpha. For ring sideroblast MDS with an SF3B1 mutation, check the baseline erythropoietin level first, if it's already above five hundred, erythropoietin therapy won't help, and luspatercept becomes the preferred choice over erythropoiesis-stimulating agents or iron supplementation.

This page revisits the ring sideroblast vignette with a which-is-true format, then adds a high-risk MDS case testing revised IPSS scoring and treatment sequencing knowledge. In the first question, the correct answer is C, luspatercept is the most appropriate treatment for this SF3B1-mutated, ring-sideroblast-predominant, transfusion-dependent patient. The distractors are worth remembering: azacitidine is not optimal for this lower-risk case, erythropoietin is not indicated once the baseline serum EPO level exceeds five hundred milliunits per milliliter, since higher endogenous levels predict a blunted response to exogenous erythropoietin, ferrous sulfate will not correct anemia driven by ineffective erythropoiesis and ring sideroblast iron trapping, and luspatercept actually binds TGF-beta superfamily ligands, not tumor necrosis factor alpha, making option E a common trap. The second case describes a forty-eight-year-old man with pancytopenia, tri-lineage dysplasia, thirteen percent blasts, and monosomy seven in twelve of twenty metaphases, placing him in a very-high-risk category by the revised IPSS. The wrong statement is D. While iron chelation is sometimes used in transfusion-dependent lower-risk MDS to reduce organ iron overload, the TELESTO trial of deferasirox showed a delay in cardiac and hepatic event-free survival but did not demonstrate a statistically significant overall survival benefit. The other statements hold: fit patients with very-high-risk disease should be considered for allogeneic transplant up front, hypomethylating agents are continued if transplant is not feasible, and oral and injectable hypomethylating agents such as azacitidine and its oral prodrug are not bioequivalent, requiring separate dosing considerations.

keypoints: Luspatercept preferred over ESA when baseline EPO exceeds 500 mU/mL
Luspatercept binds TGF-beta superfamily ligands, not TNF-alpha
Monosomy 7 with 13% blasts places a patient in the very-high-risk R-IPSS category
TELESTO trial: iron chelation delayed organ events but did not prove an overall survival benefit
segments.voiceover: Key exam traps here. Luspatercept binds TGF-beta superfamily ligands, remember that mechanism precisely, since exam writers like to swap in TNF-alpha as a distractor. Baseline EPO over five hundred rules out erythropoiesis-stimulating agents. And for high-risk MDS with monosomy seven and elevated blasts, transplant comes first if the patient is fit, while the TELESTO study on iron chelation showed event-free but not overall survival benefit.

This is a follow-up version of the ICC and WHO fifth edition MDS classification question, with slightly revised answer choices testing the same core concepts a year later. Option A remains correct, a unified ten percent dysplasia threshold for all lineages. Option B is refined further, MDS-SF3B1 in the WHO classification requires an SF3B1 mutation with low blasts, but explicitly excludes patients who also carry five q deletion, monosomy seven, or a complex karyotype, since these higher-risk cytogenetic features override the SF3B1-defined entity. Option D correctly places a patient with two-lineage dysplasia and an isolated RUNX1 mutation, without SF3B1 involvement, into the ICC category of MDS, not otherwise specified, with multilineage dysplasia. Option E again correctly applies the fifth edition WHO criteria for MDS with biallelic TP53 inactivation, demonstrated by two separate TP53 mutations at fifteen and thirty-two percent variant allele frequency alongside complex cytogenetics. The wrong statement remains option C, for the same reason as the earlier version of this question: a single TP53 mutation in a patient with a normal forty-six XY karyotype does not satisfy the ICC's multi-hit requirement for the category MDS with mutated TP53. Fellows should internalize that isolated TP53 mutations without a second hit, whether from deletion, a second mutation, or copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity, are not sufficient for this high-risk designation.

keypoints: Same core concept repeated across exam years: multi-hit TP53 required for ICC mutated-TP53 MDS
MDS-SF3B1 excludes cases with del(5q), monosomy 7, or complex karyotype
Isolated RUNX1 mutation with two-lineage dysplasia maps to MDS NOS-MLD under ICC
Single TP53 mutation plus normal karyotype is insufficient for multi-hit designation
segments.voiceover: This question repeats almost verbatim across exam years, so it is high-yield. The trap is always the same, a single TP53 mutation with a normal karyotype does not meet the multi-hit criteria the ICC requires. Also remember MDS-SF3B1 specifically excludes deletion five q, monosomy seven, and complex karyotype cases.

This question tests familiarity with the landmark New England Journal of Medicine paper by Bernard and colleagues that introduced the Molecular International Prognostic Scoring System, or IPSS-M, for myelodysplastic syndromes. Option A is correct, multivariable analysis identified TP53 multi-hit status, FLT3 mutations, and MLL partial tandem duplication as the strongest genetic predictors of adverse outcomes. Option B is correct, SF3B1 mutations were generally associated with favorable prognosis, but this benefit was attenuated when SF3B1 co-occurred with other high-risk mutations, illustrating why the model incorporates co-mutation patterns rather than treating each gene in isolation. Option C is correct, the IPSS-M showed improved prognostic discrimination compared with the revised IPSS across all major clinical endpoints, including overall survival, leukemia-free survival, and transformation to acute myeloid leukemia. Option D is correct, mutations in ASXL1, BCOR, EZH2, NRAS, RUNX1, STAG2, and U2AF1 were each independently associated with adverse risk across these same endpoints. The wrong statement is option E. The actual finding from this study was that the vast majority of MDS patients, around ninety-eight percent, carried at least one detectable molecular abnormality, not merely sixty percent as stated here. This distinction matters clinically because it underscores how comprehensive molecular profiling has become central to modern MDS risk stratification, rather than being an occasional adjunct finding.

keypoints: IPSS-M top predictors: TP53 multihit, FLT3, and MLL partial tandem duplication
SF3B1's favorable prognosis is modulated by co-mutation patterns
IPSS-M outperforms IPSS-R across overall survival, leukemia-free survival, and AML transformation
Nearly 98 percent, not 60 percent, of MDS patients carry at least one molecular abnormality
segments.voiceover: Focus on the numbers here. Almost all MDS patients, roughly ninety-eight percent, have at least one molecular abnormality detectable, so the sixty percent figure in this question is the wrong statement to catch. Also remember the top adverse predictors: TP53 multi-hit, FLT3, and MLL partial tandem duplication, and that SF3B1's good prognosis can be modulated away by co-occurring mutations.

This outline slide marks a transition point in the lecture. Having covered acute myeloid leukemia and myelodysplastic syndromes, the presentation now moves into myeloproliferative neoplasms and the overlap category of MDS slash MPN, before finishing with acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Keep this framework in mind as we shift focus toward the Philadelphia-chromosome-positive and negative myeloproliferative disorders next.

This slide details the molecular basis of chronic myeloid leukemia, focusing on the different BCR-ABL fusion isoforms that arise from the Philadelphia chromosome translocation. The reciprocal translocation between chromosome nine and chromosome twenty-two fuses the ABL1 gene from chromosome nine with the BCR gene on chromosome twenty-two, producing the derivative Philadelphia chromosome, twenty-two q minus. Depending on exactly where the breakpoint occurs within the BCR gene, three different breakpoint cluster regions produce three distinct fusion transcripts and corresponding protein isoforms. A breakpoint near the e1 locus, the minor breakpoint cluster region, generates the e1a2 transcript, which is translated into the p190 BCR-ABL protein. This p190 isoform accounts for only about one to two percent of CML cases but is the isoform most commonly seen in Philadelphia-chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia, and when it does occur in CML it tends to be associated with monocytosis and a higher frequency of additional cytogenetic abnormalities. Breakpoints near the e13 or e14 loci, the major breakpoint cluster region, generate the e13a2 or e14a2 transcripts, producing the p210 BCR-ABL protein, which is by far the most common isoform and is the classic driver of typical chronic myeloid leukemia. A rarer breakpoint near the e19 locus, the micro breakpoint cluster region, generates the e19a2 transcript and the p230 BCR-ABL protein, an uncommon CML variant characterized by prominent chronic neutrophilia and a more indolent clinical course. Understanding which isoform is present matters for interpreting quantitative PCR monitoring, since the transcript type determines which primer sets are used to track molecular response during tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy.

keypoints: Philadelphia chromosome: reciprocal translocation nine twenty-two fusing ABL1 with BCR
p210 (e13a2 or e14a2, major breakpoint region): the classic, most common CML isoform
p190 (e1a2, minor breakpoint region): more typical of Philadelphia-positive ALL, rare in CML
p230 (e19a2, micro breakpoint region): uncommon, indolent CML with prominent neutrophilia
segments.voiceover: Three isoforms to know. P210, from the major breakpoint region, is the workhorse transcript in typical CML. P190, from the minor breakpoint region, is more characteristic of Philadelphia-positive ALL, and when seen in CML brings monocytosis and extra cytogenetic changes. P230, from the micro breakpoint region, is a rare, indolent CML variant marked by chronic neutrophilia.

This slide summarizes the twenty twenty-six NCCN guideline framework for early treatment response milestones in chronic myeloid leukemia, alongside the twenty twenty European LeukemiaNet criteria. Response is tracked using BCR-ABL1 international scale transcript levels at three, six, and twelve months, and color-coded into a red, orange, yellow, light green, and green scheme that guides clinical decision-making. A BCR-ABL1 level above ten percent at three months is yellow, signaling possible TKI resistance, but the same level persisting at six or twelve months turns red, indicating TKI-resistant disease. For red and yellow zones, clinicians should evaluate medication adherence and drug interactions, consider BCR-ABL1 kinase domain mutational analysis to detect resistance mutations, and consider bone marrow cytogenetic analysis for additional chromosomal abnormalities. The recommendation for red-zone disease is to switch to an alternate tyrosine kinase inhibitor other than imatinib and evaluate the patient for allogeneic transplant. A level between one and ten percent at three to six months is green, but becomes orange by twelve months if it hasn't dropped below one percent, again prompting consideration of a TKI switch or continuing therapy if complete cytogenetic response has been achieved. Levels between zero point one and one percent are green early on and light green by twelve months, reflecting TKI-sensitive disease where the treatment goal, whether long-term survival with a one percent target or treatment-free remission with a more stringent zero point one percent target, determines whether the current regimen continues or intensifies. A level at or below zero point one percent at any timepoint is green throughout, the ideal deep molecular response. The twenty twenty ELN table on the right mirrors this same logic with slightly different transcript thresholds and explicitly flags any BCR-ABL1 kinase domain mutation or high-risk additional chromosomal abnormality, such as an extra Philadelphia chromosome, isochromosome seventeen q, trisomy nineteen, monosomy seven or seven q minus, eleven q twenty-three rearrangement, or three q thirty-six point two, as automatically red regardless of transcript level.

keypoints: BCR-ABL1 international scale levels at 3, 6, and 12 months are color-coded from green to red to guide TKI management
Greater than 10 percent BCR-ABL1 at 3 months is yellow, but turns red if it persists at 6 to 12 months
Red or yellow zones prompt adherence review, kinase domain mutation testing, and consideration of a TKI switch
Deep response at or below 0.1 percent stays green and represents the treatment-free remission target
segments.voiceover: Remember the color logic. Green means stay the course, yellow and orange are early warning signs prompting adherence checks and mutation testing, and red means switch TKI and consider transplant. A BCR-ABL1 level above ten percent that hasn't improved by six months is the classic red flag, while getting down to zero point one percent or below is the deep molecular response needed for treatment-free remission.

This hexagon diagram summarizes the toxicity spectrum across all approved CML TKIs, which is high yield for boards. In the center are the common adverse effects shared by the whole class: myelosuppression, transaminase elevation, and electrolyte disturbances. Moving outward, imatinib is associated with edema and fluid retention, hypophosphatemia, GI upset, and rarely renal effects. Dasatinib's signature toxicities are pleural and pericardial effusion, pulmonary arterial hypertension, and bleeding risk. Bosutinib tends to cause diarrhea, nausea, and transaminitis. Nilotinib and ponatinib share the highest cardiovascular risk, boxed in red here: vascular adverse events, QT prolongation, hyperglycemia, and elevated lipase, plus pancreatic enzyme elevation and hyperbilirubinemia with nilotinib, and hypertension and pancreatitis with ponatinib. Asciminib, the newest agent, mainly causes thrombocytopenia and hypertension. For boards, remember dasatinib equals pleural effusion, nilotinib and ponatinib equal vascular risk, and imatinib equals edema.

keypoints: Common class AEs: myelosuppression, transaminitis, electrolyte changes
Dasatinib: pleural effusion, pulmonary hypertension, bleeding
Nilotinib and ponatinib carry the highest cardiovascular risk
Imatinib: edema and GI effects; bosutinib: diarrhea
segments.voiceover: Key takeaway: know each TKI's signature toxicity. Dasatinib causes pleural and pericardial effusions plus pulmonary hypertension. Nilotinib and ponatinib carry the greatest cardiovascular risk, including vascular events and QT prolongation. Imatinib is linked to edema and GI symptoms, while bosutinib causes diarrhea and transaminitis. All share myelosuppression and transaminase elevation as common effects.

This table compares the 2020 European LeukemiaNet and 2023 NCCN criteria for stopping TKI therapy in chronic myeloid leukemia, a common boards topic called treatment free remission. Mandatory requirements for both guidelines include being in chronic phase disease, a motivated and well informed patient, access to high quality quantitative PCR on the international scale with rapid turnaround, and structured monitoring, monthly for the first six months, every two months through month twelve, then every three months after. For stopping to be allowed, the patient should be on first line therapy, or second line if the switch was due to intolerance, have a typical e13a2 or e14a2 BCR colon colon ABL1 transcript, and have been on TKI therapy for more than five years, with a deep molecular response, MR4 or better, for more than two years. NCCN is similar but only requires three years of therapy. Stopping is more strongly recommended when TKI duration exceeds five years and deep molecular response, MR4.5, has been sustained for more than two years.

keypoints: Mandatory: chronic phase, motivated patient, quantitative PCR, structured monitoring
Stop allowed: first line therapy, typical transcript, over five years of TKI
Stop recommended: over five years TKI with MR4.5 for over two years
NCCN allows earlier stopping consideration, at three years of TKI therapy
segments.voiceover: Remember the framework: mandatory criteria ensure safe monitoring, stop allowed criteria set the minimum bar of five years TKI therapy and two years deep molecular response, and stop recommended criteria require an even deeper and more durable response. NCCN is slightly more permissive, allowing consideration at three years of therapy instead of five.

This slide presents the Taiwan CML guideline for TKI discontinuation, which closely mirrors the international ELN and NCCN frameworks you just saw. Mandatory requirements are the same core elements: chronic phase disease only, a motivated patient with structured communication about relapse risk, access to high quality quantitative PCR testing, and the patient's agreement to more frequent monitoring after stopping. The minimal requirement, meaning stopping is allowed, requires first line therapy, or second line if intolerance was the only reason for switching, a typical e13a2 or e14a2 BCR ABL1 transcript, TKI duration greater than five years, or greater than four years for second generation TKIs, deep molecular response duration greater than two years, and critically, no prior treatment failure. The optimal requirement, where stopping is more strongly recommended, raises the bar to TKI duration over five years combined with an even deeper or more sustained molecular response, MR4 for over three years or MR4.5 for over two years. This Taiwan-specific guideline is useful to know for local practice patterns on boards style questions.

keypoints: Mirrors ELN and NCCN: mandatory, minimal, and optimal requirement tiers
Mandatory: chronic phase, motivated patient, quality PCR, close monitoring
Minimal: over five years TKI, over two years deep molecular response, no prior failure
Optimal: deeper or more durable response strengthens the case to stop
segments.voiceover: The Taiwan guideline essentially adopts the same three tier structure as ELN and NCCN. The non-negotiable mandatory items focus on disease phase and monitoring capability, the minimal requirement sets a five year therapy and two year deep response threshold with no prior treatment failure, and the optimal requirement asks for an even deeper, more durable molecular response before stopping is strongly recommended.

This is the ASC4FIRST trial design, evaluating asciminib versus imatinib or a second generation TKI as first line therapy for chronic myeloid leukemia, a new indication marked here as a new adaptation. Four hundred five newly diagnosed, Philadelphia chromosome positive, chronic phase patients with no prior TKI exposure were enrolled. Before randomization, the treating physician and patient selected which TKI the patient would receive if assigned to the investigator selected arm, either imatinib or a second generation agent. Patients were then stratified by that preselected TKI and by ELTS risk category, low, intermediate, or high, and randomized one to one. Two hundred one patients received asciminib eighty milligrams once daily, split into an imatinib stratum and a second generation TKI stratum, while two hundred four received their investigator selected TKI at label doses. The primary endpoints were major molecular response at week forty eight, both overall, asciminib versus all investigator selected TKIs, and specifically within the imatinib stratum. Key secondary endpoints repeated these comparisons at week ninety six.

keypoints: Four hundred five newly diagnosed CML chronic phase patients, TKI naive
Randomized one to one: asciminib versus investigator selected imatinib or 2G TKI
Stratified by preselected TKI and ELTS risk category
Primary endpoint: MMR at week 48, overall and in the imatinib stratum
segments.voiceover: ASC4FIRST is a first line trial testing whether asciminib beats standard TKIs, including imatinib, in treatment naive CML. The key design feature is the prerandomization TKI selection, which lets the trial compare asciminib against imatinib specifically as well as against all investigator selected TKIs. Major molecular response at week 48 was the primary endpoint, with week 96 as a durability check.

These are the week ninety six MMR results from ASC4FIRST, updating the primary week forty eight readout. Look at the overall comparison first: asciminib versus all investigator selected TKIs. At week forty eight, sixty seven point seven percent of asciminib patients achieved major molecular response versus forty nine percent on investigator selected TKIs, an eighteen point nine percent difference that was statistically significant. By week ninety six, that gap held, seventy four point one versus fifty two percent, a twenty two point four percent difference, meeting the key secondary endpoint. In the imatinib specific stratum, the difference was even larger, sixty nine point three versus forty point two percent at week forty eight, widening slightly to seventy six point two versus forty seven point one percent at week ninety six. Interestingly, in the second generation TKI stratum, the treatment difference actually grew from week forty eight to week ninety six, sixty six versus fifty seven point eight percent, up to seventy two versus fifty six point nine percent. The overall message: asciminib's molecular response advantage is durable and, in some subgroups, increases over time.

keypoints: Asciminib maintained superior MMR versus all investigator selected TKIs at week 96
Advantage versus imatinib specifically was the largest, about thirty percentage points
Treatment difference versus 2G TKIs increased between week 48 and week 96
Both primary and key secondary endpoints were met with durable benefit
segments.voiceover: The key takeaway is durability. Asciminib's molecular response advantage did not fade by week ninety six, it held or even widened across all three comparisons, overall, versus imatinib, and versus second generation TKIs. This strengthens the case for asciminib as a credible first line option, not just an early responder.

This slide summarizes the safety profile from ASC4FIRST at week ninety six, comparing asciminib, imatinib, and second generation TKIs. Grade three or higher adverse events occurred in forty four point five percent of asciminib patients, compared with forty nine point five percent on imatinib and fifty nine point eight percent on second generation TKIs, so asciminib had the lowest rate of severe toxicity. Adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation followed the same pattern, only five percent with asciminib versus thirteen point one percent with imatinib and twelve point seven percent with second generation TKIs. Dose adjustments or interruptions were needed in thirty three percent of asciminib patients versus forty one point four and fifty seven point eight percent respectively. Statistically, the hazard ratio for time to treatment discontinuation due to adverse events, asciminib versus second generation TKIs, was zero point four six, meaning a fifty four percent lower risk of stopping treatment because of toxicity. Combined with the efficacy data from the previous slide, this favorable tolerability profile is asciminib's key selling point as first line therapy.

keypoints: Grade 3 or higher AEs lowest with asciminib at 44.5 percent
AE driven discontinuation only 5 percent with asciminib, versus 13 percent with TKIs
Fifty four percent lower risk of AE related discontinuation versus 2G TKIs
Asciminib pairs better efficacy with meaningfully better tolerability
segments.voiceover: The safety data reinforce the efficacy story. Asciminib consistently caused fewer severe adverse events, fewer discontinuations, and fewer dose interruptions than either imatinib or second generation TKIs. The fifty four percent reduction in AE driven discontinuation risk versus second generation TKIs is the number to remember for boards.

This is the ASCEMBL trial, the first phase three study to test asciminib against a second generation TKI in patients who had already failed at least two prior TKIs, another new indication highlighted here. Two hundred thirty three adults with chronic phase CML, previously treated with two or more TKIs, who had either failed or were intolerant of their most recent agent, were randomized two to one, asciminib forty milligrams twice daily versus bosutinib five hundred milligrams once daily. Patients were stratified by whether they had achieved major cytogenetic response at baseline. Patients with no T315I or V299L mutations were eligible, since those confer resistance. Notably, if a patient on bosutinib met criteria for lack of efficacy, they were allowed to switch to asciminib, though that crossover population is not part of the current efficacy analysis. Median follow up was two point three years. The primary endpoint was major molecular response at twenty four weeks, with a key secondary endpoint of MMR at ninety six weeks, plus additional secondary endpoints covering cytogenetic response, time to and duration of response, and safety.

keypoints: Two hundred thirty three heavily pretreated CML patients, failed or intolerant of two or more TKIs
Randomized two to one: asciminib forty mg twice daily versus bosutinib five hundred mg daily
Excluded T315I and V299L resistance mutations
Primary endpoint MMR at week 24, key secondary MMR at week 96
segments.voiceover: ASCEMBL answers a different clinical question than ASC4FIRST, it is a later line trial, testing asciminib head to head against bosutinib in patients who already failed multiple TKIs. The two to one randomization, stratified by baseline cytogenetic response, and the twenty four week primary MMR endpoint are the design details worth remembering.

This slide shows the ASCEMBL results, and the headline is that asciminib's MMR advantage over bosutinib grew over time rather than fading. At week twenty four, the primary endpoint, twenty five point five percent of asciminib patients achieved major molecular response compared with thirteen point two percent on bosutinib, a twelve point two percent difference that was statistically significant. By week forty eight, asciminib climbed to twenty nine point three percent while bosutinib stayed flat at thirteen point two percent, widening the difference to sixteen point one percent. At week ninety six, the key secondary endpoint, asciminib reached thirty seven point six percent versus just fifteen point eight percent for bosutinib, a twenty one point seven percent difference, again statistically significant. So across three consecutive time points, asciminib's response rate kept climbing while bosutinib's plateaued early, producing a widening treatment gap. This durable and increasing benefit, in a heavily pretreated population who had already failed two or more TKIs, is why ASCEMBL supported asciminib's approval in the later line setting.

keypoints: MMR difference grew over time: 12.2 percent at week 24, 21.7 percent at week 96
Asciminib response rate kept rising, 25.5 to 37.6 percent, week 24 to 96
Bosutinib response rate plateaued, roughly 13 to 16 percent throughout
Both primary week 24 and key secondary week 96 endpoints were statistically significant
segments.voiceover: The core message is a widening, durable advantage. Asciminib's molecular response rate kept increasing from week twenty four through week ninety six, while bosutinib's largely plateaued, so the treatment difference grew from about twelve percent to nearly twenty two percent. This durability in previously treated patients is the key evidence supporting asciminib after TKI failure.

This slide details the most frequent adverse events from ASCEMBL, comparing asciminib to bosutinib. On the left, hematologic and hepatic toxicities. Thrombocytopenia occurred in about thirty percent of asciminib patients versus twenty percent on bosutinib, with grade three or higher thrombocytopenia notably more common with asciminib, twenty two percent versus nine percent. Neutropenia rates were similar between arms. Hypertension was more frequent with asciminib. In contrast, bosutinib caused far more gastrointestinal and hepatic toxicity, diarrhea in seventy two percent of bosutinib patients versus just thirteen percent with asciminib, along with more nausea, vomiting, rash, and ALT elevation. So the toxicity profiles diverge, asciminib favors cytopenias and hypertension, bosutinib favors GI and liver effects. On the right, arterial occlusive events, a known class effect of concern with second and third generation TKIs. Asciminib showed a numerically higher rate of AOEs, five percent versus one percent with bosutinib, including myocardial ischemia, coronary artery disease, and ischemic stroke, translating to an exposure adjusted rate of about three per one hundred patient years versus roughly one and a half for bosutinib. This is an important safety signal fellows should recognize, since arterial thrombosis risk is a class effect that clinicians must monitor across all TKIs, including newer agents like asciminib.

keypoints: Asciminib caused more thrombocytopenia and hypertension than bosutinib
Bosutinib caused far more diarrhea, nausea, rash, and ALT elevation
Arterial occlusive events were higher with asciminib, about five percent versus one percent
Exposure adjusted AOE rate roughly three versus one and a half per hundred patient years
segments.voiceover: Remember the toxicity split, asciminib tends toward cytopenias, hypertension, and a higher arterial occlusive event rate, while bosutinib is dominated by gastrointestinal and hepatic side effects like diarrhea and transaminitis. The arterial occlusive event signal with asciminib is a key safety point to retain, since vascular monitoring matters across TKI classes.

This is a high yield slide, the International Consensus Classification criteria for the classic myeloproliferative neoplasms, polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, prefibrotic myelofibrosis, and overt myelofibrosis. For PV, the major criteria are hemoglobin or hematocrit thresholds, presence of JAK2 V617F or exon 12 mutation, and a bone marrow biopsy showing panmyelosis with trilineage hyperplasia. Diagnosis requires all three major criteria, or the first two plus the minor criterion of a low serum erythropoietin level. For ET, the marrow shows megakaryocyte proliferation with large, mature, hyperlobulated staghorn like nuclei, notably without significant fibrosis or left shift, distinguishing it from prefibrotic myelofibrosis. Diagnosis needs all four major criteria, or the first three plus the minor criterion. Prefibrotic myelofibrosis is the critical distinction fellows must nail on boards, it shows megakaryocytic proliferation with atypia and low grade fibrosis, grade less than two, plus increased cellularity and granulocytic proliferation with often decreased erythropoiesis, features that overlap with ET but differ in marrow morphology and clinical findings like anemia and elevated LDH. Overt myelofibrosis requires higher grade reticulin or collagen fibrosis, grade two or three. Across ET, pre-PMF, and overt PMF, driver mutations in JAK2, CALR, or MPL support diagnosis, and excluding BCR-ABL1 positive CML and other myeloid neoplasms is required in every category.

keypoints: PV needs elevated Hgb or Hct, JAK2 mutation, and marrow panmyelosis, or EPO level as minor criterion
ET marrow shows mature, hyperlobulated staghorn megakaryocytes without significant fibrosis
Pre-PMF has megakaryocyte atypia plus low grade fibrosis, the key distinction from ET
Overt PMF requires reticulin or collagen fibrosis grade two or three
JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutations are shared minor to major criteria across ET, pre-PMF, and PMF
segments.voiceover: The board relevant pearl here is distinguishing ET from prefibrotic myelofibrosis. Both can present with thrombocytosis, but pre-PMF shows megakaryocyte atypia with early bone marrow fibrosis, increased cellularity, and granulocytic proliferation, while true ET has hyperlobulated mature megakaryocytes and a essentially normal, non-fibrotic marrow. This morphologic distinction predicts a very different clinical trajectory.

This slide visually reinforces the distinction between reactive thrombocytosis, essential thrombocythemia, and prefibrotic myelofibrosis using bone marrow histology and lab correlates. Reactive thrombocytosis shows a relatively normal appearing marrow without clonal megakaryocyte changes. Essential thrombocythemia typically presents without anemia, with normal red cell indices including MCV and RDW, no leukoerythroblastosis or dacrocytosis on the peripheral smear, a usually normal LDH, and a JAK2 mutant allele burden generally under twenty percent. Prefibrotic myelofibrosis, in contrast, often shows anemia with abnormal red cell indices, increased RDW and decreased MCV, may show leukoerythroblastosis and dacrocytes, teardrop cells, on the peripheral smear, an elevated LDH, and a JAK2 allele burden that can exceed twenty percent. These clinical and laboratory clues matter because outcomes diverge significantly, ET has an excellent ten year survival of eighty nine percent with low rates of leukemic transformation, zero point seven percent, and progression to myelofibrosis, zero point eight percent. Prefibrotic myelofibrosis has a lower ten year survival of seventy six percent, and substantially higher rates of leukemic transformation at five point eight percent and progression to overt myelofibrosis at twelve point three percent. So recognizing prefibrotic MF matters for prognosis and counseling, not just for pathology reports.

keypoints: ET usually lacks anemia, has normal red cell indices, and no leukoerythroblastosis
Pre-PMF often has anemia, abnormal RDW and MCV, and possible teardrop cells or leukoerythroblastosis
JAK2 allele burden tends to stay under twenty percent in ET, may exceed twenty percent in pre-PMF
Ten year survival is eighty nine percent in ET versus seventy six percent in pre-PMF
Leukemic transformation and myelofibrosis progression are markedly higher in pre-PMF
segments.voiceover: Beyond marrow morphology, simple peripheral clues separate these entities, anemia, abnormal red cell indices, teardrop cells, elevated LDH, and higher JAK2 allele burden all point toward prefibrotic myelofibrosis rather than true ET. This distinction carries real prognostic weight, since pre-PMF has meaningfully worse survival and higher transformation risk.

This algorithm from the Taiwan MPN Working Group outlines management of polycythemia vera. Every patient, regardless of risk category, gets aggressive phlebotomy targeting hematocrit below forty five percent in both men and women, plus low dose aspirin, one hundred milligrams daily, if there's no contraindication. Risk stratification then splits patients into low risk, no history of thrombosis and age sixty or under, versus high risk, history of thrombosis or age over sixty. Low risk patients are managed with phlebotomy and aspirin alone, plus aggressive control of cardiovascular risk factors like hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, and smoking. Cytoreduction can still be considered in low risk patients for specific indications, poor phlebotomy tolerance, symptomatic splenomegaly, severe symptoms, very high blood counts, symptomatic iron deficiency from phlebotomy, or new thrombosis or bleeding. High risk patients get cytoreduction added, first line hydroxyurea starting at five hundred milligrams twice daily, titrated up to two grams a day, with ropeginterferon alpha two b as an alternative to consider. If patients develop hydroxyurea intolerance or resistance, ropeginterferon becomes the next step. Patients with a history of arterial thrombosis should have twice daily aspirin or another antiplatelet agent considered, while those with venous thrombosis history get systemic anticoagulation added. Finally, ruxolitinib is reserved for severe, protracted pruritus or marked splenomegaly not otherwise controlled.

keypoints: All PV patients get phlebotomy to hematocrit under forty five percent plus low dose aspirin
Low risk equals no thrombosis history and age under sixty, high risk is thrombosis history or age over sixty
First line cytoreduction in high risk PV is hydroxyurea, with ropeginterferon as an alternative
Arterial thrombosis history favors twice daily antiplatelet therapy, venous history favors anticoagulation
Ruxolitinib is reserved for refractory pruritus or marked splenomegaly
segments.voiceover: The core PV algorithm to remember is phlebotomy to hematocrit under forty five percent plus aspirin for everyone, with hydroxyurea or ropeginterferon added for high risk patients defined by age over sixty or prior thrombosis. Reserve ruxolitinib for refractory symptoms like pruritus or splenomegaly rather than as routine cytoreduction.

This is the Taiwan MPN Working Group algorithm for essential thrombocythemia, which uses a four tier risk system rather than the simpler two tier system used in PV. Very low risk means no thrombosis history, age sixty or under, and JAK2 V617F un-mutated, these patients need no cardiovascular risk factors to simply be observed, or get aspirin if cardiovascular risk factors are present. Low risk is the same age and thrombosis criteria but with JAK2 mutation present, these patients generally receive aspirin. Intermediate risk means age over sixty without JAK2 mutation, managed with aspirin if symptomatic with cardiovascular risk factors, or observation if asymptomatic without those risk factors, since hydroxyurea is not generally recommended in this asymptomatic subgroup. High risk is defined by a history of arterial or venous thrombosis at any age, or age over sixty combined with JAK2 mutation, these patients need hydroxyurea plus aspirin as the backbone regimen. For high risk patients with arterial thrombosis history, consider twice daily aspirin or another antiplatelet; for venous thrombosis history, add systemic anticoagulation. If hydroxyurea fails due to intolerance or resistance, anagrelide is the next option. Peginterferon alfa two a or two b is noted as another option, though not yet TFDA approved in Taiwan. Note the two footnoted cautions, avoid aspirin in acquired von Willebrand disease or platelet counts at or above fifteen hundred times ten to the ninth per liter.

keypoints: Four risk tiers in ET, very low, low, intermediate, and high, based on age, thrombosis history, and JAK2 status
Very low risk without cardiovascular risk factors can simply be observed without aspirin
High risk, defined by prior thrombosis or age over sixty plus JAK2 mutation, gets hydroxyurea plus aspirin
Anagrelide is the second line option for hydroxyurea intolerance or resistance
Avoid aspirin in acquired von Willebrand disease or platelet count fifteen hundred times ten to the ninth or higher
segments.voiceover: ET risk stratification is more granular than PV, splitting into four tiers using age, thrombosis history, and JAK2 mutation status. The practical takeaway is that JAK2 mutation status shifts management even within the same age and thrombosis category, and very high platelet counts should prompt caution before starting aspirin due to acquired von Willebrand risk.

This slide covers the two IPSET prognostic models used in ET, one for thrombosis risk and one for overall survival, and these are frequently tested. The IPSET for thrombosis assigns one point for age over sixty, one point for cardiovascular risk factors like smoking, diabetes, or hypertension, two points for previous thrombosis, and two points for JAK2 V617F mutation. Scores of zero to one are low risk with an annual thrombosis rate around one percent, a score of two is intermediate risk at about two point four percent annually, and scores of three or higher are high risk at three point six percent annually. Notice that previous thrombosis and JAK2 mutation each carry double weight compared to age or cardiovascular risk factors, reflecting their stronger association with recurrent events. The separate IPSET for survival uses three variables, each scored zero to two, age under sixty scores zero while sixty or older scores two, WBC under eleven times ten to the ninth scores zero while at or above eleven scores one, and no history of thrombosis scores zero while a history scores one. Total scores define low risk at zero, intermediate at one to two, and high risk at three to four. Median overall survival is not reached in low risk, twenty four and a half years in intermediate risk, and thirteen point eight years in high risk. Notice these two scores use different variables and different weighting, so don't conflate them, thrombosis risk emphasizes JAK2 status and prior events, survival risk emphasizes age and leukocytosis.

keypoints: IPSET thrombosis score, age over sixty and CV risk factors score one point each, prior thrombosis and JAK2 mutation score two points each
IPSET thrombosis risk categories, low zero to one, intermediate two, high three or more, with rising annual thrombosis rates
IPSET survival uses age, WBC count, and thrombosis history, each scored zero to two, total defines risk category
IPSET survival risk groups, low score zero, intermediate one to two, high three to four, with markedly different median survival
