segments.voiceover: Keep these two IPSET scores distinct on boards, the thrombosis score weighs prior thrombosis and JAK2 mutation most heavily and predicts annual thrombotic event rate, while the survival score weighs age and leukocytosis and predicts median overall survival, ranging from not reached in low risk down to under fourteen years in high risk.

This slide compares three classic myelofibrosis risk stratification tools, IPSS, DIPSS, and DIPSS plus, which build on each other in a testable, layered way. IPSS, the International Prognostic Scoring System, uses five variables at diagnosis, hemoglobin under ten, WBC over twenty five thousand, age over sixty five, constitutional symptoms, and peripheral blood blasts one percent or more, each worth one point. DIPSS, the dynamic version usable at any time point during follow up, uses the same five variables but doubles the weight of hemoglobin under ten to two points, reflecting its outsized prognostic impact. DIPSS plus builds further on DIPSS by adding three more variables, unfavorable karyotype, transfusion dependency, and platelet count under one hundred thousand, each worth one point. Risk groups are defined by total score, and remember the cutoffs shift between systems, for IPSS and DIPSS plus, low is zero, intermediate one is one, intermediate two is two to three, and high is three or more for IPSS, four or more for DIPSS plus. For DIPSS specifically, because hemoglobin is worth two points, the ranges differ, intermediate one is a score of one to two, intermediate two is three to four, and high is five to six. Median survival drops sharply across risk groups, roughly one hundred thirty five months in low risk IPSS down to just twenty seven months in high risk, with DIPSS and DIPSS plus showing similarly steep declines, sixteen months median survival in DIPSS plus high risk.

keypoints: IPSS uses five variables, each worth one point, hemoglobin, WBC, age, constitutional symptoms, and blasts
DIPSS uses the same five variables but doubles hemoglobin under ten to two points
DIPSS plus adds karyotype, transfusion dependency, and platelet count under one hundred thousand as three more one point variables
Risk group cutoffs differ between IPSS, DIPSS, and DIPSS plus scoring scales
High risk median survival ranges roughly sixteen to twenty seven months across the three systems
segments.voiceover: Track the progression across these three scores, IPSS gives the baseline five clinical variables, DIPSS reweights hemoglobin to reflect its stronger prognostic pull and works at any timepoint, and DIPSS plus layers on cytogenetics, transfusion need, and thrombocytopenia for the most refined risk estimate, with high risk median survival dropping to around sixteen months.

This slide moves into the molecularly informed myelofibrosis risk models, MIPSS70, MIPSS70 plus version 2, and GIPSS, plus a separate model for secondary myelofibrosis. MIPSS70 combines clinical variables, anemia, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, blasts, constitutional symptoms, and bone marrow fibrosis, with the molecular finding of absence of a good risk CALR type one mutation, plus high risk mutations in ASXL1 and SRSF2. MIPSS70 plus version two refines this further, dropping leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and marrow fibrosis as standalone variables, but adding high risk karyotype and expanding the mutation panel to include EZH2 and IDH1 or IDH2 mutations alongside ASXL1 and SRSF2. GIPSS, the genetically inspired score, is purely genetic, no clinical variables at all, using only high risk karyotype, absence of good risk CALR type one, and high risk ASXL1 or SRSF2 mutations, plus U2AF1 mutation which appears only in GIPSS and MIPSS70 plus, not in the original MIPSS70. On the right, a completely separate tool, the MYSEC-PM, or myelofibrosis secondary to PV and ET prognostic model, designed specifically for secondary myelofibrosis rather than primary myelofibrosis. It incorporates age at secondary MF diagnosis, hemoglobin under eleven, platelet count under one hundred fifty thousand, circulating blasts three percent or more, CALR unmutated genotype, and constitutional symptoms. Fellows should recognize that secondary myelofibrosis arising from PV or ET needs this dedicated model rather than the primary myelofibrosis scores.

keypoints: MIPSS70 combines clinical variables with CALR, ASXL1, and SRSF2 mutation status
MIPSS70 plus V2.0 adds karyotype and expands mutations to include EZH2, IDH1, IDH2, and U2AF1
GIPSS is purely molecular and cytogenetic, with no clinical variables at all
Absence of good risk CALR type one mutation is a shared high risk feature across all three scores
MYSEC-PM is a separate model specifically for myelofibrosis secondary to PV or ET
segments.voiceover: The molecular progression to remember is MIPSS70 blends clinical and mutation data, MIPSS70 plus version two adds karyotype and more mutations, and GIPSS is entirely genetic with no clinical input. Absence of a good risk CALR type one mutation is the common thread across all three. And remember, secondary myelofibrosis from PV or ET gets its own dedicated tool, the MYSEC-PM, not the primary myelofibrosis scores.

This slide gives you a bird's eye view of the four JAK2 inhibitors approved for myelofibrosis, ruxolitinib, fedratinib, pacritinib, and momelotinib. Ruxolitinib and momelotinib inhibit JAK1 and JAK2, fedratinib also hits FLT3, and pacritinib and momelotinib additionally inhibit ACVR1, the receptor involved in hepcidin regulation, which explains their benefit in anemia. For first line therapy, ruxolitinib was established by COMFORT one and COMFORT two, fedratinib by JAKARTA, pacritinib by PERSIST one, and momelotinib by SIMPLIFY one. In the second line setting after ruxolitinib failure, we have FREEDOM two and JAKARTA two for fedratinib, PAC two oh three for pacritinib, and SIMPLIFY two for momelotinib. The orange box flags a new indication, highlighting that momelotinib's anemia benefit was validated in the MOMENTUM trial, and it can be used regardless of platelet count, which is unique among this drug class. For boards, remember which drug targets which kinase and which trial supports which line of therapy.

keypoints: Four approved JAK inhibitors, ruxolitinib, fedratinib, pacritinib, momelotinib
Momelotinib and pacritinib also inhibit ACVR1, helping anemia
First line pivotal trials, COMFORT one and two, JAKARTA, PERSIST one, SIMPLIFY one
Second line trials, FREEDOM two, JAKARTA two, PAC two oh three, SIMPLIFY two
Momelotinib approved via MOMENTUM trial for anemia, no platelet cutoff
segments.voiceover: Know your four JAK inhibitors by target and by trial. Ruxolitinib and momelotinib block JAK1 and JAK2, fedratinib also blocks FLT3, and pacritinib and momelotinib also block ACVR1. First line trials are COMFORT one, COMFORT two, JAKARTA, PERSIST one, and SIMPLIFY one. Second line options are backed by FREEDOM two, JAKARTA two, PAC two oh three, and SIMPLIFY two, and momelotinib's anemia benefit comes from the MOMENTUM trial.

This slide drills into the efficacy numbers from the pivotal first line phase 3 trials. Spleen volume reduction of 35 percent, called SVR35, and total symptom score reduction of 50 percent, called TSS50, at week 24 are the two key endpoints used across these studies. COMFORT one compared ruxolitinib to best available therapy and showed 41.9 percent SVR35 and 45.9 percent TSS50, in patients with platelets at least 100. COMFORT two used a similar design against best available therapy but only reported SVR35, at 32 percent. JAKARTA tested fedratinib against placebo in a similar platelet population and achieved 37 percent SVR35 and 40 percent TSS50. PERSIST one tested pacritinib against best available therapy with no platelet restriction at all, which is its defining feature, but showed lower response rates, around 19 percent for both endpoints. Finally SIMPLIFY one was a non-inferiority trial comparing momelotinib against ruxolitinib itself, in patients with platelets at least 50, and momelotinib was non-inferior for spleen response but numerically lower for symptom response. The key exam point is that pacritinib is the only drug in this group studied with truly no platelet floor, making it the go to choice for severely thrombocytopenic patients.

keypoints: COMFORT one and two, ruxolitinib vs BAT, platelets over 100, SVR35 32 to 42 percent
JAKARTA, fedratinib vs placebo, SVR35 37 percent, TSS50 40 percent
PERSIST one, pacritinib vs BAT, no platelet limit, response around 19 percent
SIMPLIFY one, momelotinib non-inferior to ruxolitinib, platelets over 50
Pacritinib uniquely has no platelet count restriction in its pivotal trial
segments.voiceover: Remember the platelet thresholds. COMFORT one and two and JAKARTA required platelets over 100 or 50 respectively. SIMPLIFY one required platelets over 50 and showed momelotinib is non-inferior to ruxolitinib for spleen response. PERSIST one stands out because pacritinib had no platelet floor, giving roughly 19 percent SVR35 and TSS50 even in severely thrombocytopenic patients.

This slide covers the second line and salvage setting after ruxolitinib failure or intolerance. JAKARTA two was a phase 2 study of fedratinib in ruxolitinib relapsed, refractory, or intolerant patients, showing 31 percent SVR35 and 27 percent TSS50. FREEDOM two confirmed this in a phase 3 design against best available therapy, with similar numbers around 35.8 and 34.1 percent. SIMPLIFY two tested momelotinib against best available therapy, mostly continued ruxolitinib, in a non-inferiority design for ruxolitinib suboptimal or intolerant patients, with no platelet limitation. Spleen response was actually lower for momelotinib, 7 percent versus 6 percent for BAT, but transfusion independence at week 24 was markedly better, 43 percent for momelotinib versus 21 percent for ruxolitinib, underscoring that momelotinib's niche is anemia control rather than spleen shrinkage. Finally, PAC two oh three was a phase 2 dose finding study of pacritinib in ruxolitinib relapsed or refractory patients, testing 100 once daily, 100 twice daily, and 200 twice daily doses, which ultimately supported the 200 milligram twice daily dose used in later development. For boards, the take home message is that in the second line setting, momelotinib is chosen primarily for anemia and transfusion independence, not for spleen response.

keypoints: JAKARTA two and FREEDOM two, fedratinib after ruxolitinib failure, SVR35 around 31 to 36 percent
SIMPLIFY two, momelotinib vs BAT, non-inferiority for suboptimal ruxolitinib response
Momelotinib's strength is transfusion independence, 43 percent vs 21 percent for ruxolitinib
PAC two oh three, pacritinib dose finding after ruxolitinib failure, supported 200mg BID
segments.voiceover: In the second line, after ruxolitinib fails, fedratinib is supported by JAKARTA two and FREEDOM two, with SVR35 around one third of patients. Momelotinib in SIMPLIFY two was non-inferior for spleen response, but its real strength was transfusion independence, 43 percent versus 21 percent. Pacritinib's second line dosing came from the PAC two oh three dose finding study, landing on 200 milligrams twice daily.

This is a high yield slide, literally flagged as a must know for the exam. It's the Taiwan MPN working group's management algorithm for myelofibrosis, based on the NCCN MPN guideline version 2 2025. Patients are first stratified by DIPSS or DIPSS-plus into low, intermediate, and high risk categories, and driver and non-driver mutation testing plus cytogenetics is used to refine that risk further into low risk, intermediate one, and intermediate two or high risk groups. For low risk patients, if asymptomatic you simply observe; if symptomatic, options include a clinical trial, a JAK inhibitor in select circumstances, hydroxyurea for cytoreduction, or ropeginterferon alfa two b. For intermediate one risk, symptomatic patients receive ruxolitinib, fedratinib, or momelotinib off label, while allogeneic transplant is reserved for those with adverse cytogenetics or high risk mutations. For intermediate two and high risk disease, the central question becomes transplant candidacy. If yes, proceed to allogeneic transplant, using a JAK inhibitor as bridging therapy beforehand. If not a transplant candidate, treatment is guided by platelet count and anemia status, momelotinib is preferred with symptomatic anemia, especially with platelets under 50, while ruxolitinib and fedratinib are used when platelets are preserved above 50. Disease progression or transformation to AML triggers a switch to systemic chemotherapy, hypomethylating agents like azacitidine or decitabine, or venetoclax. This algorithm tests three things at once, your ability to risk stratify with DIPSS, your knowledge of which JAK inhibitor fits which platelet and anemia profile, and knowing when transplant is the right call.

keypoints: Risk stratify with DIPSS or DIPSS-plus, refine with driver and cytogenetic mutations
Low risk asymptomatic, observe; symptomatic, JAKi, hydroxyurea, or ropeginterferon
Intermediate two or high risk, central decision is transplant candidacy
Not a transplant candidate, momelotinib favored if anemic with low platelets
Disease progression to AML, chemo, azacitidine, decitabine, or venetoclax
segments.voiceover: This algorithm is exam gold. Stratify with DIPSS or DIPSS-plus, then refine using mutation and cytogenetic data. Low risk and asymptomatic means observation. For intermediate two or high risk disease, the fork in the road is transplant eligibility. Transplant candidates get allogeneic HSCT with a JAK inhibitor as a bridge, non-candidates get momelotinib if anemic with low platelets, or ruxolitinib and fedratinib if platelets are adequate. Progression to AML shifts management to chemotherapy or hypomethylating agents.

This slide presents another treatment algorithm for higher risk myelofibrosis, published in Blood in October 2024, organized around splenomegaly and constitutional symptoms as the entry point. If the patient has no cytopenias, first line therapy is ruxolitinib, and the dose is tailored to the platelet count, 20 milligrams twice daily if platelets exceed 200, 15 milligrams twice daily for platelets between 100 and 200, and just 5 milligrams twice daily for platelets between 50 and 100. If platelets are under 50, ruxolitinib is skipped altogether in favor of pacritinib. On first line ruxolitinib, if the patient develops worsening splenomegaly or symptoms without cytopenias, the next step is fedratinib; if cytopenias develop instead, the pathway moves to momelotinib or pacritinib, chosen again by anemia and platelet status. Separately, if the presenting problem includes anemia with transfusion dependence right from the start, momelotinib is the first line choice, and if it fails, the second line choice bifurcates by platelet count into ruxolitinib or fedratinib for higher platelets, or pacritinib territory for lower platelets. On the right side of the diagram, if the primary problem is anemia plus thrombocytopenia with platelets 25 or above, momelotinib is again favored, while pacritinib is favored if platelets are below 50. The unifying concept is that drug selection in myelofibrosis is really a three way negotiation between spleen and symptom burden, platelet count, and anemia or transfusion dependence, and this diagram is a nice practical companion to the Taiwan algorithm from the previous slide.

keypoints: Ruxolitinib dosing is platelet tiered, 20mg BID over 200, down to 5mg BID for 50 to 100
Platelets under 50 at baseline, skip ruxolitinib, start pacritinib
Anemia with transfusion dependence, momelotinib preferred first line
Second line after ruxolitinib failure depends on cytopenias vs spleen or symptom progression
Drug choice balances spleen response, platelet count, and anemia
segments.voiceover: Think of drug selection in MF as balancing three variables, spleen and symptom burden, platelet count, and anemia. Ruxolitinib dosing scales down as platelets drop, from 20 milligrams twice daily above 200,000 to 5 milligrams twice daily between 50 and 100,000. Below 50,000 platelets, skip straight to pacritinib. If transfusion dependent anemia dominates the picture, momelotinib is the first choice, both up front and after ruxolitinib failure.

This slide reviews two board style questions on myeloproliferative neoplasms. Question 11 asks which statement about MPN is not correct, and the answer is A, the driver mutations are not the same across PV, ET, and MF, since although JAK2, CALR, and MPL mutations overlap across all three entities, their frequencies differ substantially, and importantly, triple negative disease, meaning none of the three, is essentially only seen in ET and MF, not PV, since a JAK2 mutation is required for essentially all PV cases. Options B through E are all true, ET does have the best survival among the three MPNs, transplant is not used in low risk disease, watchful waiting is reasonable for low risk asymptomatic patients, and ruxolitinib can be considered even in select low risk symptomatic patients. Question 19 asks which statement about genetic changes in myeloid neoplasms is wrong, and the answer is E, CSF3R mutation is actually strongly associated with chronic neutrophilic leukemia, not chronic myelomonocytic leukemia, which is instead characterized by mutations in genes like SRSF2, TET2, and ASXL1. The other options are correct, SETBP1 and ETNK1 mutations do characterize atypical CML, SF3B1 mutation is classic for MDS slash MPN with ring sideroblasts and thrombocytosis, and JAK2 V617F is strongly linked to polycythemia vera.

keypoints: Q11 answer A, driver mutation frequencies differ across PV, ET, and MF, not identical
Triple negative disease occurs in ET and MF but essentially never in PV
Q19 answer E, CSF3R mutation defines CNL, not CMML
SETBP1 and ETNK1 for atypical CML; SF3B1 for MDS/MPN-RS-T; JAK2 V617F for PV
segments.voiceover: Two quick genetics pearls. First, driver mutation frequencies differ across PV, ET, and MF, and triple negative status essentially rules out PV since a JAK2 mutation drives nearly all PV cases. Second, know your genotype phenotype pairs, CSF3R with chronic neutrophilic leukemia, SETBP1 and ETNK1 with atypical CML, SF3B1 with MDS slash MPN with ring sideroblasts and thrombocytosis, and JAK2 V617F with polycythemia vera.

This slide covers two more board questions. Question 21 concerns treatment free remission in CML, asking which requirement is not adequate for TKI discontinuation per the Taiwan CML treatment guideline, and the answer is C, patients who failed first line TKI but achieved deep molecular response on second line therapy are not automatically good candidates for discontinuation, because prior TKI failure predicts a higher relapse risk after stopping. The genuinely required criteria include chronic phase only disease, access to a high quality quantitative PCR laboratory, typical e13a2 or e14a2 BCR-ABL1 transcripts so PCR monitoring is reliable, and a sustained deep molecular response of more than 3 years for MR4 or more than 2 years for MR4.5 before attempting discontinuation. Question 22 presents a 45 year old heavy smoking male with essential thrombocythemia, platelet count 2000, JAK2 V617F positive, and a history of hypertension and prior myocardial infarction, asking which statement is wrong, and the answer is B. It's wrong because with an extreme platelet count above 1500, this patient is at risk for acquired von Willebrand syndrome, and starting aspirin without first checking von Willebrand studies could cause bleeding rather than prevent thrombosis; cytoreduction with hydroxyurea should be the priority given his very high risk IPSET thrombosis score, and aspirin needs to be added cautiously. Options A, C, and D are correct, this patient truly is high risk by IPSET thrombosis, smoking cessation and blood pressure control matter greatly, and hydroxyurea induced skin ulcers are a recognized reason to permanently discontinue the drug.

keypoints: Q21 answer C, second line TKI deep response does not guarantee safe TFR candidacy
TFR requires chronic phase, reliable qPCR, typical transcripts, and sustained deep MR
Q22 answer B, extreme thrombocytosis needs von Willebrand workup before aspirin
Very high platelet counts risk acquired von Willebrand syndrome and bleeding
Hydroxyurea induced skin ulcers mean permanent drug discontinuation
segments.voiceover: For TFR eligibility in CML, remember chronic phase only, a reliable PCR lab, typical BCR-ABL1 transcripts, and durable deep molecular response, over 3 years for MR4 or over 2 years for MR4.5. And for extreme thrombocytosis in ET, always rule out acquired von Willebrand syndrome before starting aspirin, since untreated it can cause bleeding instead of preventing clots. Also remember that hydroxyurea induced skin ulcers mean permanent discontinuation, not dose reduction.

The final slide in this set covers two more questions. Question 23 asks which statement about ruxolitinib use in MPN is wrong, and the answer is D, anemia is not a contraindication to ruxolitinib, it's simply a common side effect that requires monitoring and dose adjustment, not a reason to withhold the drug entirely. The correct facts are that ruxolitinib is indicated for intermediate and high risk primary myelofibrosis and post PV or post ET myelofibrosis, the starting dose is 20 milligrams twice daily for platelets above 200, 5 to 10 milligrams twice daily for platelets between 50 and 100, and physicians must watch for opportunistic infections, since JAK inhibition impairs cell mediated immunity and raises risk for things like herpes zoster, tuberculosis reactivation, and atypical infections. Question 24 is a case of a 40 year old man diagnosed with primary myelofibrosis, initially asymptomatic with hemoglobin 13 and WBC 15 without blasts, who 5 years later at age 45 develops fever, weight loss, hemoglobin drops to 8, and WBC rises to 28 with 5 percent blast cells. The question asks which statement is not adequate, and the answer is B, this patient should not have been treated with ruxolitinib initially, because at diagnosis he was asymptomatic with preserved counts, meaning low risk disease by IPSS, and current guidelines support observation rather than upfront JAK inhibitor therapy for asymptomatic low risk patients, since ruxolitinib has not been shown to prevent disease progression in this setting. The other statements are true, initial IPSS was low risk, and at age 45 with new cytopenias, constitutional symptoms, and circulating blasts, DIPSS becomes high risk, and at that point both allogeneic transplant and ruxolitinib become appropriate considerations.

keypoints: Q23 answer D, anemia is a side effect to monitor, not a contraindication to ruxolitinib
Ruxolitinib requires vigilance for opportunistic infections like zoster and TB
Q24 answer B, asymptomatic low risk PMF should be observed, not treated upfront
Progression to symptomatic disease with blasts and cytopenias converts risk to high
At high risk conversion, both transplant and ruxolitinib become appropriate
segments.voiceover: Ruxolitinib pearls, anemia is a side effect to manage, not a contraindication, and watch for opportunistic infections like shingles or TB reactivation. And for asymptomatic low risk primary myelofibrosis, the right move is observation, not early JAK inhibitor therapy, since ruxolitinib hasn't been proven to delay progression in that group. Once symptoms, cytopenias, and blasts appear, risk reclassifies as high and both transplant and ruxolitinib become appropriate.

This vignette asks which risk classification or treatment statement is wrong for a 55 year old heavy smoker with essential thrombocythemia, a JAK2 V617F allele burden of 23.4 percent, a platelet count of 2000 times 10 to the 9 per liter, and a history of hypertension and myocardial infarction. Walk through the revised IPSET thrombosis score first. Points come from age over 60, prior thrombosis, cardiovascular risk factors, and JAK2 V617F positivity. This patient is only 55, so no age point, but hypertension counts as a cardiovascular risk factor for one point, and JAK2 positivity adds two points, bringing the total to three, which lands him in the high risk category. So option A, saying he should be classified high risk, is actually a true statement, not the wrong one. The wrong answer here is option B. For high risk ET, the correct first line cytoreductive agent is hydroxyurea, not anagrelide. Anagrelide is reserved as a second line option for patients who are refractory to or intolerant of hydroxyurea. The remaining options are all correct, aggressive cardiovascular risk factor control and smoking cessation matter enormously in this thrombosis prone patient, and when hydroxyurea causes a non healing leg ulcer, the drug must be permanently discontinued since rechallenge risks worsening the ulcer.

keypoints: IPSET thrombosis score adds points for age over 60, prior thrombosis, cardiovascular risk factors, and JAK2 V617F
This patient reaches high risk through hypertension plus JAK2 positivity, despite being under 60
Hydroxyurea, not anagrelide, is the correct first line cytoreductive therapy for high risk ET
Anagrelide or interferon alpha are second line choices after hydroxyurea failure or intolerance
Hydroxyurea induced leg ulcers require permanent drug discontinuation, never rechallenge
segments.voiceover: The trap in this question is assuming a 55 year old cannot be high risk, but cardiovascular risk factors plus JAK2 positivity alone reach the threshold. The actual error is prescribing anagrelide as first line therapy when hydroxyurea is the guideline recommended first choice for high risk essential thrombocythemia.

This question tests understanding of primary myelofibrosis pathophysiology by asking which statement is not true. Option A is correct, median age at diagnosis is 65 to 70 years, though rare pediatric and even neonatal cases occur. Option B is correct, case reports of myelofibrosis in lupus patients support an immune mediated mechanism of marrow connective tissue hyperplasia in some cases. Option C is the false statement, and this is the one to focus on for boards. It claims that neoplastic myeloproliferation dominates in the erythroid and megakaryocytic lineages, producing an intensely cellular marrow with only mild granulocytosis and thrombocytosis. That is backwards from the true biology. In primary myelofibrosis, the dominant proliferating lineages are megakaryocytic and granulocytic, while erythropoiesis is typically reduced, contributing to anemia. And critically, as the disease progresses, the marrow becomes progressively fibrotic and hypocellular, not intensely cellular. Option D is correct, massive increases in splenoportal blood flow from extramedullary hematopoiesis, combined with decreased hepatic vascular compliance or hepatic vein thrombosis, can produce severe portal hypertension and ascites. Option E is correct, extramedullary hematopoietic foci on serosal surfaces can cause pleural, pericardial, or abdominal effusions, sometimes massive.

keypoints: Megakaryocytic and granulocytic lineages proliferate in PMF, while erythropoiesis is typically reduced
Progressive PMF marrow becomes fibrotic and hypocellular, not intensely cellular as option C claims
Median age at diagnosis is 65 to 70, but pediatric and neonatal cases are reported
Splenoportal hyperperfusion plus reduced hepatic vascular compliance can cause severe portal hypertension
Extramedullary hematopoiesis on serosal surfaces can cause massive pleural or pericardial effusions
segments.voiceover: Remember the biology backwards from option C, PMF is driven by megakaryocytic and granulocytic proliferation with reduced erythropoiesis, and the marrow trends toward fibrosis and hypocellularity over time rather than staying intensely cellular.

This question asks which statement about polycythemia vera is not true. Option A is correct, patients homozygous for JAK2 V617F tend to have longer disease duration, higher hemoglobin levels, more pruritus, and a higher likelihood of transforming to post PV myelofibrosis, reflecting a gene dosage effect. Option B is the false statement to focus on. It claims the marrow shows increased erythroid precursors with normal granulocytic precursors. In reality, PV marrow shows panmyelosis, a hypercellular marrow with increases in all three myeloid lineages, erythroid, granulocytic, and megakaryocytic, not just the erythroid line with a normal granulocytic compartment. Option C is correct, thrombosis is the most common and clinically important complication of PV, occurring in roughly one third of patients over the disease course. Option D is correct, platelet count is elevated in about half of patients at diagnosis, and in about ten percent it exceeds 1000 times 10 to the 9 per liter. Option E is correct, clonality studies using X chromosome inactivation patterns confirm that red cells, granulocytes, platelets, monocytes, and B lymphocytes all arise from the same neoplastic clone, demonstrating that PV originates at the level of a multipotent hematopoietic stem cell.

keypoints: PV marrow shows panmyelosis, hypercellularity across erythroid, granulocytic, and megakaryocytic lineages together
Homozygous JAK2 V617F predicts longer disease duration, higher hemoglobin, and higher risk of post PV myelofibrosis
Thrombosis is the leading complication of PV, occurring in about one third of patients
Platelet count exceeds 1000 times 10 to the 9 per liter in roughly ten percent of patients at diagnosis
X inactivation clonality studies show red cells, granulocytes, platelets, monocytes, and B cells all share the neoplastic clone
segments.voiceover: The key teaching point is panmyelosis, PV involves all three myeloid lineages in the marrow, not just erythroid expansion with a normal granulocytic compartment, which is what makes option B the false statement.

This question addresses chronic myeloid leukemia management principles, largely extrapolated from adult data since pediatric CML is rare, and asks which combination of statements is correct. Statement one is true, specialty care for chronic tyrosine kinase inhibitor complications is now essential, and CML is no longer fatal within a few years the way it was in the pre TKI era. Statement two is false, it claims the Sokal score remains very powerful for predicting death from CML now that most patients die of other causes while in remission. The Sokal score was developed and validated in the pre TKI, interferon and chemotherapy era, and its prognostic power for CML specific mortality is far weaker in the modern TKI era. Statement three is true, this is the standard definition, a BCR-ABL1 transcript level of 0.1 percent or less on the international scale defines major molecular response, also called MR3. Statement four is a numeric distractor, the widely accepted MR4.5 cutoff is a BCR-ABL1 transcript level of 0.0032 percent or less, not 0.0035 percent as stated, with the caveat of at least 35,000 ABL1 transcripts in the same cDNA volume. Combining the two true statements, one and three, gives answer B.

keypoints: Statement 1 is true, TKI therapy transformed CML into a chronic disease requiring specialty toxicity management
Statement 2 is false, the Sokal score was designed for the pre TKI era and predicts CML death poorly today
Statement 3 is true, major molecular response or MR3 equals BCR-ABL1 transcript level 0.1 percent or less
Statement 4 is a numeric trap, the accepted MR4.5 cutoff is 0.0032 percent, not the 0.0035 percent stated
Correct combination is statements 1 and 3, answer B
segments.voiceover: Watch for numeric distractors in molecular response definitions, MR3 at 0.1 percent is correct, but the MR4.5 threshold quoted here is slightly off from the accepted 0.0032 percent, and remember the Sokal score has lost its prognostic power in the TKI era.

This page has two linked CML questions. The first asks which mRNA transcripts form the functional junction of p210 BCR-ABL1, the fusion protein found in the overwhelming majority of CML patients. The p210 fusion protein arises from either the e13a2 junction, sometimes called b2a2, or the e14a2 junction, sometimes called b3a2, corresponding to statements two and four, giving answer C. The other two options are distractors from different fusion isoforms, e19a2 produces the rarer p230 fusion protein, which is associated with a CML variant featuring prominent neutrophilic maturation, and e1a2 produces p190, the fusion typically seen in Philadelphia chromosome positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia rather than classic CML. The second question addresses treatment free remission, asking which requirement is not adequate for TKI discontinuation under Taiwan's CML guideline. The correct answer is option D. It states that patients who failed first line TKI therapy but later achieved a deep molecular response on second line TKI are also acceptable candidates for discontinuation. That is not adequate, because failing first line therapy reflects a more resistant, biologically aggressive clone, and the guideline restricts discontinuation candidacy to patients who switched TKI only because of intolerance, not resistance or treatment failure.

keypoints: p210 BCR-ABL1 arises from e13a2 or e14a2 junctions, statements 2 and 4, giving answer C
e19a2 produces the rarer p230 fusion, linked to CML with prominent neutrophilic maturation
e1a2 produces p190, typically associated with Philadelphia chromosome positive ALL, not classic CML
TFR eligibility requires that any TKI switch was due to intolerance, not resistance or treatment failure
Patients who failed first line TKI and later reached deep response on second line are not adequate discontinuation candidates
segments.voiceover: Know your BCR-ABL1 junctions, e13a2 and e14a2 give p210, e1a2 gives p190, e19a2 gives p230. For treatment free remission, the critical eligibility rule is that switching TKI must have been for intolerance, never for resistance or treatment failure.

This page repeats similar concepts from a past board exam year. The first question asks which statement about treating Philadelphia negative myeloproliferative neoplasms is wrong, and the answer is option B. It claims aspirin at 80 to 100 milligrams daily can be used safely without any complication even when the platelet count exceeds 1500 times 10 to the 9 per liter. That is wrong, because extreme thrombocytosis above roughly 1000 to 1500 raises the risk of acquired von Willebrand syndrome, and aspirin in that setting can worsen bleeding risk, so ristocetin cofactor activity should be checked before assuming aspirin is safe. The other options are all correct, reducing hematocrit below 0.45 in PV lowers vascular events, ruxolitinib improves symptoms and quality of life particularly with myelofibrotic transformation, pegylated interferon alfa can reduce the JAK2 V617F allele burden, and long term hydroxyurea carries a very low leukemogenic risk, similar to phlebotomy alone. The second question on this page repeats the treatment free remission discontinuation criteria question, and again the requirement describing patients who failed first line TKI but achieved deep response on second line therapy as adequate for discontinuation is the incorrect one, this time labeled option C.

keypoints: Extreme thrombocytosis above 1000 to 1500 times 10 to the 9 per liter raises acquired von Willebrand syndrome risk with aspirin
Hematocrit under 0.45 is the target in PV to reduce vascular events, per landmark trial data
Ruxolitinib helps symptoms and quality of life in PV, especially with myelofibrotic transformation
Long term hydroxyurea carries very low leukemogenic risk, comparable to phlebotomy alone
TKI discontinuation candidacy still requires that any prior TKI switch was for intolerance, not treatment failure
segments.voiceover: Two recurring board pearls here, do not assume aspirin is automatically safe at extreme platelet counts without checking for acquired von Willebrand syndrome, and TFR discontinuation candidates must have switched TKI for intolerance, never because first line therapy failed.

This page has two primary myelofibrosis treatment questions from a past exam. The first asks which treatment statement is true, and the answer is option C, for a transplant ineligible, high risk patient with constitutional symptoms, ruxolitinib is the recommended therapy since JAK inhibition is the mainstay for symptom control when transplant is not an option. The other options are incorrect, asymptomatic intermediate 1 risk patients are generally observed rather than started on erythropoiesis stimulating agents, and allogeneic transplantation is typically reserved for higher risk categories rather than being the default for intermediate 1 risk with symptomatic splenomegaly. The second question compares secondary myelofibrosis, meaning post essential thrombocythemia and post polycythemia vera myelofibrosis, against primary myelofibrosis, and the correct answer combines statements one and four, option D. The risk of transformation to acute myeloid leukemia is relatively lower in secondary myelofibrosis compared with primary myelofibrosis, and the MYSEC-PM model is the risk stratification tool specifically validated for secondary myelofibrosis rather than the standard primary myelofibrosis scoring systems. Overall survival is not simply lower in secondary MF, and transfusion dependence actually tends to be higher in primary myelofibrosis, not secondary MF, making statements two and three false.

keypoints: For transplant ineligible, high risk PMF with constitutional symptoms, ruxolitinib is the recommended therapy
MYSEC-PM is the risk stratification model specifically validated for secondary myelofibrosis
AML transformation risk is relatively lower in secondary MF compared with primary myelofibrosis
Transfusion dependence tends to be higher in primary myelofibrosis than in secondary MF
Post-ET secondary MF generally has a better prognosis than post-PV secondary MF
segments.voiceover: Keep these secondary versus primary myelofibrosis distinctions straight for boards, use MYSEC-PM for secondary MF risk stratification, secondary MF has lower AML transformation risk and less transfusion burden than primary myelofibrosis, and among secondary MF, post-ET carries a better prognosis than post-PV.

This page packs three rapid fire MPN questions from a recent exam. The first asks which statement about MPN clinical care is wrong, and the answer is option B. It claims that CALR type 2 mutations with platelet counts over one million per cubic millimeter carry a higher thrombosis risk than CALR type 1 or MPL mutations. That relationship is actually reversed, CALR type 1 like mutations and MPL mutations tend to carry relatively higher thrombosis risk, while CALR type 2 mutations, despite often presenting with higher platelet counts, are generally associated with lower thrombotic risk. The second question asks about myelofibrosis drug efficacy and side effects, and the correct combination is statements one, two, and three, option A. Fedratinib carries a boxed warning for Wernicke's encephalopathy, so thiamine status should be checked before starting it. Ruxolitinib and fedratinib produce the most pronounced spleen size reduction among available agents. Pacritinib and momelotinib are preferred choices for patients with significant anemia since they are less myelosuppressive to red cells. Statement four is false, patients with significant thrombocytopenia should be steered toward pacritinib, not fedratinib. The third question asks which factor is not part of the revised IPSET thrombosis model for essential thrombocythemia, and the answer is option C, CALR mutation, since the actual risk factors are age over 60, prior thrombosis history, and JAK2 V617F mutation, while CALR mutation is generally linked to lower thrombosis risk.

keypoints: CALR type 1 like and MPL mutations carry relatively higher thrombosis risk than CALR type 2 mutations
Fedratinib requires thiamine screening due to its Wernicke's encephalopathy boxed warning
Ruxolitinib and fedratinib give the most pronounced spleen size reduction among myelofibrosis drugs
Pacritinib suits thrombocytopenic patients, while pacritinib and momelotinib suit patients with significant anemia
Revised IPSET thrombosis risk factors are age over 60, prior thrombosis, and JAK2 V617F, not CALR mutation
segments.voiceover: Three quick pearls, CALR type 2 actually carries lower thrombosis risk despite higher platelet counts, fedratinib needs a thiamine check before starting, pacritinib is the go-to for thrombocytopenic myelofibrosis patients, and CALR mutation is not one of the IPSET thrombosis risk factors for essential thrombocythemia.

This page reviews two exam favorites. First, treatment free remission, or TFR, in CML. The Taiwan guideline requires chronic phase disease, a high quality quantitative PCR lab, typical BCR-ABL1 transcripts like e13a2 or e14a2, and a sustained deep molecular response, more than three years for MR4 or more than two years for MR4.5, before attempting TKI discontinuation. The trap here is option C. Patients who fail first line TKI due to resistance and later achieve a deep response on second line therapy are not considered adequate TFR candidates, because failure implies an unstable, resistant clone even if it looks quiet now. Second, polycythemia vera management. Remember the ELN definitions of hydroxyurea resistance and intolerance. Leg ulcers that develop after starting hydroxyurea are explicitly classified as hydroxyurea intolerance, which is why the statement denying that link is the wrong one.

keypoints: TFR needs chronic phase, deep molecular response duration, and quality PCR
Resistance to first-line TKI disqualifies TFR even after later deep response
Hct target below 0.45 reduces vascular events in PV
Leg ulcers on hydroxyurea count as hydroxyurea intolerance
segments.voiceover: Key takeaways. TFR candidacy requires chronic phase disease, a validated PCR lab, and a documented deep molecular response held for at least two to three years. A history of TKI resistance, not just intolerance, generally excludes a patient from attempting discontinuation. For polycythemia vera, keep hematocrit under zero point four five to cut vascular risk, and remember that leg ulcers occurring on hydroxyurea are a recognized sign of drug intolerance, not a separate unrelated finding.

Two more classification-heavy questions. Question one asks which mutation is not high risk under MIPSS seventy version two for primary myelofibrosis. The high molecular risk category includes ASXL1, SRSF2, EZH2, and IDH1 or IDH2 mutations, each carrying prognostic weight in the calculator. DNMT3A, despite being one of the most common myeloid mutations overall, is not counted among these high-risk drivers, so it's the correct answer. Question two tests the fifth edition WHO and ICC criteria for Philadelphia-negative MPNs, which stayed largely similar to the fourth edition. The wrong statement here is option C, because it borrows features that actually define prefibrotic early myelofibrosis, things like increased age-adjusted marrow cellularity, granulocytic proliferation, and reduced erythropoiesis, and misattributes them to true essential thrombocythemia. True ET marrow should not show those proliferative, hypercellular changes; that distinction between ET and prePMF is exactly what the morphologic criteria are designed to catch.

keypoints: MIPSS70v2 high-risk mutations: ASXL1, SRSF2, EZH2, IDH1/2 (not DNMT3A)
5th WHO/ICC MPN criteria largely mirror the 4th edition
True ET marrow lacks hypercellularity, granulocytic proliferation, or decreased erythropoiesis
Those proliferative features actually define prefibrotic early myelofibrosis
segments.voiceover: Remember the MIPSS seventy version two high molecular risk set, ASXL1, SRSF2, EZH2, and IDH1 or IDH2, while DNMT3A sits outside that high-risk group. And when you see hypercellular marrow with granulocytic proliferation and reduced erythropoiesis attributed to essential thrombocythemia, recognize that as prefibrotic early myelofibrosis instead, since true ET marrow stays comparatively bland.

This question tests the ASC4FIRST trial, which compared asciminib against investigator-selected standard of care TKIs in newly diagnosed chronic phase CML. Overall, asciminib produced significantly higher major molecular response rates at week forty eight compared with the pooled investigator-selected TKI arm, and specifically outperformed imatinib. However, when the comparison was narrowed to second generation TKIs alone, asciminib did not reach statistical significance for that particular subgroup difference, which is why option C, claiming a significantly higher response with asciminib over second generation TKIs, is the wrong statement. On safety, asciminib was consistently better tolerated, with fewer grade three or higher adverse events and fewer treatment discontinuations than both imatinib and second generation TKIs. This distinction between the pooled comparison, the imatinib-specific comparison, and the second-generation-specific comparison is a classic place exam writers hide the trap.

keypoints: ASC4FIRST: asciminib beat pooled investigator-selected TKI and imatinib for MMR at week 48
Asciminib vs 2nd-gen TKI alone did not reach significance for MMR
Asciminib had fewer grade 3+ adverse events and discontinuations overall
Watch which comparator subgroup a trial claim refers to
segments.voiceover: Key point, asciminib in ASC4FIRST showed a significant major molecular response advantage over the pooled TKI group and over imatinib specifically, but not a statistically significant advantage over second generation TKIs alone. Meanwhile its safety profile was favorable across the board, with fewer severe adverse events and discontinuations than either comparator.

This question bundles four statements about CML and asks which combination is correct. Statement one is true, cytogenetics combined with FISH or RT-PCR remains standard for confirming the Philadelphia chromosome or BCR-ABL1 fusion in every new CML diagnosis. Statement two is false, asciminib's approval was for adult patients, not as pediatric first-line therapy, so that claim about children is fabricated for the exam. Statement three is false, ASXL1 mutations are generally associated with a worse, not better, response to TKI therapy and portend higher risk disease. Statement four is true, pediatric CML patients treated with front-line imatinib do tend to achieve molecular responses more slowly than adults, yet their overall survival ends up comparable. Combining the two correct statements, one and four, gives answer D.

keypoints: Cytogenetics plus FISH or RT-PCR confirms CML diagnosis in all cases
ASXL1 mutation predicts worse, not better, TKI response
Pediatric CML on imatinib responds more slowly but has similar survival to adults
Watch for fabricated drug approval claims in exam distractors
segments.voiceover: Remember, standard CML diagnosis always pairs cytogenetics with FISH or RT-PCR. ASXL1 mutations flag a worse, not favorable, response to TKI therapy. And children with CML on front-line imatinib show slower molecular responses than adults but reach comparable long-term survival, which is why statements one and four are the correct pair here.

This table breaks down mutation frequencies across the MDS/MPN overlap syndromes, chronic myelomonocytic leukemia, atypical CML, MDS/MPN with ring sideroblasts and thrombocytosis, and MDS/MPN unclassifiable, organized by functional gene class. A few patterns are worth memorizing. TET2, DNMT3A, and ASXL1, the epigenetic class three genes, dominate CMML, each mutated in a third to over half of cases. Atypical CML stands out for its high rate of SETBP1 and ASXL1 mutations, along with frequent splicing gene involvement, particularly SRSF2. RARS-T, now folded into MDS/MPN with ring sideroblasts and thrombocytosis, is defined by its striking splicing mutation burden, especially ZRSR2 at eighty percent and SF3B1, reflecting its close relationship to ring sideroblast morphology. MDS/MPN unclassifiable shows a more mixed signature with relatively higher RUNX1 involvement. Recognizing which gene class dominates which entity helps you triangulate the diagnosis on a board vignette even before the full clinical picture is spelled out.

keypoints: CMML is driven by TET2, DNMT3A, ASXL1 epigenetic mutations
Atypical CML enriched for SETBP1 and ASXL1
RARS-T defined by high splicing mutation burden, especially ZRSR2 and SF3B1
MDS/MPN-U shows relatively higher RUNX1 involvement
segments.voiceover: For boards, anchor each MDS/MPN overlap entity to its signature mutation class. CMML pairs with TET2, DNMT3A, and ASXL1. Atypical CML pairs with SETBP1 and ASXL1. RARS-T pairs with splicing mutations, ZRSR2 and SF3B1 especially. And MDS/MPN unclassifiable tends to show more RUNX1 involvement than the others.

The fifth edition WHO classification refines CMML diagnosis in several testable ways. First, the absolute monocytosis threshold was lowered, persistent monocytosis of at least five hundred per microliter, together with monocytes making up at least ten percent of the white count, now satisfies the prerequisite criterion, a lower bar than before. Second, flow cytometry showing abnormal partitioning of peripheral blood monocyte subsets is now a recognized supporting criterion, with a characteristic increase in classical monocytes above a ninety four percent cutoff serving as a reproducible, objective marker in CMML. Third, subtyping still splits into myelodysplastic CMML, with a white count under thirteen, and myeloproliferative CMML, at or above thirteen, and the proliferative subtype is notably enriched for activating RAS pathway mutations along with worse clinical outcomes. Finally, note that the CMML-zero category, which existed under the blast and promonocyte based grading in earlier schemes, has been eliminated in this edition, leaving CMML-1 and CMML-2 as the only subgrouping tiers.

keypoints: Absolute monocytosis threshold lowered to 500/uL for CMML prerequisite criteria
Classical monocyte fraction over 94% by flow supports CMML diagnosis
MP-CMML (WBC 13 or higher) enriched for RAS pathway mutations, worse outcomes
CMML-0 category no longer exists; only CMML-1 and CMML-2 remain
segments.voiceover: High yield changes in the fifth edition CMML criteria, the monocytosis cutoff dropped to five hundred per microliter, monocyte subset flow cytometry with a classical monocyte cutoff above ninety four percent is now a supporting criterion, myeloproliferative CMML links to RAS pathway mutations and worse prognosis, and the CMML-zero grade has been retired, leaving just CMML-1 and CMML-2.

This algorithm walks through CMML risk-adapted management, referencing a 2022 Haematologica risk model. Median overall survival ranges dramatically by risk group, from ninety seven months in low risk down to just sixteen months in high risk disease. Low risk patients without autoimmune features are simply observed, though autoimmune manifestations may warrant prednisone, anti-cytokine agents, or DNA methyltransferase inhibitors. For high risk and intermediate-2 risk patients, allogeneic stem cell transplant is the preferred curative approach whenever the patient is eligible. Transplant-ineligible patients are then split by CMML subtype, dysplastic CMML with TET2 mutated, ASXL1 wild type biology is managed with DNA methyltransferase inhibitors, while proliferative CMML, marked by ASXL1 or RAS pathway mutations, is steered toward clinical trials targeting pathways like MEK, PLK1, CD123, or GM-CSF signaling. Intermediate-1 risk and symptomatic intermediate-2 patients get treatment tailored to their dominant problem, erythropoiesis stimulating agents or luspatercept for anemia, hydroxyurea or off-label ruxolitinib for splenomegaly or constitutional symptoms, and for thrombocytopenia, options range from clinical trials in proliferative disease to immune-mediated therapies like rituximab, eltrombopag, or romiplostim.

keypoints: CMML risk stratifies from median OS 97 months (low) to 16 months (high)
High and intermediate-2 risk: allogeneic transplant if eligible
Transplant-ineligible: DNMTi for dysplastic CMML, clinical trials for proliferative CMML
Symptom-directed therapy for intermediate-1 risk: anemia, splenomegaly, thrombocytopenia each have distinct options
segments.voiceover: The core logic, risk stratify first using the survival-based model, send high and intermediate-2 risk patients to transplant if eligible, and if not, split by dysplastic versus proliferative biology for DNMTi versus clinical trials. Lower risk or symptomatic intermediate-1 disease gets managed by dominant symptom, anemia, splenomegaly, or thrombocytopenia, each with its own directed therapy.

This classic association question pairs specific mutations with their myeloid neoplasm entities. CSF3R mutations are strongly linked to chronic neutrophilic leukemia, that pairing is correct. PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1 rearrangements, and PCM1-JAK2 fusions are the defining lesions of myeloid or lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia, also correct, and importantly these entities, apart from PCM1-JAK2 to some extent, are exquisitely imatinib sensitive. KIT D816V is the hallmark mutation of systemic mastocytosis, correct as well, and JAK2 V617F is essentially synonymous with polycythemia vera, found in the vast majority of cases. The wrong pairing is option E. SETBP1 mutations are actually characteristic of atypical CML and CMML, not MDS/MPN with ring sideroblasts and thrombocytosis, which is instead defined by its high rate of SF3B1 mutations often co-occurring with JAK2 V617F. Mixing up SETBP1 with the wrong overlap syndrome is exactly the kind of gene-disease mismatch these questions test.

keypoints: CSF3R mutation strongly associated with chronic neutrophilic leukemia
PDGFRA/B, FGFR1, PCM1-JAK2 define myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia
KIT D816V hallmark of systemic mastocytosis; JAK2 V617F hallmark of PV
SETBP1 belongs to aCML/CMML, not MDS/MPN-RS-T (which is SF3B1 driven)
segments.voiceover: Lock in these gene-disease pairs, CSF3R with chronic neutrophilic leukemia, PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, and PCM1-JAK2 with eosinophilic myeloid neoplasms, KIT D816V with systemic mastocytosis, and JAK2 V617F with polycythemia vera. SETBP1 belongs to atypical CML and CMML, not to MDS/MPN with ring sideroblasts and thrombocytosis, which is really an SF3B1 story.
This outline shows where we are in the talk. After covering AML, MDS, MPN, and MDS-MPN overlap syndromes, we're now moving into the acute lymphoblastic leukemia section, highlighted here in red.

This marked must-know table compares prognostic factors in adult versus pediatric ALL, and the boards love testing these age and immunophenotype cutoffs. In adults, age under 35 is favorable while over 60 is adverse; white count under 30 for B-cell disease is good, but over 100 for T-cell disease is bad. Thymic T-ALL is a favorable immunophenotype, whereas early T-cell precursor ALL is adverse. On genotype, there's no strong favorable marker in adults, but BCR-ABL1, MLL-AF4 rearrangement, and hypodiploidy under 44 chromosomes are all adverse, and MRD under 0.01% after induction is the favorable cutoff. In children, the sweet spot age is one to nine years, with under one or over ten being higher risk. B-lymphoblastic immunophenotype is favorable while early T-cell precursor is again adverse. Hyperdiploidy over 50 chromosomes and ETV6-RUNX1 fusion are the classic favorable pediatric markers, while hypodiploidy under 44, MLL-AF4, and IKZF1 alterations are adverse, and pediatric MRD thresholds flag anything over 1% as adverse.

keypoints: Adult favorable: age <35, thymic T-ALL, MRD <0.01%
Adult adverse: BCR-ABL1, MLL-AF4, hypodiploidy <44
Pediatric favorable: age 1-9, hyperdiploidy >50, ETV6-RUNX1
Pediatric adverse: age <1 or >10, hypodiploidy <44, IKZF1
segments.voiceover: Remember the mirrored pattern: extremes of age are bad in both groups, and early T-cell precursor immunophenotype is adverse whether you're looking at kids or adults. Favorable genetics differ by age group, hyperdiploidy and ETV6-RUNX1 in children, while adults lack a strong favorable marker but share the same adverse hits, BCR-ABL1, MLL-AF4, and hypodiploidy under 44 chromosomes.

This more granular table from a 2024 Blood review breaks adult ALL prognostic factors into three tiers: patient-related, disease-related, and treatment-response dynamics. Patient-related factors are age, treated as a continuous variable but especially adverse over 55 to 60, and poor ECOG performance status. Disease-related factors include a high white count, over 30 for B-cell or over 100 for T-cell disease, unfavorable immunophenotypes like pro-B, CD20 positive, early T-cell precursor, and mature T, and the key cytogenetic elements, Philadelphia chromosome positive disease, KMT2A rearrangement, hypodiploidy, and complex karyotype. Ph-like ALL with mutated CRLF2, TP53, or JAK-STAT pathway genes is also increasingly recognized as high risk. The most clinically important section is treatment-response dynamics, because how the leukemia responds trumps static baseline features. Poor prednisone response during the prephase, incomplete blast clearance by day eight to fifteen or persistent bone marrow blasts at end of induction, needing more than one cycle to reach complete remission, and above all, minimal residual disease positivity from end of induction onward, are the unifying factors that predict outcome and guide transplant decisions.

keypoints: Patient-related: age (continuous variable), ECOG >1
Disease-related: high WBC, Ph+, KMT2A rearranged, Ph-like ALL
Treatment-response: poor prednisone response, slow blast clearance
MRD positivity is the key unifying prognostic factor
segments.voiceover: Baseline features matter, but response to therapy matters more. Track corticosteroid sensitivity in the prephase, how fast blasts clear by day eight to fifteen, how many cycles it takes to reach remission, and above all, MRD status, since persistent MRD after induction or before transplant is the single strongest predictor of relapse.

This NCCN table lays out cytogenetic risk stratification for B-ALL, and you should be able to sort any karyotype into good or poor risk on sight. Good risk includes hyperdiploidy with fifty-one to sixty-five chromosomes, especially when trisomies of chromosomes four, ten, and seventeen are present together, and the translocation twelve;twenty-one producing ETV6-RUNX1. Poor risk is a longer, high-yield list: hypodiploidy under forty-four chromosomes, KMT2A rearrangements including translocation four;eleven, any IGH translocation, the Philadelphia chromosome translocation nine;twenty-two producing BCR-ABL1, which was defined as high risk in the pre-TKI era, and complex karyotype with five or more abnormalities. Ph-like or BCR-ABL1-like ALL is its own poor-risk category, subdivided into JAK-STAT pathway lesions like CRLF2, EPOR, and JAK rearrangements, ABL-class fusions involving ABL1, ABL2, PDGFRA, PDGFRB, or FGFR, and other kinase fusions like NTRK, FLT3, LYN, and PTK2B. Round out the poor-risk list with intrachromosomal amplification of chromosome twenty-one, translocation seventeen;nineteen producing TCF3-HLF, and IKZF1 alterations.

keypoints: Good risk: hyperdiploidy 51-65 (trisomy 4/10/17), ETV6-RUNX1
Poor risk: hypodiploidy <44, KMT2A rearranged, BCR-ABL1
Poor risk: Ph-like ALL (JAK-STAT, ABL-class, other kinase fusions)
Poor risk: complex karyotype, iAMP21, TCF3-HLF, IKZF1 alterations
segments.voiceover: Two good-risk entities to memorize: hyperdiploidy, especially with trisomy four, ten, and seventeen, and ETV6-RUNX1. Everything else on this slide is poor risk, hypodiploidy, KMT2A rearrangements, Philadelphia chromosome, complex karyotype, Ph-like ALL with its JAK-STAT or ABL-class fusions, iAMP21, TCF3-HLF, and IKZF1 alterations.

This slide reproduces the International Consensus Classification, or ICC, entity list for ALL, and while you don't need to memorize every line, you should recognize the pattern. B-ALL with recurrent genetic abnormalities includes the classic translocation entities, BCR-ABL1, KMT2A rearranged, ETV6-RUNX1, and TCF3-PBX1, the ploidy-defined entities, hyperdiploid, low hypodiploid, and near haploid, and less common fusions like IL3-IGH, iAMP21, and rearrangements of MYC, DUX4, MEF2D, ZNF384, NUTM1, and HLF. The BCR-ABL1-like category is split into ABL-class rearranged, JAK-STAT activated, and not-otherwise-specified subtypes. Newer provisional entities added in the ICC include ETV6-RUNX1-like, PAX5-altered, mutated ZEB2 with IGH-CEBPE, ZNF384-rearranged-like, and KMT2A-rearranged-like B-ALL, plus B-ALL with mutated IKZF1 N159Y or mutated PAX5 P80R. On the T-ALL side, the categories are simpler: early T-cell precursor ALL, with or without BCL11B rearrangement, T-ALL not otherwise specified, and a set of provisional entities.

keypoints: Classic B-ALL entities: BCR-ABL1, KMT2A-r, ETV6-RUNX1, TCF3-PBX1
Ploidy entities: hyperdiploid, low hypodiploid, near haploid
Provisional entities: PAX5-altered, ZNF384-r-like, KMT2A-r-like
T-ALL: early T-cell precursor, NOS, provisional entities
segments.voiceover: Group ICC B-ALL entities into buckets: classic fusion-defined subtypes like BCR-ABL1 and KMT2A rearranged, ploidy-defined subtypes like hyperdiploid and hypodiploid, and a growing list of newer fusion and mutation subtypes such as DUX4, MEF2D, and PAX5-altered disease. T-ALL classification stays comparatively simple, centered on early T-cell precursor status.

This table drills into the newer structurally-defined B-ALL subtypes, and the annotated summary on the right is the fastest way to learn it: DUX4 rearrangement, NUTM1 rearrangement, and PAX5 P80R mutation are favorable, while MYC rearrangement, MEF2D rearrangement, HLF rearrangement, and CDX2/UBTF are poor risk. DUX4-rearranged B-ALL is actually excellent prognosis despite looking aggressive, it's more common in adolescents and young adults, shows CD371 and CD2 positivity, and often has associated ERG and IKZF1 deletions. MEF2D-rearranged disease, by contrast, is CD10-negative or dim with CD38 and cytoplasmic mu positivity, and carries a poor prognosis. HLF-rearranged B-ALL is very rare but very poor prognosis, though it may respond to anti-CD19 therapy. ZNF384 or ZNF362 rearranged disease is notable for aberrant myeloid antigen expression and overlaps significantly with B-myeloid mixed phenotype acute leukemia. NUTM1-rearranged ALL is enriched in infants who lack KMT2A rearrangements and, unlike most infant ALL, actually carries a good prognosis.

keypoints: Favorable structural subtypes: DUX4-r, NUTM1-r, PAX5 P80R
Poor structural subtypes: MYC-r, MEF2D-r, HLF-r, CDX2/UBTF
DUX4-r: CD371+/CD2+, excellent prognosis despite aggressive look
NUTM1-r: infant ALL without KMT2A rearrangement, good prognosis
segments.voiceover: Memorize this favorable-versus-poor split: DUX4, NUTM1, and PAX5 P80R are favorable, while MYC, MEF2D, HLF, and CDX2/UBTF are poor. The classic trap is DUX4-rearranged ALL, it can look alarming but actually carries an excellent prognosis, so don't confuse it with the genuinely high-risk MYC or HLF rearranged subtypes.

This chart shows how ALL subtype distribution shifts across the age spectrum, and the key takeaway is that Ph-like ALL becomes progressively more common as patients get older within the AYA range. In standard-risk childhood ALL it makes up only about ten percent of cases, dominated instead by ETV6-RUNX1 and hyperdiploid disease. That proportion climbs through childhood high-risk and adolescent groups, peaks at nearly twenty-eight percent in young adults aged twenty-one to thirty-nine, and stays above twenty percent through the older adult groups. Ph-like ALL is biologically important because it shares a gene expression profile strikingly similar to Philadelphia-chromosome-positive ALL, activating the same JAK-STAT and kinase signaling pathways, but without the actual BCR-ABL1 rearrangement. That means these patients often respond to tyrosine kinase inhibitors or other targeted therapy directed at their specific fusion partner, even though a standard BCR-ABL1 test would come back negative. Recognizing Ph-like ALL clinically is essential because missing it means missing a targetable lesion.

keypoints: Ph-like ALL rises with age: ~10% childhood SR to ~28% young adults
Ph-like shares JAK-STAT signaling with Ph-positive ALL
No BCR-ABL1 rearrangement despite similar gene expression
Often targetable with TKI or JAK inhibitor therapy
segments.voiceover: Ph-like ALL is the great mimic, it behaves like Philadelphia-positive disease genomically but tests negative for BCR-ABL1, and it becomes more prevalent as patients move from childhood into the young adult range, peaking near twenty-eight percent. Always screen for it in AYA patients since it often has a targetable kinase fusion.

This donut chart breaks down what actually drives Ph-like ALL at the molecular level, since it's not one lesion but a whole family of kinase-activating events that converge on similar downstream signaling. The single largest group, roughly half of cases, is CRLF2 deregulation, through IGH-CRLF2 or P2RY8-CRLF2 rearrangements or activating CRLF2 point mutations. ABL-class fusions make up about twelve percent, involving ABL1, ABL2, CSF1R, or PDGFRB, and these are important clinically because they can respond to ABL-directed tyrosine kinase inhibitors like imatinib or dasatinib. JAK2 fusions account for about seven percent, and truncating EPOR rearrangements make up another three to ten percent, both of which activate JAK-STAT signaling and may respond to JAK inhibitors. Beyond that, there's a long tail of rarer kinase abnormalities, FLT3, NTRK3, BLNK, TYK2, and PTK2B, plus additional JAK-STAT pathway mutations and Ras pathway lesions involving NRAS, KRAS, PTPN11, and NF1. The clinical takeaway is that Ph-like ALL is genomically heterogeneous, so comprehensive fusion and mutation testing, not just a single marker, is needed to identify the specific targetable lesion in each patient.

keypoints: CRLF2 deregulation (IGH/P2RY8-CRLF2, mutations) is ~50% of Ph-like ALL
ABL-class fusions (ABL1/2, CSF1R, PDGFRB) ~12%, TKI-responsive
JAK2 fusions ~7%, EPOR rearrangements ~3-10%
Ras pathway (NRAS/KRAS/PTPN11/NF1) mutations ~6%
segments.voiceover: Half of Ph-like ALL is driven by CRLF2 deregulation, so that's the single most important lesion to test for. The rest splits among ABL-class fusions, which are TKI-targetable, JAK2 fusions and EPOR rearrangements feeding JAK-STAT signaling, and a smaller Ras-pathway mutant group. Comprehensive genomic testing is required since no single assay catches them all.

This slide from MD Anderson tracks survival in Philadelphia chromosome positive ALL across five treatment eras spanning nineteen eighty four to twenty twenty three, and it's a beautiful illustration of how targeted therapy transformed a once dismal disease. In the pre tyrosine kinase inhibitor era, five year overall survival was only about nine percent with a median survival of just fourteen months. Adding imatinib to hyper C-VAD chemotherapy pushed five year survival to forty two percent, and switching to dasatinib nudged that further to forty eight percent. But the real leap came with ponatinib plus hyper C-VAD, reaching seventy six percent five year survival, and the most recent era combining blinatumomab with ponatinib is tracking even higher, with three year survival around eighty nine percent, essentially chemotherapy free induction. The panel on the right shows a randomized comparison confirming ponatinib beats dasatinib head to head, with event free survival of sixty nine versus forty six percent and overall survival of eighty three versus fifty six percent. The board takeaway is that in Ph positive ALL, potent third generation TKIs like ponatinib, especially paired with immunotherapy, have essentially closed the survival gap that used to separate this subtype from Philadelphia negative disease.

keypoints: Pre-TKI 5yr OS ~9%, median 14 months
Imatinib + HyperCVAD -> 42% 5yr OS
Dasatinib + HyperCVAD -> 48% 5yr OS
Ponatinib + HyperCVAD -> 76% 5yr OS, beats dasatinib head to head
Blina + ponatinib era -> ~89% 3yr OS, chemo-light
segments.voiceover: Remember the survival ladder in Ph positive ALL: roughly nine percent in the pre TKI era, climbing through imatinib and dasatinib into the forties, then jumping to seventy six percent with ponatinib, and now approaching ninety percent when ponatinib is paired with blinatumomab. Ponatinib beat dasatinib directly in a randomized trial for both event free and overall survival.

This is the PhALLCON trial, a global phase three study that earned ponatinib a new frontline indication, marked here with the red new indication flag. The question was whether frontline ponatinib beats imatinib when each is combined with reduced intensity chemotherapy in adults with newly diagnosed Philadelphia chromosome positive ALL. Two hundred forty five patients were randomized in a two to one fashion, one hundred fifty four to ponatinib at thirty milligrams daily, dropping to fifteen after achieving MRD negative complete remission, and seventy eight to imatinib at six hundred milligrams daily, both layered onto reduced intensity chemotherapy. The primary outcome was MRD negative complete remission at the end of induction, defined as BCR-ABL1 by MR4, meaning point zero one percent or less. The result favored ponatinib decisively, thirty four point four percent achieving MRD negative CR compared to just sixteen point seven percent with imatinib, a statistically significant absolute risk difference of eighteen percentage points with a p value of point zero zero two. For boards, remember this trial name, PhALLCON, established ponatinib as the preferred frontline TKI partner in Ph positive ALL when paired with reduced intensity chemotherapy rather than the older imatinib backbone.

keypoints: PhALLCON: phase 3, ponatinib vs imatinib + reduced-intensity chemo
Newly diagnosed Ph+ ALL, N=245, 2:1 randomization
Primary endpoint: MRD-negative CR at end of induction
Ponatinib 34.4% vs imatinib 16.7% MRD-negative CR
New frontline indication for ponatinib
segments.voiceover: PhALLCON is the trial to know here: ponatinib plus reduced intensity chemotherapy roughly doubled the MRD negative complete remission rate compared to imatinib, thirty four percent versus seventeen percent, and that's what earned ponatinib its new frontline approval in Philadelphia positive ALL.

This slide gives the updated survival data from the same PhALLCON trial, now looking at event free and progression free survival with longer follow up. Ponatinib enrolled one hundred sixty four patients and imatinib eighty one. For event free survival, censored for transplant, ponatinib had fewer events, twenty eight point seven percent versus thirty four point six percent with imatinib, and median event free survival was not even estimable in the ponatinib arm compared to twenty nine months with imatinib, though the hazard ratio of point six five had a confidence interval crossing one, so this difference didn't reach statistical significance. Progression free survival told a clearer story, ponatinib's median was twenty months versus just seven point nine months for imatinib, with a hazard ratio of point five eight and a tighter confidence interval of point four one to point eight three, which is statistically significant. Visually, both Kaplan-Meier curves separate early and the ponatinib line consistently sits above imatinib throughout follow up. The key nuance for boards is that while MRD negative CR and progression free survival clearly favor ponatinib, the event free survival benefit trended favorably but wasn't statistically definitive in this analysis, which is a common testable detail examiners like to probe.

keypoints: Ponatinib n=164 vs imatinib n=81, PhALLCON follow-up data
EFS: median not estimable vs 29 months, HR 0.65 (CI crosses 1)
PFS: median 20 months vs 7.9 months, HR 0.58 (significant)
PFS benefit is statistically robust; EFS trend not yet significant
segments.voiceover: Keep two numbers straight from this trial: progression free survival was clearly better with ponatinib, twenty months versus about eight months, and that result was statistically significant. Event free survival also favored ponatinib but its confidence interval crossed one, so it wasn't formally significant, a nuance worth remembering.

This slide is a high yield summary of every FDA approved indication for blinatumomab, the CD19 by CD3 bispecific T cell engager, and it's worth memorizing this list verbatim for boards. First, adult B-ALL relapse, established by the TOWER trial published in the New England Journal in twenty seventeen. Second, pediatric B-ALL relapse, based on a twenty sixteen Journal of Clinical Oncology study. Third, and this is a big bucket, B-ALL with positive MRD as a bridge to allogeneic stem cell transplant, supported by three separate trials, the phase two BLAST trial in Blood twenty eighteen, the AALL1331 trial for younger patients aged one to thirty one with relapsed B-cell ALL, and the twenty one twenty zero two one five trial for pediatric patients with high risk B-precursor ALL in first relapse, published in JAMA twenty twenty one. Finally, the newest indication, B-ALL with negative MRD used as consolidation therapy, based on a twenty twenty four New England Journal publication. So the four indication categories to remember are relapsed disease in adults, relapsed disease in children, MRD positive bridging to transplant, and now MRD negative consolidation, which represents blinatumomab moving earlier into frontline consolidation therapy.

keypoints: Adult B-ALL relapse: TOWER trial, NEJM 2017
Pediatric B-ALL relapse: JCO 2016
MRD-positive bridging to allo-HSCT: BLAST, AALL1331, trial 20120215
MRD-negative consolidation: NEJM 2024, newest indication
segments.voiceover: Four FDA indications for blinatumomab to memorize: relapsed B-ALL in adults from the TOWER trial, relapsed B-ALL in children, MRD positive disease bridging to transplant across three supporting trials, and the newest one, MRD negative consolidation from the twenty twenty four New England Journal publication.

This is the pivotal TOWER trial, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in twenty seventeen, comparing blinatumomab to standard chemotherapy in relapsed or refractory Philadelphia chromosome negative ALL. Overall survival was significantly longer with blinatumomab, a median of seven point seven months versus four months with chemotherapy, a hazard ratio of point seven one, p equals point zero one, an absolute gain of three point seven months highlighted right on the slide. Event free survival showed an even more dramatic relative benefit, with a hazard ratio of point five five and six month event free survival estimates of thirty one percent for blinatumomab against just twelve percent for chemotherapy. The response table below breaks down hematologic outcomes at twelve weeks, complete remission with full hematologic recovery was achieved in thirty three point six percent of the blinatumomab group versus fifteen point seven percent with chemotherapy, and when you include partial or incomplete recovery, complete remission rates were forty three point nine versus twenty four point six percent, both differences highly significant. This is the trial that put blinatumomab on the map for boards, remember the numbers, roughly double the remission rate and nearly double the median overall survival compared to salvage chemotherapy in relapsed refractory Ph negative ALL.

keypoints: TOWER trial, NEJM 2017, relapsed/refractory Ph- ALL
Median OS 7.7 vs 4.0 months, HR 0.71, gain of 3.7 months
6-month EFS 31% vs 12%, HR 0.55
CR with full hematologic recovery 33.6% vs 15.7%
segments.voiceover: TOWER established blinatumomab over chemotherapy in relapsed refractory Ph negative ALL: median overall survival nearly doubled from four to seven point seven months, and complete remission with full recovery roughly doubled too, thirty four percent versus sixteen percent.

This slide addresses a distinct clinical scenario, patients who are in morphologic complete remission but still have measurable residual disease, meaning MRD of ten to the negative three or greater after at least three blocks of intensive chemotherapy. Eligibility required first or later complete remission plus that persistent or recurrent MRD. The primary endpoint was MRD complete response after just one cycle of blinatumomab at fifteen micrograms per meter squared daily for up to four cycles, and the key secondary endpoint was relapse free survival at eighteen months. Looking at the patient characteristics table, this was a heavily pretreated population of one hundred sixteen patients, sixty five percent were in their first complete remission and thirty four percent in their second, with baseline MRD levels mostly clustered between ten to the negative one and ten to the negative three. The Kaplan-Meier curve at the bottom is the clinically important part, patients treated in first CR had dramatically better relapse free survival than those treated in second or third CR, a median of twenty four point six months versus eleven months, hazard ratio two point zero nine, p equals point zero zero four. The board pearl here is that blinatumomab converts MRD positive to MRD negative status, and treating earlier, in first remission rather than waiting for a second relapse, meaningfully improves relapse free survival.

keypoints: Eligibility: CR with persistent MRD >= 10^-3 after >=3 chemo blocks
Blinatumomab 15 mcg/m2/day, up to 4 cycles, MRD-CR after cycle 1
Primary endpoint MRD-CR; secondary RFS at 18 months
1st CR: median RFS 24.6 months vs 2nd/3rd CR: 11.0 months, HR 2.09
segments.voiceover: For MRD positive B-ALL in remission, blinatumomab converts MRD status and buys real relapse free survival, but timing matters, treating in first complete remission gave a median of nearly twenty five months versus only eleven months when given after a second or third relapse.

This flowchart lays out the design of E1910, the randomized phase three trial that established blinatumomab as consolidation therapy in MRD negative B-ALL, again flagged as a new indication. Patients first receive induction chemotherapy for two cycles, and if they don't achieve complete remission or CRi they're discontinued from the study. Those who respond move to one cycle of intensification chemotherapy, and if their MRD becomes negative, defined as less than point zero one percent, they're randomized. The blinatumomab arm receives two cycles of blinatumomab with a two week rest between cycles, followed by four cycles of consolidation chemotherapy interspersed with two more cycles of blinatumomab, then blood or marrow transplant if a suitable donor exists, and maintenance chemotherapy continuing for two and a half years from the start of intensification. The control arm skips blinatumomab entirely, going straight from randomization to four cycles of standard consolidation chemotherapy, then transplant if eligible, then the same maintenance schedule.
